attributes.name: Frost Free Season
attributes.description:
Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: Social Vulnerability Index (2006-2010) -- U.S. (Michigan)
attributes.description: SoVI® is a valuable tool for policy makers and practitioners. It graphically illustrates the geographic variation in social vulnerability. It shows where there is uneven capacity for preparedness and response and where resources might be used most effectively to reduce the pre-existing vulnerability. SoVI® also is useful as an indicator in determining the differential recovery from disasters.The index synthesizes 27 socioeconomic variables, which the research literature suggests contribute to reduction in a community’s ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from hazards. SoVI® data sources include primarily those from the United States Census Bureau.The data are compiled and processed by the Hazards and Vulnerability Research Institute at the University of South Carolina. The data are standardized and placed into a principal components analysis to reduce the initial set of variables into a smaller set of statistically optimized components. Adjustments are made to the components’ cardinality (positive (+) or negative (-)) to insure that positive component loadings are associated with increased vulnerability, and negative component loadings are associated with decreased vulnerability. Once the cardinalities of the components are determined, the components are added together to determine the numerical social vulnerability score for each county.SoVI® 2006-10 marks a change in the formulation of the SoVI® metric from earlier versions. New directions in the theory and practice of vulnerability science emphasize the constraints of family structure, language barriers, vehicle availability, medical disabilities, and healthcare access in the preparation for and response to disasters, thus necessitating the inclusion of such factors in SoVI®. Extensive testing of earlier conceptualizations of SoVI®, in addition to the introduction of the U.S. Census Bureau’s five-year American Community Survey (ACS) estimates, warrants changes to the SoVI® recipe, resulting in a more robust metric. These changes, pioneered with the ACS-based SoVI® 2005-09 carry over to SoVI® 2006-10, which combines the best data available from both the 2010 U.S. Decennial Census and five-year estimates from the 2006-2010 ACS.

attributes.name: soc.007 Natural Resource Protection and Child Health Indicators
Natural Resource Management Index
attributes.description: As one of the four indicators in the Natural Resource Management Index, NRPI shows the degree to which a country protects at least 17% of terrestrial biome within its borders. It is computed as a standardized proximity-to-target ranging from 0 (worst performance) to 100 (at target or best performance). Biomes are broad ecological regions (e.g., a desert or deciduous forest). CIESIN utilized the 2016 World Database of Protected Areas (WDPA), ISciences coastline data set, and WWF's Terrestrial Ecoregions of the World data set (Olson et al. 2001) to compute the proportion of each biome in a country that is protected. The WDPA includes polygons that provide the actual boundaries of protected areas. The biome data, provided by the WWF data set, are manually matched with ISciences coastline data to ensure that all areas, particularly along the coast or small islands, are assigned a biome type. A composite layer consisting of all three data sets was created and the percentage of each biome that is protected was calculated. The percentage was capped at 17%, so that additional "credit" does not accrue where protection exceeds 17%. The countries' overall scores are a weighted average of the protection score for each biome. The weights are derived by calculating the biome area as a fraction of a country’s overall land area. Greater weights are applied to larger biomes. The indicator covers 237 countries and is updated based on the most recent monthly release of UNEP's World Conservation Monitoring WDPA.   For more information, please see http://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/nrmi-natural-resource-protection-child-health-indicators-2016/docs Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

Uncertainty about the exact location of boundaries of some protected areas, especially those represented by creating circles around points, and the potential spatial mismatch between the protected areas layer and the biome-country layer represent potential sources of error. Additionally, the WDPA database has been a work in progress since 2006; over the years, as relatively accurate boundary data become available, point protected areas are replaced with boundary delineations that often result in a changes in total area under protection.

attributes.description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data cover select regions from East, West, and Central Africa; Central America; and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. attributes.name: Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts
attributes.description: The Coral Reef Watch (CRW) program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAH) produces this daily 5 km product of coral reef bleaching alert areas, allowing direct monitoring of 95% of global coral reefs. This 7-day composite product shows the maximum stress level that an ocean pixel has experienced due to high sea surface temperature (SST) during the most recent 7 consecutive days, and are dated on the last day of the period. These data are used as the core of NOAA's CRW coral bleaching management program.    These coral bleaching alerts are derived from the NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-Only SST Analysis. Long-term satellite data of SST is used to define the "usual" SST for a given grid cell. This is taken to be the maximum monthly mean SST over that grid cell. For example, if September is the month with the hottest average SST, the September mean SST will be taken as that grid cell's "usual" value. A HotSpot is then defined as temperatures that are higher than this average. A Degree Heating Week is defined as a grid cell being week degree C hotter than usual for a period of one week.     The Bleaching Alert Levels are defined as below. This product shows the maximum bleaching alert level that a grid square has reached in the past 7 consecutive days.    Stress Level Definition Effect  No Stress HotSpot <= 0   Bleaching Watch 0 < HotSpot < 1   Bleaching Warning 1 <= HotSpot and 0 < DHW < 4 Possible Bleaching  Bleaching Alert Level 1 1 <= HotSpot and 4 <= DHW < 8 Bleaching Likely  Bleaching Alert Level 2 1 <= HotSpot and 8 <= DHW Mortality Likely    Full technical details on the types of satellites used, data collected, and analyses performed are available at the following sites: http://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/6/11/11579 and https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/methodology/methodology.php#sst. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

info.cautions: These data layers do not contain any information about the history of exposure to damaging sea surface temperatures, only the current and recent past (within 1 week). Therefore, a region could be considered at Alert Level 2 (the highest level of alert) for several weeks and then drop down to No Stress in 2 weeks. It is important to consult the historical record in order to determine cumulative stress that regions have been exposed to.

Satellite-Detected Vegetation Health
attributes.description: MODIS NDVI data are provided by NASA through its Terra and Aqua satellites and made available through the Global Agricultural Monitoring (GLAM) project. Data are released in 8-day periods, with January 1 always being the starting date of the first period of each year. The data are released on a 0.00225 x 0.00225 degree grid, resulting in ~250-meter square sections that cover the entire globe. This data can be, and are operationally, used to classify land cover on the Earth's surface. This classification can be used to monitor crop health and forest cover around the world through programs like USAID's FEWS NET and WRI's Global Forest Watch (GFW).    The Terra and Aqua satellites each carry a MODIS instrument, image the same areas on the Earth approximately 3 hours apart, and return to each point on Earth every 1-2 days. The data shown here are for the Terra satellite only. The Terra MODIS sensors collect data on several spectral bands, one of which corresponds to the reflectance of visible red spectrum of light (Band 1, 620-670 nm, VIS) and one of which corresponds to the reflectance near infrared spectrum of light (Band 2, 841-876 nm, NIR). The NDVI is calculated based on differences in reflectance of these bands of light off the Earth's surface. NDVI = (NIR - VIS) / (NIR + VIS). For additional information, please see https://glam1.gsfc.nasa.gov, https://nsidc.org/data/modis/terra_aqua_differences/, and https://arset.gsfc.nasa.gov/land/webinars/advancedNDVI. info.technical_title: Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Terra 8-Day Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)
info.functions: MODIS NDVI data provide estimates of vegetation health using satellite remote sensing. This data is used by disaster monitoring agencies such as USAID's Famine Early Warning System Network (FEWS NET) to monitor crop health, and by WRI's Global Forest Watch program to monitor deforestation.
info.cautions: The NDVI is chlorophyll sensitive and saturates at high levels of vegetation, making the results less accurate in high biomass regions. The Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) has improved sensitivity in high-biomass regions and reduced effect of atmosphere compared with the NDVI. The NDVI is featured here because of its popularity among practitioners in the remote-sensing field.    MODIS measurements are published on a consistent grid, which does not align perfectly with recorded measurements as these measurements drift over time with changes in the Terra satellite orbit. This introduces a degree of uncertainty in the resampling of data taken from measurements to the published grid.

attributes.description:
These data were used to create Figure 19.5 in the Third National Climate Assessment report.
See: http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/regions/great-plains#graphic-16884

This figure shows the average of projections of the number of consecutive dry days from several climate models. On the global scale, climate model simulations show consistent projections of future annual precipitation conditions under a range of emissions scenarios. Models are in complete agreement in showing decreases in annual precipitation in the subtropics and increases in annual precipitation at higher latitudes.
The contiguous U.S. straddles the transition zone between drier conditions in the subtropics (south) and wetter conditions at higher latitudes (north). Because the precise location of this zone varies somewhat among models, projected changes in annual precipitation in central areas of the U.S. range from small increases to small decreases. A clear direction of annual precipitation change occurs only in Alaska and the far north of the contiguous U.S. where increases are projected, and in the far Southwest where decreases are projected.
Although this means that changes in overall precipitation are uncertain in many U.S. areas, there is more certainty regarding dry spells. The annual maximum number of consecutive dry days is projected to increase in most areas, especially the southern portions of the contiguous United States.

Child Malnutrition
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The child malnutrition datasat shows child malnutrition estimates for 152 countries in 2018. This dataset demonstrates child malnutrition using five indicators: stunting, wasting, severe wasting, underweight, and overweight among children under 5 years old. The indicators are based on height, weight, and age ratios of children compared to World Health Organization (WHO) Growth Standards. The dataset utilizes the information collected from 854 household nutritional surveys and is presented in tabular format on a global scale.

  
  
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), UN World Health Organization (WHO), and World Bank interagency team regularly update this dataset. Malnutrition robs children’s futures and hinders their growth, chance of survival, and development. Ultimately, this severely reduces their ability to contribute to their local communities and the world as a whole. According to UNICEF, nearly half of all deaths in children under five are attributable to undernutrition. Analysis from this dataset reveals that malnutrition rates remain alarmingly high. To improve children’s nutrition requires multi-sectoral programming with long term planning strategies. Regular data collection is essential to monitor trends and progress, and to raise awareness of nutritional problems. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was created using estimates from 854 nationally representative household nutritional surveys that were reviewed against a set of quality control criteria. These surveys are typically carried out every three to five years, so yearly estimates were created using data trends. Survey data was checked for validity and consistency. Additionally, to ensure that survey estimates were comparable over time, survey data was compared to an international standard reference population, the WHO Child Growth Standards. 

  
  
The WHO Child Growth Standards were used to compare five malnutrition indicators to those collected in surveys. Survey data for each indicator was presented using z-scores (how many standard deviations away from the mean) based on the WHO Child Growth Standards. For example, stunting is calculated as the proportion of children with height-for-age below two standard deviation of the reference population based on WHO Child Growth Standards. 

  
  


For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.unicef.org/resources/dataset/malnutrition-data/).   
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for global and regional level malnutrition, as well as indicator-specific national and disaggregated data are also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.   
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Child Malnutrition
info.technical_title: Global Database on Child Growth and Malnutrition 2019 Edition
info.functions: Child malnutrition for 152 countries in 2018
info.cautions:
This dataset is mainly comprised of estimates from nationally representative household surveys. Since data are collected infrequently and measure malnutrition at one point in time, it is challenging to capture the sudden fluctuations in wasting that can occur over the course of a given year. Additionally, some national surveys begin in one calendar year and end in the next. When this occurs, the data from these surveys is assigned to whichever year more of the survey took place in. 

  
  
During the process of standardization, estimates are adjusted where necessary to be nationally representative and to cover the age range 0 to 5 years. As a result of making these adjustments, prevalence might be slightly different from the survey results reported elsewhere.

  
  
The majority of data available on child malnutrition is from low and middle income countries. Footnotes in the source document state which high income countries and which measurements should be interpreted with caution due to low coverage. There is an effort being made to increase data for high income countries for future reports.

attributes.description:
The updated world map of Köppen-Geiger climate classification is produced by the University of Veterinary Medicine, Vienna, Austria, and the Carinthian Institute for Climate Protection. This series of digital world maps for the period 1901-2100 depicts global trends in observed climate and projected climate change scenarios with 0.5 degree spatial resolution. World maps for the observational period 1901-2002 are based on recent data sets from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU) at the University of East Anglia and the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) at the German Weather Service. World maps for the period 2003-2100 are based on ensemble projections of global climate models provided by the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research and can be found on the original site. The main results comprise an estimation of the shifts of climate zones in the 21st century by considering different scenarios formulated by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](ad218d82-058b-4b8e-b790-44fb6d4b531f) as a replacement.**_
  
The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. attributes.name: Active Fires (VIIRS)
attributes.description:
The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGTDL_NRT) produced by NASA are the latest fire monitoring product of the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375-meter pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. This higher resolution enables detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters than the previously available MODIS data. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspots or fire pixels. Fires over the past 24 hours are accessible on this site, and information for older fires is available on the NASA FIRMS website.

attributes.name: Average Temperature
attributes.description:
Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: [Archived] Erosion Risk
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](dc5db1e0-12bb-4d4d-b84f-37fa492060b6) as a replacement.**_
  
This layer shows the risk of erosion around the world, from low to high. Erosion and sedimentation by water involves the process of detachment, transport, and deposition of soil particles, driven by forces from raindrops and water flowing over the land surface. Because soil erosion is difficult to measure at large scales, soil erosion models are crucial estimation tools to extrapolate limited data to other localities and conditions. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), which predicts annual soil loss from rainfall and runoff, is the most common model used at large spatial scales due to its relatively simple structure and empirical basis. The model takes into account rainfall erosivity, topography, soil erodibility, land cover and management, and conservation practices. Because the RUSLE model was developed based on agricultural plot scale and parameterized for environmental conditions in the USA, modifications of the methods and data inputs are necessary to make the equation applicable to the globe. We estimated erosion potential based on the RUSLE model, adjusted to extend its applicability to a global scale. Conservation practices and topography information were not included in this model to calculate global erosion potential, due to data limitation and their relatively minor contribution to the variation in soil erosion at the continental to global scale compared to other factors. The result of the global model was categorized into five quantiles, corresponding to low to high erosion risks.  
  
### Additional Information

The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP dataset includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. attributes.name: prep_0109 U.S. Projected Change in Number of Warm Nights - Lower Emissions (2041-2070)
U.S. Projected Change in Number of Warm Nights - Lower Emissions (2041-2070)
attributes.description:
These data were used to create Figure 19.3 in the Third National Climate Assessment report.
See: http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/regions/great-plains#graphic-16882
 
This figure shows the average of projections of the number of warm nights from several climate models. On the global scale, climate model simulations show consistent projections of future temperature conditions under a range of emissions scenarios. All models show warming by late this century that is much larger than historical variations nearly everywhere globally. For the U.S., models unequivocally project large and historically unprecedented future warming in every region of the U.S. under all of the scenarios used in this assessment. The amount of warming varies substantially between higher versus lower scenarios, and moderately from model to model, but the amount of projected warming is much larger than historical variations. Likewise, the models project unequivocal increases in the number of warm nights that are larger than historical variations.
 
Citation:
Melillo, Jerry M., Terese (T.C.) Richmond, and Gary W. Yohe, Eds., 2014: Climate Change Impacts in the United States: The Third National Climate Assessment. U.S. Global Change Research Program, 841 pp. doi:10.7930/J0Z31WJ2.

attributes.name: Adult Literacy Rate
attributes.description:
The UNESCO Institute for Statistics compiled statistics on global adult literacy based on national censuses and household surveys and, for countries without recent literacy data, using the Global Age-Specific Literacy Projection Model (GALP). Literacy rates are outcome indicators to evaluate educational attainment. These data can predict the quality of a future labor force and can be used in ensuring policies for life skills for men and women. They can be also used as a proxy instrument to see the effectiveness of education system: a high literacy rate suggests the capacity of an education system to provide a large population with opportunities to acquire literacy skills. The accumulated achievement of education is fundamental for further intellectual growth and social and economic development, although it doesn't necessarily ensure the quality of education. Literacy statistics for most countries cover the population age 15 and older, but some include younger ages or are confined to age ranges that tend to inflate literacy rates. Generally, literacy also encompasses numeracy, or the ability to make simple arithmetic calculations. The reference period for aggregates is 1985-1994 for 1990, 1995-2004 for 2000, and 2005-2014 for 2010. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: World Hydro Reference
attributes.description:
This tile layer of the world's hydrological features was created by ESRI and is designed to provide a hydrologically oriented set of features to use with the World Terrain Base Layer or other simple base maps. The map features a hydrocentric design based on the amount of water flowing within the drainage network such that symbols of the same size and color represent roughly the same amount of water. Surface water flow is shown as a linear phenomenon even over and through bodies of water. Using the best available, these data show relative flow accurately, so that if one river carries more water downstream than another river, the result will be that the first river will have a thicker symbol on the map. This map is used as an overlay for content such as elevation from the World Terrain Base service or thematic services such as soil units, vegetation, or ecoregions. Combined with a basemap and map services, this map provides a frame of reference for showing regional, national, and continental hydrologic phenomena such as drought, runoff, river-level monitoring, and flood forecasting. River names are collected in the UTF8 character set so river names are collected in their original language but are written in the Roman alphabet. Sources for all river names are from the open source geonames.org project, so they are international by nature. The map is compiled from several sources. The global scales (very small scales through 1:2,300,000) include content from HydroSHEDS, GTOPO30 Global Topographic Data, SRTM, GLWD, WorldClim, GRDC, and WWF Global 200 Terrestrial Eco Regions, with the latter 3 providing the inputs and basis for calculating flow. At medium scales (1:36,000 to 1:2,000,000) this service currently contains only U.S. data from the NHDPlusV2 that was jointly produced by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). attributes.name: foo.005 Crop Land Area and Production [Archived]
[Archived] Crop Land Area and Production
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](54af072c-7bb5-4bb1-af84-ea7ba0b4fc22) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Crop Land and Production dataset shows global harvested area and production for four major crops: wheat, soybean, rice and maize. The dataset was derived from the 2005 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and subnational crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. 

  
  
Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. 

  
  
The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Crop Land Area and Production dataset shows production and harvested area for global wheat, soybean, rice and maize crops. Production and harvested area were derived from crop physical area generated by the SPAM mathematical model. The SPAM model outputs were distinguished by crop production system. This was done to account for differences in resource use (i.e., type and quantity of seeds, water, labor, machinery, fertilizer and pesticides). Industrialized farming is considered to be high input and uses large amounts of outside resources. Low input and subsistence farming typically use resources directly from the farm (i.e., manure and cover crops) for crop management. The four production systems were defined by water and management type:
- Irrigated – high input (I)
- Rainfed – high input (H)
- Rainfed – low input (L)
- Rainfed – subsistence (S)

  
  
The primary inputs for the SPAM were crop harvested area, production and yield statistics. This data was collected at the smallest available administrative level (i.e., region, district). Crop statistics at the national level were provided by the [United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAOSTAT)](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home). Subnational statistics were drawn from these additional FAO datasets:  
- [the global information system on water and agriculture (AQUASTAT)](http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/)
- [AgroMaps](http://www.fao.org/land-water/land/land-governance/land-resources-planning-toolbox/category/details/en/c/1026341/) 
- [CountrySTAT](http://www.fao.org/in-action/countrystat/en/)
  
  
Subnational crop data was also provided by the global dataset of [monthly irrigated and rainfed crop areas around the year 2000 (MIRCA2000)](https://www.uni-frankfurt.de/45218023/MIRCA), country statistics offices, published literature and expert judgments. The national and subnational crop production statistics were then allocated to 5 arc minute pixels via a cross-entropy optimization model. The cross-entropy approach quantifies the difference between two probability models and was used to minimize modeling uncertainty. The output of this model were pre-allocated physical areas for each crop and production system. 

  
  
The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included:
- Cropland extent: Satellite imagery was used to distinguish cropland from other land types (forest, grassland, waterbodies) and delineate the geographic extent within which crop production could be allocated. Satellite imagery was provided by the [International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA-IFPRI) cropland map](https://iiasa.ac.at/web/home/research/ResearchPartners/IFPRI.en.html). The satellite imagery was upscaled from a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds to fit the 5 arc minute resolution of the SPAM model.
- Crop suitability: Crop suitability measured whether cropland met the specific temperature, moisture and soil requirements of each crop. Areas were categorized as very suitable, suitable, moderately suitable and marginally suitable using data from the [Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZV3.0) dataset](https://webarchive.iiasa.ac.at/Research/LUC/GAEZ/index.htm). 
- Irrigated areas: Locations of areas equipped for irrigation from the [FAO’s Global Map of Irrigated Areas (GMIA 5.0)](http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/geospatial-information/global-maps-irrigated-areas) were used to further refine production system and cropland definitions. 
- Crop prices: Crop prices were used to understand the location and extent of crops, based on the assumption that farmers choose to grow crops that generate the highest revenue. Crop prices were based on FAOSTAT Gross Production Value data from 2004-2006. 
- Market accessibility: Rural population density was used as a proxy for market accessibility, a factor that affects a farmer’s decision to plant a crop. Population density from the [Global Rural and Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1)](https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/collection/grump-v1) was used to classify pixels as rural or urban at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data was aggregated and reclassified to the 5 arc minute pixel resolution of the SPAM model.
- Potential yield: Crop yield is the amount of crop grown per area of land. Potential crop yield information was derived from GAEZ data and used to further direct the allocation optimization process. 
- Cropping intensity and multiple crops: The cropping intensity parameter accounted for the fact that more than one crop can be grown simultaneously on a plot and that crops can be rotated throughout the year. 

  
  
The SPAM model allocated the crops within each administrative unit with pre-allocated crop statistics within a country using an iterative cross-entropy optimization approach in the [General Algebraic Modeling Software (GAMS)](https://www.gams.com/). The model worked by iteratively minimizing the error between the pre-allocated shares of physical area and the allocated shares of physical area in each pixel. 

  
  
Harvested area and production were calculated from crop physical area in each pixel. Physical area was converted to harvested area using the cropping intensity variable. Total harvested area of each crop in each pixel was calculated by summing estimates across the four production systems. Production was calculated by multiplying harvested area with yield (the amount of production per harvested area in kilograms/hectare). Total production was the sum of production from all of a crop’s production systems and was reported in metric tons. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the [SPAM 2005 Technical Documentation](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/DHXBJX).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2005 Version 3.2 has data for 38 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area, yield and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer

info.functions: Production and harvested area of wheat, soybean, rice and maize crops
info.cautions:
- The variety and sheer volume required to run the SPAM (and related) models raises questions of reliability and comprehensiveness of estimates across different cropping statistics, geographic areas and countries. 
- Different sources of information may lead to inconsistent and incompatible information. 
- Input data was often not available at the smallest administrative level, so national-level data was used.
- If necessary, adjustments were made to the SPAM input data using the following hierarchy of credibility: statistical drop data, cropland, irrigated area and crop suitability area.
- Cropping intensity and production system data were not validated for reliability.
- FAO’s 2004-2006 average international crop prices were used for all countries. Averages likely misrepresent the local economic realities and associated cropping choices faced by farmers.
- Crop distribution maps were not widely available and are mostly for countries with sophisticated agriculture and monitoring systems.
- The reliability of land cover data used for measuring cropland can have significant implications on the overall reliability of MapSPAM allocations. 
- Crop production sometimes occurs within protected areas such as national parks, wilderness areas and nature reserves. During the initial allocation process, SPAM allowed for crop allocation in protected areas. It did not allow increases of areas designated as cropland, suitable areas or irrigated land in protected areas.

attributes.name: U.S. Sea Level Rise Inundation
attributes.description:
This data set was created as part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Office for Coastal Management's efforts to create an online mapping viewer depicting potential sea level rise and its associated impacts on the nation's coastal areas. The purpose of the mapping viewer is to provide coastal managers and scientists with a preliminary look at sea level rise and coastal flooding impacts. The viewer is a screening-level tool that uses nationally consistent data sets and analyses. Data and maps provided can be used at several scales to help gauge trends and prioritize actions for different scenarios.

The purpose of this data set is to show inundation from current Mean Higher High Water (MHHW), as well as potential sea level rise inundation of 1 ft, 2 ft, 3 ft, 4 ft, 5 ft, and 6 ft above the current MHHW for the area. Tiles have been cached down to Level ID 15 (1:18,055).

This data set illustrates the scale of potential flooding, not the exact location, and does not account for erosion, subsidence, or future construction. Inundation is shown as it would appear during the highest high tides (excludes wind driven tides). The data set should be used only as a screening-level tool for management decisions. As with all remotely sensed data, all features should be verified with a site visit. The data set is provided "as is," without warranty to its performance, merchantable state, or fitness for any particular purpose. The entire risk associated with the results and performance of this data set is assumed by the user. This data set should be used strictly as a planning reference and not for navigation, permitting, or other legal purposes.

For more information visit the Sea Level Rise Impacts Viewer (http://coast.noaa.gov/slr). 

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

The National Map transportation data is commonly combined with other data themes, such as boundaries, elevation, hydrography, and structures, to produce general reference base maps. attributes.name: Extreme Precipitation Days
attributes.description:
Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d9034fa9-8db0-4d52-b018-46fae37d3136) as a replacement.**_
  
The Terrestrial Ecoregions data set released by The Nature Conservancy (TNC), and updated in 2008 from compilations of previous studies, classifies land into 14 major habitat types (MHTs). MHTs reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in terrestrial systems.   
  
MHTs are broadly broken down by latitude, ranging from boreal and tundra, temperature, and tropical regions. Temperate and tropical forests are further broken down into broadleaf and conifers. These regions are also distinguished by moisture level, ranging from desert, xeric, and dry, to moist habitats. Finally, shrublands are distinguished by elevation, from high altitude montane shrublands to flooded lowlands. The ecoregions, originally developed by Olson and Dinerstein (2002), Bailey (1995), and Environment Canada (Wiken 1986), were modified by TNC. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Air Quality: Population Exposed to Unhealthy Levels of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Population Exposed to Unhealthy Levels of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) dataset shows the percentage of a country’s population living in places with unhealthy levels of PM2.5 in the air. Particulate matter (PM) are air pollutants such as dirt, dust, soot or smoke. The [EPA categorizes](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) PM by size. Pollutants that are 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter can be inhaled by humans and can be harmful to human health. Fine particulate matter (less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter) poses a greater health risk than PM10. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines state that ambient air concentrations exceeding 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic meter (m3) are unhealthy. Estimates of annual PM2.5 concentrations were generated by combining data from atmospheric chemistry transport models, satellite observations of aerosols in the atmosphere and ground-level particulate monitoring. These estimates were then overlain with gridded population data. This data was collected globally at the country level for select years between 1990 and 2017.

  
  
PM2.5 occurs in many shapes and chemical compositions. Some particulates are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks. Others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. Cooking and heating with solid fuel sources, such as coal, wood or dung, creates harmful smoke and particulate matter. Around 40% of the world’s population relies on solid fuels for cooking and heating. The small size of PM2.5 allows particulates to get deep into the lungs and even into the bloodstream. [Scientific studies](https://www.thelancet.com/gbd?source=post_page) have linked particulate pollution exposure to various health problems including lung cancer, heart disease and respiratory disease. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particulate pollution exposure. The [Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study](http://www.healthdata.org/gbd/2019) estimates that air pollution causes 6.5 million deaths every year. PM2.5 also negatively affects the environment causing haze, acid rain and damage to sensitive forests or farm crops. Additionally, air pollution can hinder development for low and middle-income countries and vulnerable populations. 

  
  
This dataset is part of the GBD study, an international scientific effort led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington. The World Bank Group commissioned the first GBD study as part of its 1993 World Development Report. The GBD believes that everyone deserves to live a long, healthy life. Their study aims to help achieve this by providing a dataset to improve health systems and eliminate disparities. A consortium of more than 3,600 researchers from more than 145 countries contributed to the GBD study. The WHO was a major contributor as well. The study quantifies the health effects of diseases and injuries and analyzes the risk factors for death and disease. Air quality is among the study’s 84 environmental, behavioral, occupational and metabolic risk factors.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was derived from a gridded model of air quality and population. Estimates of annual PM2.5 concentration were generated by combining data from three sources: atmospheric chemistry transport models, [satellite observations of aerosols](http://fizz.phys.dal.ca/~atmos/martin/?page_id=140) in the atmosphere, and ground-level particulate monitoring. [Harvard University’s GEOS Chem](http://acmg.seas.harvard.edu/geos/) atmospheric chemistry model was used to simulate atmospheric transport of chemical air pollutants such as organic carbon, nitrate, sulfate, ammonium and mineral dust. Atmospheric aerosol observations collected by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) satellites were combined with the GEOS Chem model to estimate atmospheric particulate concentration. Data was available at a resolution of 0.1 degrees (°). Ground-level particulate monitoring data for PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations were also used. This data was measured by 9,960 ground monitors in 108 countries. Air quality data from each of the three measurements was calibrated by country and modeled using a hierarchical statistical method.

  
  
The GBD used high resolution population data from NASA’s [Gridded Population of the World](https://beta.sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/collection/gpw-v4) (GPW) dataset. The GPW data was upscaled from its resolution of 0.0417° to fit the GBD’s model grid cell sizes of 0.1°. GPW data was then overlaid with gridded PM2.5 estimates to determine the percentage of a country’s population living in an area with unhealthy air quality. The WHO’s definition of unhealthy air quality are air concentrations greater than 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per m3. In grid cells where PM2.5 concentrations exceeded this threshold, the population data was summed and divided by the country’s total population. The data from all grid cells was aggregated by population-based weighted averaging to calculate each country’s population percentage figure. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(18)32225-6/fulltext#supplementaryMaterial) (supplementary appendix 1, page 67).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. 
See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). 
This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

attributes.name: Ecoregions Prioritized for Conservation
attributes.description:
The Ecoregions Prioritized for Conservation released by The Nature Conservancy (TNC) provides a vision for conservation success for ecological systems, natural communities, and species representative of an ecoregion by showing the boundaries of areas that TNC has prioritized for conservation in 2011. Many portfolio areas were derived from ecoregional assessments, but other priorities derived using other planning methodologies are included in this global data set. Ecoregional assessment is a method for setting geographic priorities based on the status of biodiversity, habitat condition, threats, and sociopolitical conditions in an ecoregion. In more detail, ecoregional assessments use ecoregions as the unit of analysis.   
  
For an ecoregion or collection of ecoregions, TNC develops and disseminates finer-scale data on the distribution and status of biodiversity, habitat condition, current and future threats, and the sociopolitical conditions that influence conservation success within those ecoregions. These finer-scale data allow TNC to set long-term conservation goals for ecosystems, natural communities, and imperiled or declining species representative of an ecoregion, and to establish ecoregional priorities for resource allocation—specific landscapes, threats to biodiversity, and strategic opportunities that affect one or more ecoregions and demand immediate attention. Ecoregional data also provide a baseline against which TNC can measure progress toward the long-term goals for the representative ecosystems and species within an ecoregion. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2ac1f43c-30bc-4ed9-846c-8443ce4987a9) as a replacement.**_
  
Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,200 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. attributes.name: [Archived] Political Violence Risk Assessment
attributes.description:
The Political Violence Risk Assessment dataset was originally published by The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS). Its purpose is to forecast the onset of large-scale political violence. Countries are evaluated to determine their "risk" of experiencing a large-scale political violence event in the next month using structural data (infant mortality, regime type, conflicts in neighboring countries, and state-led discrimination) and automated event data (protests, assaults, and expressions of disapproval) from the previous month, which are combined in a logistic regression model. The score is normalized between 0 and 100 and indicates the percentile rank of probability of onset. Infant mortality data are from World Development Indicators; other structural data are from the Center for Systemic Peace; event data are from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone; and normalization and aggregation were done by the HCSS. attributes.name: Impaired Waters (U.S.)
attributes.description:
This data set was created by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and shows bodies of waters that have been identified as impaired based on the current approved Clean Water Act 303(d) lists submitted by states. The goal of the Clean Water Act (CWA) is "to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation's waters" (33 U.S.C. §1251(a)). Under section 303(d) of the CWA, states, territories, and authorized tribes, collectively referred to in the act as "states," are required to develop lists of impaired waters. These are waters for which technology-based regulations and other required controls are not stringent enough to meet the water quality standards set by states. The law requires that states establish priority rankings for waters on the lists and develop total maximum daily loads (TMDLs) for these waters. A TMDL includes a calculation of the maximum amount of a pollutant that can be present in a waterbody and still meet water-quality standards. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. attributes.name: Frost Free Season
attributes.description:
Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA). 

LOCA is a technique for downscaling climate model projections of the future climate. The method estimates finer-scale climate detail using the systematic historical effects of topography on local weather patterns. The LOCA downscaled climate projections provide temperature and precipitation on pixels that are six kilometers (3.7 miles) across. The data are daily, covering the period 1950-2100 for 32 global climate models. LOCA attempts to better preserve extreme hot days and heavy rain events than the previous generation of downscaling approaches. While previous downscaling techniques typically formed the downscaled model day using a weighted average of 30 similar historical days, LOCA looks locally around each point of interest to find the one best matching day. The data spans from Mexico through southern Canada and can be used to assess climate impacts across much of North America, including the entire conterminous U.S. The work represents a collaboration across many groups, including SIO, the California Energy Commission, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Geological Survey, the Bureau of Reclamation, the NOAA Regional Integrated Sciences and Assessments (RISA) program, the Climate Analytics Group, the nonprofit group Climate Central, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, NASA Ames Research Center, Santa Clara University, the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder, and the Southwest Climate Science Center.

The LOCA data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 32 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the LOCA data set. For access to the original LOCA data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: Frost Free Season
attributes.description:
Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding & Sea Level Rise (m)
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Areas Likely Flooded by Sea Level Rise dataset shows on a global scale which areas can be flooded at different amounts of water rise due to sea level rise, tide, and storm surge. The map presents sea level rise at 30-Meter, 20-Meter, 10 Meter, 5 Meter, 3-Meter, 2.5 Meter, 2-Meter, 1.5-Meter, 1.0- Meter, 0.5-Meter options. Areas that are inundated at each sea level rise value are masked in blue. The data used for surface elevation was collected from multiple sources that range from satellite imagery to flood maps between 1929 and 2015. The resolution of the dataset varies based on region in the world, with the contiguous United states being the highest resolution at 5 m and much of the rest of the world at 90 m.

  
  
This dataset was created by Climate Central under their project Surging Seas. It has been cited in over 5,000 articles, highlighted on the front page of the White House Climate Initiative website, and accessed by more than 60 federal agencies. It plays an important role in helping world governments understand the effects of climate change, make policies, and develop tools to effectively help communities in the instance of flooding. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset was created by first combining multiple digital elevation models to create global coverage. Elevation data was then altered to be expressed relative to local high tide lines. High tide lines used were the average high tide line based on seasonal and monthly fluctuations (Mean Higher High Water). Next, two layers showing standard ocean water coverage and flood control methods for the United States were applied. Lastly, an algorithm was added to show how water coverage would increase based on different amounts of sea level rise, storm surge, and tides. The “bathtub method” algorithm shows water coverage in all areas below a given water height threshold that is input by the user. The final data was projected using raster and tabular data between 60 degrees north and 56 degrees south.

  
  
Elevation data for the contiguous United States came from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Coastal Lidar collection at 5 m horizontal resolution and information on Alaska came from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) at 60 m resolution. Elevation data for Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Corn Island (Nicaragua), Dominica, Dominican Republic, Grenada, Guyana, Haiti, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, San Blas (Panama), Suriname, The Bahamas, and Trinidad and Tobago came from Climate Central’s CoastalDEM database at 10 m resolution. Data for the rest of the world was taken from NASA’s Shuttle Radar Topography Missions (SRTM) at a resolution of 90 m. High tide data was taken from the VDatum tidal model for the contiguous United States and a global tidal model supplied by Mark Merrifield of the University of Hawaii for the rest of the world.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

info.functions: Global representation of areas that will likely be flooded at different amounts rising water due to a combination of sea level rise, tide, and storm surge
info.cautions:
- SRTM is known to overestimate earth elevations. It originally collects data on surface elevation and not bare earth elevation. The surface elevation data is corrected to show bare earth elevation, but it can be difficult to process and ultimately the values are just estimations. Areas with large buildings, vegetation, or other obstructions are most at risk of errors.
- The USGS map on Alaska is from 1929 and does not have a reliable conversion to current reference frames. Additionally, it does not show any tectonic action, uplifting or subduction, that is common in the state and has occurred over the last 100 years.
- Data on flood control methods is sparse. This study only included levees for within the United States and even then it did not consider the state of which the levees are in and if they are functional enough to control severe flooding.
- Isolated areas of low-lying elevation are only shown to be protected from sea level rise if they are protected by a ridge of at least 20 m above the high tide line. Data with this precision was challenging to collect because flood maps in many areas have poor resolution and artifacts from rendering. It is likely that some of these areas are misclassified and some areas not classified in this category should be.
- The dataset does not consider future changes like erosion or construction. Additionally, it does not consider the geology of the region and some areas with porous bedrock can be affected by sea level rise even if they are protected based on elevation data. This dataset should be used in conjunction with local site visits to get the best results.

attributes.name: foo.010 Crop Harvested Area Yield Production
Crop Harvested Area and Production
attributes.description:
The Crop Harvested Area and Production data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It shows the harvested area, yield and production amount of 175 crops in 206 countries for the year 2000 (average of census data between 1997 and 2003). Harvested area represents the fractional proportion of hectares harvested per gridcell. Production is calculated by multiplying harvested area in hectares and crop yield in tons per hectare. The data were collected from agricultural census and survey information on the areas and yields of 175 crops from the smallest political units reasonably obtainable for 206 countries. Data availability varies for different crops within each country, with most countries having subnational statistics for some crops but national statistics for others. The largest single source of subnational data is Agro-MAPS, a joint project between the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the International Food Policy Research Institute and the Center for Sustainability and the Global Environment. Croplands cover about 15 million km² of the planet and provide the bulk of the food and fiber essential to human well-being. Most global land cover data sets from satellites group croplands into just a few categories, thereby excluding information critical for answering key questions on subjects ranging from biodiversity conservation to food security to biogeochemical cycling. Information about agricultural land use practices like crop selection, yield and fertilizer use is even more limited. These EarthStat data present land use data sets created by combining national, state and county-level census statistics with a recently updated global data set of croplands on a 5 minute by 5 minute (~10 km x 10 km) latitude/longitude grid. attributes.name: Average Low Temperature
attributes.description:
Annual average low temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

These data were used to create Figure 16.2 in the Third National Climate Assessment report.
See: http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/regions/northeast#graphic-17071
 
This figure shows the average of projections of the number of days over 90 degrees Fahrenheit from several climate models. On the global scale, climate model simulations show consistent projections of future temperature conditions under a range of emissions scenarios. All models show warming by late this century that is much larger than historical variations nearly everywhere globally. For the U.S., models unequivocally project large and historically unprecedented future warming in every region of the U.S. under all of the scenarios used in this assessment. The amount of warming varies substantially between higher versus lower scenarios, and moderately from model to model, but the amount of projected warming is much larger than historical variations. Likewise, the models project unequivocal increases in the number of days over 90 degrees Fahrenheit that are larger than historical variations.

attributes.name: Gray Water Footprint and Pollution Levels
attributes.description: The Twente Water Centre at the University of Twente (TWC) created a global assessment of nitrogen-related water pollution in river basins, with the option to specify the pollution source by economic sector, and by crop for the agricultural sector. Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) loads to freshwater are estimated to calculate the resultant gray water footprints (GWFs), and relate the GWFs per river basin to runoff to calculate the N-related water pollution level (WPL) per catchment. These calculations were created at a 5-by-5 arc minute spatial resolution over the period 2002-2010.   The GWF is calculated by dividing the N load by the difference between the ambient water quality standard for N (the maximum acceptable concentration) and the natural concentration of N in the receiving water body. The water pollution level (WPL), which measures the degree of pollution within a catchment, is estimated as the ratio of the total of GWF in a catchment to the actual runoff from that catchment. The artificial fertilizer application rate data came primarily from the International Fertilizer Industry Association (IFA) and was supplemented with data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
