attributes.name: bio.047a Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquitoe Aedes aegypti
Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes aegypti
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmission by one of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible under baseline conditions, as well as in the years 2050 and 2080. The mosquito is *Aedes aegypti*, and it transmits diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the baseline temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. On Resource Watch, we display the RCP 8.5 “business as usual” scenario, which represents how the climate is predicted to change if we continue our current emissions trends.

  
  
According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. 


  
  
The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows temperature suitability data for one of the other most common-disease-carrying mosquitoes, [*Aedes albopictus*](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio047b-Temperature-Suitability-for-Disease-Carrying-Mosquitoe-Aedes-albopictus). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate,  human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data.

  
  
As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for three other climate change scenarios (RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 6.0), as well as results produced by different climate models, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes aegypti
info.technical_title:
Global expansion and redistribution of Aedes-borne
virus transmission risk with climate change
info.functions: The number of months per year the temperature is suitable for disease-carrying mosquito Aedes aegypti
info.cautions: No models can precisely predict the global climate suitability for transmission risk. Models used in this dataset only set an outer spatiotemporal bound on where transmission is thermally plausible, given climate projections. Other environmental, biological, and social factors can also impact disease transmission by mosquitoes. In addition, the relationship between climate change and burdens of diseases carried by mosquitoes is a complex process. Climate change is likely to change the relationship between transmission risk and disease burden at fine scales within those zones of transmission nonlinearly, such that areas with shorter seasons of transmission could still experience increased overall disease burdens, or vice versa.
info.citation: Ryan, S.J., C.J. Carlson, E.A. Mordecai, L.R. Johnson. 2019. “Global Expansion and Redistribution of Aedes-Borne Virus Transmission Risk with Climate Change.” PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 13 (3): e0007213. ene.001a Global Reservoir and Dam GRanD v1.3
Reservoirs and Dams
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the locations of dams and the areas covered by the reservoirs that they create upstream. The information used to create this dataset is compiled from a variety of sources, creating a global, harmonized account of dams and reservoirs. The current version maps 7,320 dams that were built as recently as 2017, with a combined storage capacity of 6,864 km³. These include reservoirs with a storage capacity of more than 0.1 km³; smaller dams and reservoirs were added if data was available. 
  
  

The production of this dataset was led by a consortium of partners through the Global Water System Project (GWSP) in Bonn, Germany, and is a joint project of the Earth System Science Partnership (ESSP).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Datasets were contributed by 11 participating institutions to serve as the foundation for creating the first version of this dataset. The current version of the dataset adds new dams and reservoirs that were mostly derived from data sources available online. These included national repositories, the Clean Development Mechanism project registry of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), some privately maintained databases like Roller Compacted Concrete Dams, and, for validation purposes, information listed by the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD).
  
  

To consolidate the datasets and improve accuracy, the locations of all dams included in the source datasets were verified, updated, and/or newly georeferenced. This process was guided by maps, atlases, and online resources (including Google Earth).
  
  

Each dam (with a few exceptions, see source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125)) was assigned to a polygon that depicts the reservoir surface. In the first version of the dataset, most polygons used for this procedure were provided by the SRTM Water Body Database (SWBD), a near-global, public mapping product created at 30 m resolution from remote sensing imagery. Additional reservoir outlines were added from various alternative sources or digitized from scratch. In the newest version of the dataset, most of the new reservoir polygons that were added were delineated from the surface water maps produced by the Joint Research Center (JRC) of the European Commission from Landsat imagery at 30 m resolution for the period 1984-2015.
  
  

Cross-validation of the information provided by different sources was performed, and records with suspicious information were flagged and individually verified. Data gaps were filled by comparing and merging attributes from different databases. If inconsistencies, uncertainties, or data gaps remained, the “Quality” index of the record was lowered accordingly. 
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/ene_001a_reservoirs_and_dams).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Reservoirs and Dams

sources.source-description: European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (EC JRC)
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)

info.technical_title: Global Reservoir and Dam Database, Version 1.3
info.functions: Dam locations and areas of the associated reservoirs
info.cautions:
The most comprehensive global dam database, the World Register of Dams, is compiled by the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD) and currently lists more than 58,000 records of large dams. This inventory is not georeferenced and therefore cannot be displayed on Resource Watch, but the number of dams it has recorded indicates the large data gaps that exist in this dataset.
  
  

The various sources used to create this dataset showed different characteristics regarding their resolution, accuracy, comprehensiveness, and the type of attributes—mostly due to the different objectives and needs when assembling them.
  
  

While no criterion for minimum height of dams was applied in the generation of this dataset, many of the source datasets used a threshold of 15 m in their original collections, introducing a bias in the initial selection toward higher dams.
  
  

Reservoir outlines are typically subject to strong seasonal fluctuations. As most polygons in the first version of this dataset are originally depicted from remote sensing imagery (i.e., a snapshot in time) they may reflect a low-fill or dry-season state with significantly smaller than maximum area.
  
  

Not all data sources provided a clear distinction on whether their attribute data refers strictly to a physical dam or to the impounded reservoir behind it, or both.
info.citation: Lehner, B., C. Reidy Liermann, C. Revenga, C. Vörösmarty, B. Fekete, P. Crouzet, P. Döll, et al. 2011. “High-Resolution Mapping of the World’s Reservoirs and Dams for Sustainable River-Flow Management.” Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment 9 (9): 494-502. Accessed through Resource Watch, (date). [www.resourcewatch.org](https://www.resourcewatch.org).

year.description: Year in which the dam was built (not further specified: year of construction; year of completion; year of commissioning; year of refurbishment/update; etc.)

res_name.description: Name of reservoir or lake (i.e. impounded water body)

alt_name.alias: Alternative Name of Reservoir or Dam

sec_admin.description: Indicates dams or reservoirs that lie within or are associated with multiple administrative units

sec_cntry.description: Indicates international dams or reservoirs that lie within or are associated with multiple countries

alt_year.description: May indicate a multi-year construction phase, an update, or a secondary dam construction

rem_year.description: Year in which the dam was removed, replaced, subsumed, or destroyed; see also column ‘Timeline’ below

alt_hgt_m.description: May indicate update or secondary dam construction

alt_len_m.description: May indicate update or secondary dam construction

area_skm.description: Representative surface area of reservoir in square kilometers (km²); consolidated from other ‘Area’ columns in the following order of priority: ‘Area_poly’ over ‘Area_rep’ over ‘Area_max’ over ‘Area_min’; exceptions apply if value in ‘Area_poly’ column seems unreliable; see also notes below

area_poly.description: Surface area of associated reservoir polygon in square kilometers (km²)

area_rep.description: Most reliable reported surface area of reservoir in square kilometers (km²)

area_max.description: Maximum value of other reported surface areas in square kilometers  (km²)

area_min.description: Minimum value of other reported surface areas in square kilometers (km²)

cap_mcm.description: Representative maximum storage capacity of reservoir in million cubic meters (m³, millions); consolidated from other ‘Cap’ columns in the following order of priority: ‘Cap_max’ over ‘Cap_rep’ over ‘Cap_min’; exceptions apply if value in ‘Cap_max’ column seems unreliable or rounded; see also notes below

cap_max.description: Reported ‘maximum storage capacity’ in million cubic meters (m³, millions); see notes below

cap_rep.description: Reported ‘storage capacity’ in million cubic meters (m³, millions); value may refer to different types of storage capacity; see notes below

cap_min.description: Minimum value of other reported storage capacities in million cubic meters (m³, millions)

depth_m.description: Average depth of reservoir in meters; calculated as ratio between storage capacity (‘Cap_mcm’) and surface area (‘Area_skm’); values that are somewhat higher than the dam height (‘Dam_hgt_m’) may still be reasonable, e.g. if the storage capacity refers to the maximum volume yet the reservoir polygon represents a low-fill status; values capped at 1000 indicate exceedingly high values which may be due to inconsistencies in the data

dis_avg_ls.description: Long-term (1971-2000) average discharge at dam location in liters per second; value derived from HydroSHEDS flow routing scheme combined with WaterGAP runoff estimates (Döll et al. 2003) at 15s resolution at point location of dam

dor_pc.description: Degree of Regulation (DOR) in percent (%); equivalent to “residence time” of water in the reservoir; calculated as ratio between storage capacity (‘Cap_mcm’) and total annual flow (derived from ‘Dis_avg_ls’); values capped at 10,000 indicate exceedingly high values, which may be due to inconsistencies in the data and/or incorrect allocation to the river network and the associated discharges

elev_masl.description: Elevation of reservoir surface in meters above sea level; value derived from EarthEnv-DEM90 data set (Robinson et al. 2014) at 15s resolution at point location of dam

catch_skm.description: Area of upstream catchment draining into the reservoir in square kilometers (km²); value derived from HydroSHEDS at 15s resolution at point location of dam

catch_rep.description: Reported area of upstream catchment draining into reservoir in square kilometers (km²)

main_use.description: Main purpose of reservoir: Irrigation; Hydroelectricity; Water supply; Flood control; Recreation; Navigation; Fisheries; Pollution control; Livestock; or Other

lake_ctrl.description: Indicates whether a reservoir has been built at the location of an existing natural lake using a lake control structure; currently this column only contains limited entries; ‘Yes’ = lake control structure raises original lake level; ‘Enlarged’ = lake control structure enlarged the original lake surface area; ‘Maybe’ = not sure, but data seems to indicate a lake control structure

multi_dams.description: Indicates whether there is more than one dam associated with this reservoir (e.g. main and saddle dam); if ‘Yes’, then columns ‘Alt_year’, ‘Alt_hgt_m’, and ‘Alt_len_m’ refer to the secondary dam

timeline.description: Indicates whether the status of a dam has changed or will change over time: ‘Destroyed’ (dam got destroyed or failed); ‘Modified’ (dam was modified from an earlier status, e.g. raised, expanded, refurbished, but the earlier status is not individually recorded in GRanD); ‘Planned’ (dam is planned to be built in the future); ‘Removed’ (dam record and point are retained but the dam itself has been removed and not replaced); ‘Replaced’ (dam record and point are retained in data set but the dam itself has been replaced; the new dam is recorded as a new GRanD point); ‘Subsumed’ (dam record and point are retained but the dam and reservoir themselves were subsumed by larger infrastructure constructed further downstream; the old reservoir polygon has been removed in version 1.3 and the new dam and reservoir are recorded as a new GRanD point and polygon) ‘Under construction’ (dam is currently under construction)

quality.description: 1: Verified (location and data have been verified); 2: Good (location and data seem good but have not all been verified); 3: Fair (some data discrepancies; missing data; or uncertainties); 4: Poor (significant data discrepancies of various kinds that indicate errors); 5: Unreliable (severe data discrepancies without reasonable explanation)

long_dd.description: Longitude of point location of dam in decimal degrees; the point location is only an approximation of the actual dam location

lat_dd.description: Latitude of point location of dam in decimal degrees; the point location is only an approximation of the actual dam location

poly_src.description: ‘CanVec’ = Canadian hydrographic dataset (Natural Resources Canada 2013); ‘ECRINS’ = European Catchments and Rivers Network System (EEA 2012); ‘GLWD’ = Global Lakes and Wetlands Database (Lehner and Döll 2004); ‘JRC’ = polygon digitized from European Commission Joint Research Centre’s surface water layer (Pekel et al. 2016); ‘JRC modified’ = initial polygon digitized from JRC surface water layer and then modified by McGill University; ‘McGill’ = polygon digitized from scratch or majorly modified by McGill University; ‘NHD’ = US National Hydrography Dataset (US Geological Survey 2013); ‘SWBD’ = SRTM Water Body Database (Slater et al. 2006); ‘UY’ = polygon provided by University of Yamanashi; ‘Other’ = other sources, including remote sensing imagery and GIS repositories; ‘No polygon’ = no polygon available

editor.description: ‘McGill’ = McGill University (BL = B. Lehner; PB = P. Beames); ‘UNH’ = University of New Hampshire

data_info.alias: Supporting information on certain data issues
data_info.description: ‘Capacity from statistics’ = capacity derived from Eq. 1 or Eq. 2; ‘Capacity estimated’ = capacity estimated from other available information

grand_id.description: Unique ID for each dam and associated reservoir; IDs correspond between dam (point) and reservoir (polygon) layers of the GRanD database; IDs up to 6862 refer to dams and reservoirs included in version 1.1; IDs 6863 and above were added in version 1.3

attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Terrorism Index (GTI) is a quantification of the impact of terrorism in a country. It provides a comprehensive summary of the key global trends and patterns in terrorism over the last 50 years. A higher GTI represents a higher impact of terrorism in a country.

  
  
 GTI measures the impact of terrorism in a country by combining data for all terrorist incidents occuring in a country for a given year. Each possible terrorist event is analyzed to make sure it is within GTI’s requirements to be qualified as a terrorist incident and is given a score based on four indicators.

  
  
The Global Terrorism Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace (IEP) using data from the Global Terrorism Database (GTD) and other sources. Data for the GTD was collected and composed by the National Consortium for the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism (START) at the University of Maryland. 

  
  
The GTI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2002 to 2018 for 163 countries or independent territories covering 99.7% of the world’s population. This data can help to create a discussion about the future of terrorism and the necessary policy measures to mitigate it.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Terrorism Index (GTI) utilzed data from the Global Terorism Database, which has information on 170,000 terrorist incidents from 1970 to the end of 2018. The GTI dataset contains information  from 2012 to 2018. Three criteria were used to determine whether an incident qualified to be included in the Global Terrorism Database. To be included in the database the incident had to meet the points outlined below:

  
  
1. The incident was intentional - the result of a conscious calculation on the part of a perpetrator.
  
  
2. The incident involved some level of violence or threat of violence - including property damage as well as violence against people.
  
  
3. The perpetrators of the incidents were sub-national actors. This database did not include acts of state terrorism.

  
  
 Incidents with insufficient information were not included in the database. 

  
  
The GTI was developed in consultation with the Global Peace Index Expert Panel. Country scores were calculated on a scale from 0 to 10; where 0 represented no impact from terrorism and 10 represented the highest measurable impact of terrorism. Scores were determined by analyzing each terrorism incident using four indicators:

- total number of terrorist incidents in a given year 
- total number of fatalities caused by terrorists in a given year 
- total number of injuries caused by terrorists in a given year
- a measure of the total property damage from terrorist incidents in a given year


  
  
Each indicator was given a different weight between zero and three for every incident, and a five year weighted average was applied to the country score to reflect the long term psychological impact of terrorist incidents. Psychological impacts of terrorist incidents often last in a society for many years after the incident.  Finally, a base 10 logarithmic banding system between 0 and 10, at 0.5 intervals, was applied to each country score to get the final GTI value. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/11/GTI-2019web.pdf)  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_093_global_terrorism_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.  
  
### Disclaimer

sources.source-description: The Institute for Economics and Peace

info.technical_title: Global Terrorism Index 2019
info.functions: A comparable measure on the impact of terrorism in 163 countries from 2002 to 2018
info.cautions:
Defining terrorism is not a straightforward matter. There is no single internationally accepted definition of what constitutes terrorism and academic literature has many competing definitions and typologies. The definition used in the GTI is the same that is used for the GTD, which includes the idea that there are long term psychological effects on a community that experiences a terrorist incident. Other terrorism resources likely use varying definitions.

Multiple incidents that occur in both the same geographic location and temporal point are regarded as a single incident. If either the time of the incidents or their locations are different, the events are recorded as separate incidents. For example, if multiple events are caused by the same perpetrator and occur at the same time, but in different places they are counted as separate incidents.
info.citation: Institute for Economics & Peace. Global Terrorism Index 2019: Measuring the Impact of Terrorism, Sydney, November 2019. attributes.name: req.009b Annual Rate of Change for Energy Intensity
Annual Rate of Change in Energy Intensity
attributes.description:
This analysis shows the annual rate of change in energy intensity. Energy intensity indicates how much primary energy is needed to produce one unit of gross domestic product (GDP). Having a low energy intensity indicates that a country can increase its economic growth without having to rely as heavily on energy consumption. A negative percentage for the annual rate of change in energy intensity means that the energy intensity had decreased since the previous year.

  
  
The Resource Watch data team calculated the annual rate of change in energy intensity using the [Energy Intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/2c444596-2be3-4786-bdfc-24010f99b21e) dataset on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch analyzed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/blog-analysis/tree/master/req_009_energy_decarbonization_leaders).

attributes.name: Electricity Consumption
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the net electricity consumption in 230 countries from 1980 to 2016. This dataset is published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), [which calculates net electricity consumption](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=Net%20electricity%20consumption) as “generation, plus imports, minus exports, minus transmission and distribution losses.”
  
  

Electricity consumption is a key indicator of the environmental impact and input costs of economic activity. The intensity of electricity consumption and the sources of energy are among the key indicators of sustainable energy, as defined by Sustainable Development Goal 7.  
  
### Methodology  
  
EIA collected and analyzed consumption data from multiple external sources. The estimates in this dataset are based on a time series analysis, and the performance of the model was evaluated with hold‐out validation.
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.eia.gov/beta/international/images/International_Energy_Statistics_Estimation_for_Lagged_Data.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [total energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/67cf410f-4cdf-4437-aa09-187e5fa590ae) dataset by EIA.
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ene_034_electricity_consumption).

Agriculture, Value Added
attributes.description:
The Agriculture, Value Added data set was created by the World Bank and displays the net output of agriculture sectors in most countries and various other regional entities (e.g., geographic regions, economic output, members of certain economic/political unions) after adding up all outputs and subtracting the value of intermediate goods and services consumed in production. Agriculture corresponds to International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC) divisions 1-5 and includes forestry, hunting, and fishing, as well as cultivation of crops and livestock production. The value added is calculated without making deductions for depreciation of fabricated assets or depletion and degradation of natural resources. The origin of value added is determined by the ISIC, revision 3. National data are available for some countries beginning in 1960 and available for an increasing number of countries up until present, when all but a few countries are represented. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

info.technical_title: Agriculture, value added (% of GDP)
info.functions: Net output of agriculture sector, after adding up all outputs and subtracting intermediate inputs, as share of total economic output
info.cautions: Among the difficulties faced by compilers of national accounts is the extent of unreported economic activity in the informal or secondary economy. In developing countries a large share of agricultural output is either not exchanged (because it is consumed within the household) or not exchanged for money. Agricultural production often must be estimated indirectly, using a combination of methods involving estimates of inputs, yields, and area under cultivation. This approach sometimes leads to crude approximations that can differ from the true values over time and across crops for reasons other than climate conditions or farming techniques. Similarly, agricultural inputs that cannot easily be allocated to specific outputs are frequently "netted out" using equally crude and ad hoc approximations.

attributes.name: Snow Cover
attributes.description:
The MODIS Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI) snow cover layer, from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), shows the presence of snow cover over land and water bodies as an index related to the presence of snow. NDSI snow cover is derived from the cloud free snow reflectance sensed by the MODIS instrument, and hence this layer shows presence of snow during day time and under cloud clear condition only. NDSI snow cover though could be retrieved in the valid range of (0, 1.0) at every pixel, additional tests like surface temperature screening linked with the surface height is used for accurate detection. Snow is precipitation that forms from water vapor in the atmosphere where temperatures are below 0° Celsius. If the ground temperature is also below freezing, snow will accumulate on the ground as bright, white layer of snowpack. Snow cover reflects sunlight back into the atmosphere, helping to cool the Earth’s surface. Snowmelt is used for drinking water and crop irrigation, and can moisturize soil to reduce the risk of wildfire in many areas in the world. When snow melts in the spring, too much snow can cause springtime flooding. The MODIS Snow Cover (Normalized Difference Snow Index) layer is available from both the Terra (MOD10) and Aqua (MYD10) satellites. The sensor and imagery resolution is 500 m, the geographic coverage is global, and the temporal resolution is daily. Monthly averages for each CMG cell are calculated from the corresponding 28 – 31 days of observations in the MOD10C1 daily maximum snow cover extent data set. The input data are filtered to utilize only the clearest surface views in the average and to remove low magnitude snow cover fractions in the output that likely reflect erroneous snow detections.Algorithm Description
Average snow cover is calculated for each cell in the CMG using the 28 – 31 days of MOD10C1 (daily snow cover) for the month. Data is filtered so that the most relevant days of snow cover are used to calculate the average and to filter out data that is of low magnitude i.e. low occurrence of snow during the month. The latter filter works to remove some occurrences of erroneous snow from the monthly snow average. The daily snow data is used to compute the monthly average snow cover. A daily cell must have a Clear Index (CI) of > 70% to be included in the average. Clear index is defined as the number of cells without clouds divided by the total number of cells.That filter is applied so that only the clearest of the daily observations are included in the average. (See the MOD10C1 section for description of the CI.) A daily observation contributes to the monthly average for a cell as follows: 
Daily contribution to monthly mean = 100 * snow%/CI  For daily observations that are cloud free the snow contribution to the mean is the observed snow fraction in a grid cell. For daily observations of mixed snow and cloud fractions with a high CI it is assumed that there is some fraction of snow cover obscured by cloud. In that case the daily snow observation is increased in that equation so that the contribution to the monthly mean will be greater than the daily snow observation. For example, a cell has 25% snow cover and the CI = 75 then the cell is determined to have (25%/75 * 100) = 33% fractional snow cover. Daily observations with a CI ≤ 70 are assigned either as 100% cloudy, night, missing or no decision. There must be at least one day in the month for each cell with the CI > 70 in order for the mean snow cover to be computed for that cell of the monthly CMG. If that restriction is not met then the cell is reported as no decision.  A second filter is applied to the calculated mean fractional snow cover of each cell to filter out those cells in which the magnitude of snow cover is less than 10%. Cells failing the filter are assigned 0% snow for the month. Cells with a low magnitude are considered suspect of being erroneous snow originating in the MOD10_L2 algorithm and being propagated through the sequence of snow products. The magnitude of snow is calculated as an average snow for all days with snow passing the first filter of CI > 70. Data displayed on Resource Watch is filtered to only show snow cover greater than 20 percent. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information

info.functions: Monthly average percentage of snow-covered land
info.cautions: Analysis of the quality of the MOD10CM has been limited to visual and qualitative comparative analysis of the monthly snow maps. Overall the MOD10CM appears to be a reasonable representation of mean monthly snow cover when compared to other sources of global or regional snow maps. However there are notable amounts of spurious snow cover in places that did not have snow which is the result of compounding of daily snow commission errors over the month. Such snow commission errors can be seen in the monthly snow cover in Fig.12. In some situations the snow commission errors may be indicative of anomalous surface conditions, or frequent snow/cloud confusion. Users may choose to screen out low amounts of snow cover to reduce probable snow commission errors or interpret the data in other ways relevant to their interest. The validation status of this product is Stage 1 but may change as evaluation and validation analysis is done. Data displayed on Resource Watch is filtered to only show snow cover greater than 20 percent.

attributes.name: Life Expectancy at Birth
attributes.description:
Life expectancy at birth is derived from male and female life expectancy at birth and compiled by the World Bank from sources such as (1) UN Population Division: World Population Prospects; (2) Census reports and other statistical publications from national statistical offices; (3) Eurostat: Demographic Statistics; (4) UN Statistical Division: Population and Vital Statistics Report (various years); (5) U.S. Census Bureau: International Database; and (6) Secretariat of the Pacific Community: Statistics and Demography. It is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if mortality patterns at the time of its birth remain constant in the future. It reflects the overall mortality level of a population and summarizes the mortality pattern that prevails across all age groups in a given year. It is calculated in a period life table, which provides a snapshot of a population's mortality pattern at a given time. It therefore does not reflect the mortality pattern that a person actually experiences during his or her life, which can be calculated in a cohort life table. High mortality in young age groups significantly lowers the life expectancy at birth. But if a person survives his or her childhood of high mortality, he or she may live much longer. For example, in a population with a life expectancy at birth of 50, there may be few people dying at age 50. The life expectancy at birth may be low due to high childhood mortality, so that once a person survives his or her childhood, he or she may live much longer than 50 years. This data set of country-level figures is global in scope and spans 1960-present. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: cit.047 Urban Land Use - Mexico - 6 Category (In review)
Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for nine cities in Mexico. The nine cities are Culiacán, Guadalajara, León, Mérida, Mexico City, Monterrey, Reynosa, Tijuana, and Tuxtla Gutiérrez. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. (For full definitions of these categories, see [this working paper](https://marroninstitute.nyu.edu/uploads/content/Measuring_the_Quality_of_Urban_Layouts_December_1_2016_Reduced_new.pdf) or the [technical note](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).) These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The data is available for the year 2018 and has a resolution of 5 meters (m).
  
  

The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. The dataset can be used to measure the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identify what types of land use have been affected by natural disasters. Although this particular LULC dataset captures only one moment in time, when available there is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset was produced in an automated way via supervised machine learning techniques. Automating urban LULC classification reduced the resource and time requirements by orders of magnitude, relative to manual mapping, thus making the process highly scalable. The machine learning model used for classification required two primary ingredients: satellite imagery and ground-truth data. Ground-truth is the observation or measurements about what actually exists at a specific location.This data was collected from the Atlas of Urban Expansion, a multiphase research effort conducted by the New York University (NYU) Urban Expansion Program in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. The Sentinel-2 constellation of the European Space Agency was used as the source of satellite imagery. The original resolution of the imagery was 10 m; this was later upsampled to 5 m to utilize as much information as possible from the ground-truth data.
  
  

The satellite imagery was combined with the ground-truth data to create training samples required for training the model. The models were relatively small, straightforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The trained models were finally used to map selected cities in Mexico. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [roads](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e1c519d3-16ea-400a-a71c-9033ba5f490b) for the same nine cities in Mexico and LULC (areal) data for [India](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e354f7b8-0fca-422f-bf12-fc6189812bec).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.
  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Seychelles Female Share of Population
attributes.description:
This data set displays the female share of the population per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics 2010 Population and Housing Census Report. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020. 

There are over 600 enumeration areas on the 3 main islands of Seychelles; this data set focuses on the enumeration areas on Mahé. Enumeration areas are composed of approximately 50-70 dwelling units each. The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households. 

The female share of the population was calculated by dividing the number of females in an enumeration area by the population of the respective enumeration area and converted into a percentage. This data represents the percentage of the population in each enumeration area that identifies as female.

attributes.description:
It is a vector layer corresponding to tree coverage at the country level, obtained as a result of the restitution made with the production of orthoimages between 2015 and even 2018, whose formal flight began operations on November 19, 2014. It is part of the project 2013LN-000002-00100 "Recruitment for the taking of images and the production of ortho images and digital cartography of the entire national territory", with the aim of updating the existing photogrammetric products at 1:5,000 scale. The main reason for the project was the taking of images for the production of orthophotos and digital cartography of the entire continental National Territory and the spatial expansion of Coco Island and Caño Island, at 1:1,000 scale in urban areas and 1:5,000 in the rest of the country.

Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Satellite Measurements
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²).

  
  
Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 

  
  
1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor.

  
  
2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset.

  
  
3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo.

  
  
The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.functions: Average monthly density of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) in the troposphere
info.cautions:
- The current surface albedo climatology used has a spatial resolution of 0.5° x 0.5° (approximately 55 x 55 km), which is coarse compared to the much higher spatial resolution used by S5p TROPOMI of 3.5 x 5.5 km. As a consequence, the albedo grid affects the NO₂ column products quality, especially in coastal areas.

  
  
- In general, TROPOMI underestimates the tropospheric NO₂ densities at polluted sites. The median negative biases of the daily comparisons are generally less than 50% (the product requirement for tropospheric NO₂), but can be quite variable depending on station and NO₂ level. 

  
  
- Good coherence is found between TROPOMI and Multi Axis Differential Absorption Spectroscopy (MAX-DOAS) NO₂ datasets with a correlation coefficient of 0.84.
  
  
- For more information on the data quality, please see the [product readme file](https://sentinel.esa.int/documents/247904/3541451/Sentinel-5P-Nitrogen-Dioxide-Level-2-Product-Readme-File).

attributes.name: Origin Countries of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Origin Countries of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons dataset shows the populations of concern that originate from each country worldwide. This dataset utilizes a subset of the categories used in the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees’ (UNHCR) definition for populations of concern and includes refugees, asylum-seekers, internally displaced persons (IDPs), stateless persons, and others of concern. The dataset is available for every year from 1951 to 2020 at a national spatial resolution. It shows the results in millions of people.

  
  
[According to the UNHCR](https://www.unhcr.org/en-us/figures-at-a-glance.html), there are over 70 million persons forcibly displaced worldwide. This includes 25.9 million refugees, 41.3 million IDPs, 3.5 million asylum seekers, and over 3.9 million stateless people. Out of the world’s displaced people, 80% live in countries or territories affected by acute food insecurity and around 13 million are people under the age of 18. 

  
  
The dataset is part of the UNHCR’s [population statistics database](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/). It was created as a way to provide open source data on populations of concern. Data on a person's country of residence or origin and their status (refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, etc.) are included. The UNHCR uses the information to help meet their mission of working to ensure that everybody has the right to seek asylum and find safe refuge in another country.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The UNHCR’s population statistics database provides information on people of concern’s country of residence or origin and their status. It was created and is updated using information from reliable sources including censuses, government reports, international agencies, and UNHCR estimates. The [populations of concern](https://www.unhcr.org/en-us/statistics/country/45c06c662/unhcr-statistical-online-population-database-sources-methods-data-considerations.html#refugees) used in the database include:

1. Refugees: Individuals recognized under the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees; its 1967 protocol; the 1969 Organization of African Unity Convention Governing the Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa; the definition contained in the 1984 Cartagena Declaration on Refugees; those recognized in accordance with the UNHCR statute; individuals granted complementary forms of protection; or those enjoying temporary protection. Since 2007, the refugee population also includes people in refugee-like situations.
 
2. Asylum-seekers: Individuals who have sought international protection and whose claims for refugee status have not yet been determined, irrespective of when they may have been lodged.
 
3. Internally displaced persons (IDPs): people or groups of individuals forced to leave their homes or places of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of, armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights, or natural or man-made disasters, and who have not crossed an international border. For the purposes of the UNHCR's statistics, this population only includes conflict-generated IDPs to whom the UNHCR extends protection and/or assistance. Since 2007, the IDP population also includes people in an IDP-like situation. For global IDP estimates, see [www.internal-displacement.org](https://www.internal-displacement.org/).
 
4. Returned refugees: Former refugees who have returned to their country of origin spontaneously or in an organized fashion but are yet to be fully integrated. Such return would ideally take place in conditions of safety and dignity.
 
5. Returned IDPs: IDPs who were beneficiaries of the UNHCR's protection and assistance activities and who returned to their areas of origin or habitual residence during the year.
 
6. Stateless persons: Defined under the 1954 Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons as those not considered as nationals by any state under the operation of its law. In other words, they do not possess the nationality of any state. UNHCR statistics refer to persons who fall under the agency’s statelessness mandate because they are stateless according to this international definition, but data from some countries may also include persons with undetermined nationality.
 
7. Others of concern: Individuals who do not necessarily fall directly into any of the groups above, but to whom the UNHCR extends its protection and/or assistance services, based on humanitarian or other special grounds. 

  
  
The dataset was created by adding these individual categories together to show the populations of these groups that have left each country. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows UNHCR data on the [Host Countries of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc043a-Host-Countries-Refugees-and-Displaced-Persons).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Further data on returned refugees and returned IDPs are available, as well as the status of current asylum seekers shown as monthly and yearly values. Additionally, data for every year between 1951 and 2017 are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: cit.038.nrt Air Quality - Modeled Forecast - WACCM (Black Carbon)
Air Quality: Black Carbon Modeled Next-day Forecast
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted black carbon (BC) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). Black carbon is a particulate emitted from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels and biomass. Major [sources include](https://www.c2es.org/document/what-is-black-carbon/) diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, cook stoves, wood burning and forest fires. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research), black carbon is a “global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate.”  
  
Inhalation of black carbon is associated with [cardiovascular disease, respiratory problems, cancer, and even birth defects](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research). Black carbon makes up a significant portion of particulate matter pollution.  
  
Although black carbon is not a greenhouse gas, it contributes to climate change in a few ways. Its dark color absorbs solar radiation, which warms up the atmosphere. Black carbon also settles on snow and ice, darkening these surfaces that would normally reflect a lot of solar radiation. According to research published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo473), black carbon may have caused more than 30% of the recent rapid warming in the Arctic.   
  
WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted black carbon concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps.  
  
WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution.  
  
### Methodology  
  
WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). 
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_038_waccm_atmospheric_chemistry_model).  
  
### Disclaimer

attributes.name: ene.004 Renewable Energy Share of Total Energy Consumption
Percentage of Energy Consumption from Renewable Sources
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the percentage of total final energy consumption(TFEC) that comes from renewable sources in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. 

  
  
The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. 


  
  
Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database.  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was compiled using data from IEA and UNSD. Renewable energy consumption was divided by total final energy consumption to calculate the share of renewable energy in the total final energy consumption of each country.

  
  
Renewable energy consumption was defined as the final consumption of renewables plus the amount of electricity and heat consumption estimated to have come from renewable energy sources. Total final energy consumption was defined as the sum of the final energy consumption in the transport, industry, residential, services, and other sectors. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database.   
  
 Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data related to electricity access and renewable energy electricity is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: wat.064 Cost of Sustainable Water Management
Cost of Sustainable Water Management
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset represents the cost of action to deliver sustainable water management as outlined in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 6(SDG6). The datasets presented on Resource Watch encompass the water challenges within SDG6 and show the cost percentage each category requires out of the total cost to achieve sustainable water management. Total Estimated Cost is the annual cost in 2015 USD to deliver on each aspect of sustainable water management, calculated for each country as the cost of action required to close the gap between current and desired conditions.

  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to provide a visual representation of the cost to achieve sustainable water management. Water related issues are already a serious concern and will only worsen given the combined effects of population growth, economic growth, and climate change. SDG6 works to “ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all” by 2030. Sustainable water management includes access to drinking water, access to sanitation services, water pollution, water scarcity, and water management. Each of these categories has specific "estimated cost"  and its percentage of the "total estimated cost" can communicate the relative magnitude of the issue, from a financial perspective. This cost does not fully account for the social and economic benefits of resolving each water challenge and should not be used to inform local policy decisions.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset calculates the cost of action to close the gap between current and desired sustainable water management conditions by 2030. Where possible, the calculation method builds off of existing research and methods rather than developing new approaches to calculating the cost of action. The dataset shows values for the total estimated cost to deliver drinking water, deliver access to sanitation services, eliminate industrial water pollution, eliminate agricultural water pollution, address water scarcity, and address water resource management. Each of these categories was created using the formula below:
  
  
Total Estimated Cost = Projected Gap x Solution Cost
                                                                                                                                                    
  
The projected gap is the gap between current and desired conditions. The solution cost is the cost, in 2015 US dollars, that it will take to change each unit of the current condition to the desired condition for the population in 2030. 

  
  
Water management is a quantity that is based on population, so to determine the amount of water required for the population in 2030 estimated population data was taken from 2030 gridded population data in Downscaling Drivers of Global Environmental Change: Enabling Use of Global SRES Scenarios at the National and Grid Levels (Hutton and Varughese 2016). Values for the solution cost of creating access to drinking water and sanitation were taken from the World Bank for 140 low-income countries and estimated for all other countries. Solution costs for industrial water pollution were taken from Hutton and Varughese 2016, for agricultural water pollution from a combination of eight academic articles, and for water scarcity from 2030 Water Resources Group (WRG) reports. The proposed method was designed to be reproducible with data at any scale, however this dataset has been developed using global, comparable data. For full discussion of the calculation method, see the Achieving Abundance Technical Appendix.

  
  
The final datasets were presented as the percentage of costs to achieve each individual form of water management out of the total cost of water management by 2030. The datasets were projected on a global map at a national resolution using vector format. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/resources/data-sets/achieving-abundance).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
The percentage of the total estimated cost to address water resources management is 17% for each country, but this indicator was not shown on Resource Watch map. Please click on the “Table” button in the “Customize Visualization” section to find this data on Resource Watch.  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_064_cost_of_sustainable_water_management).

There are many pathways to resolving existing water challenges, and this dataset has developed only one pathway. The pathway proposed relies on global models that do not fully reflect local data, policy, or other contextual factors. The proposed method may be replicated on a local level with more precise data, but this dataset should not be used to inform local decisions on water resource management.

- This dataset calculates the cost of action, but does not discuss the financing mechanisms used to deliver funding to achieve these costs, whether from public sector, private sector, tariffs, or other financing mechanisms.

- Data used to determine sanitation and water access costs assumes that current water related infrastructure is fully functional and working at maximum capacity. Additionally, access rates are assessed differently in each country. Lastly, the data used for these values were only for 140 countries and the rest of the world rates were estimated using rates from similar countries.

- The costs calculated to reduce water scarcity were estimated based on each country's purchasing power parity and cost of the most efficient water saving solutions. It does not consider that some water saving solutions are not viable in every country.

attributes.name: Fires
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes near-real-time active fires as points that represent the center of a 375 m resolution pixel and is being updated twice daily. 

  
  
The data is collected from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) sensor on Suomi-National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi-NPP) satellite. 

  
  
This dataset is provided through the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) Fire Email Alerts. This dataset provides improved response for smaller fires, mapping of large fire perimeters, and better detection at night, when fire activities usually occur. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of detection. This dataset is well suited for use in near-real time alert systems, fire tracking, and management. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Fire detections are determined using a multispectral contextual algorithm to identify subpixel fire activity and other thermal anomalies in the Level 1 (swath) input data. The algorithm uses all five 375 m VIIRS channels to detect fires and separate land, water, and cloud pixels in the image. Fire locations are then given as the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm.

  
  
The algorithm first screens for cloud and water pixels. Next potential fires are found using criteria based on brightness detected by the channels. These fires are then filtered by the algorithm to find the distinct radiometric signatures associated with active fires. Finally custom filters are applied to reduce false alarm rates. False alarms usually come from areas of high solar reflection such as metallic rooftops in industrial parks or bright surfaces such as concrete pavement.

  
  
Confidence values are available for each fire detection. They are based on a collection of intermediate algorithm quantities used in the detection process and are intended to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot/fire pixels. Confidence values are set to low, nominal, and high. Low confidence daytime fire pixels are typically associated with areas of sun glint and lower relative temperature anomaly (<15K) in the mid-infrared channel I4. Nominal confidence pixels are those free of potential sun glint contamination during the day and marked by strong (>15K) temperature anomaly in either day or nighttime data. High confidence fire pixels are associated with day or nighttime saturated pixels.

  
  
For the full documentation of the initial algorithm methodology, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425713004483).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Resource Watch displays the most recent fires in the past week. Data older than the last seven days or within the temporal coverage of January 20, 2012, to the present is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.

Not all fires are detected. There are several reasons why VIIRS may not have detected a certain fire. The fire may have started and ended between satellite overpasses. The fire may have been too small or too cool to be detected in the 375 m pixel. Cloud cover, heavy smoke, or tree canopy may completely obscure a fire. It is not recommended to use active fire locations to estimate burned area due to spatial and temporal sampling issues.

attributes.name: Plastic Inputs from Rivers into Oceans
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows a global estimate of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans for 2010, expressed in kilograms per year. The authors used data on waste management, population density, and hydrological information to create this model. The dataset includes information on 40,760 watersheds and 182 different countries. The data is presented in a vector format. 
  
  
Plastic pollution in our oceans and on our coastlines have become a major threat to ocean health worldwide. A better understanding and quantification of marine plastic sources can help in implementing mitigation strategies to alleviate the issue. The dataset can help in identifying places that require higher attention in terms of plastic waste monitoring and mitigation plans. This data can also be used as a baseline measurement for ocean plastic mass balance exercises. 
  
  
This data was developed by researchers funded by The Ocean Cleanup Foundation. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The amount of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans was estimated by using data on mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) per country, population density, topographic elevation, and location of artificial barriers (weirs and dams).
  
  
For each catchment area mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) rates per day were calculated by combining data on waste generation by inhabitant per day and population density for the area. This data was combined with water flow per river catchment area to provide a final value for the mass of plastic released at the river’s mouth. This data was extrapolated using seasonal variations in water flow to create a year dataset. Data on population density was derived from the dataset Global 15 x 15 Minute Grids of the Downscaled Population by the Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) for 182 countries. Data used to calculate MPW rates were collected from seven peer reviewed studies. Topographic information was taken from Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) hydrological model for surface/subsurface runoff and location of artificial barriers was taken from AquaStat and Global Reservoir and Dam Database (GRanD).
  
  
In total the dataset includes information for 40,760 watersheds worldwide. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15611#Sec6).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for plastic input in tonnes per year, plastic input in tonnes per month, and average monthly water runoff in catchment area in mm per day are also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.

info.name: Plastic Inputs from Rivers into Oceans
info.technical_title: River Plastic Emissions to the World's Oceans
info.functions: Global estimate of river plastic discharge into the world’s oceans for 2010
info.cautions:
The study considers only debris larger than their net mesh sizes (usually 0.3 mm) and smaller than the aperture size of their sampling devices (usually 0.5 m). Debris outside of this size range are neglected in this study, but they can still enter the ocean in extreme events such as turbulent river flows and large flood events. 
  
  
The studies reviewed to calculate MPW rates were based on only buoyant plastic on the surface of rivers. They did not consider buoyant plastic below the surface that may have submerged from turbulent waters. Additionally, they do not consider non-buoyant plastic that may eventually make it to the ocean through strong turbulents or water movement.  The model assumes that all types of plastic materials are trapped by artificial obstacles such as dams, but in reality, the trap efficiency of these barriers is based on a variety of factors.
  
  
There is inherently a large amount of uncertainty when dealing with plastic in water systems. Plastic degradation and deposition are still poorly understood topics and likely play an important role in plastic movement in freshwater ecosystems.
