attributes.name: Positive Peace Index
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Positive Peace Index (PPI) is a quantitative approach to measure Positive Peace. Positive Peace is defined as the attitudes, institutions, and structures that lead to a more peaceful society. A country with a higher PPI is more capable of building and maintaining peace. 

  
  
The Positive Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure a country’s success in building and maintaining peace.  Positive peace is used to create resilient and adaptive communities that prevent conflict and help societies channel disagreements productively. The framework for PPI is based on eight domains:

  
  
1. *Acceptance of the Rights of Others:* This requires countries to have formal laws that can guarantee basic human rights and freedoms, ensure gender equality, and worker’s rights.
  
  
2. *Equitable Distribution of Resources:* This ensures everyone has equal access to resources, such as education and health.
  
  
3. *Free Flow of Information:* This is measured by the extent to which citizens can gain access to information, whether the media is free and independent, and how well-informed citizens are.
  
  
4. *Good Relations with Neighbours:* A country’s relationship with other countries is an important indicator of how peaceful and politically stable the country is.
  
  
5. *High Levels of Human Capital:*  The employment rate among young citizens and the number of people engaged in research activities shows the level of social capital in a country.
  
  
6. *Low Levels of Corruption:*  High levels of corruption leads to a shortage of funding for essential services, which creates unrest in a society.
  
  
7. *Sound Business Environment:*  This is measured by the presence of regulatory systems and formal institutions in a country to support a good business environment.
  
  
8. *Well-Functioning Government:*  A government that delivers high-quality public and civil services, creates trust and participation, maintains political stability, and promotes the rule of law is necessary for a peaceful country.

  
  
The PPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2009 to 2018 for 163 countries covering 99.6% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand and make progress towards global peacefulness along with other interrelated areas such as:  improved economic productivity and social advancement.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Positive Peace Index (PPI) uses 24 indicators in eight domains to measure Positive Peace. The eight domains range from the flow of information within a country to levels of corruption. PPI is interconnected to the Global Peace Index (GPI) which is another measurement for global peacefulness. GPI is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence in a country. The internal measures of the Global Peace Index were statistically compared to approximately 25,000 national data series, indices, and attitudinal surveys to determine the initial set of indicators for Positive Peace Index. These indicators were then qualitatively assessed. If there were multiple indicators for similar cases, the least important ones were discarded. 

  
  
Finally, the remaining indicators were aggregated into the eight domains of Positive Peace and given a correlation coefficient to their value in GPI using statistical approaches. The correlation coefficient represented how important the indicators were in the PPI measurement compared to GPI. The correlation coefficient was used to weight GPI Internal Peace scores for each indicator and create a final score out of 5.  For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/10/PPR-2019-web.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_092_positive_peace_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

Urban Extent for Select Cities
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the physical urban extent and population of a global random sample of 200 cities, circa 2014. The urban extent of a city was defined as the extent of a city’s contiguous built-up area. While these extents can cover large areas and multiple municipalities, they often represent one shared labor market. 

  
  
This dataset was created as part of the Atlas of Urban Expansion, which aims to monitor both the quantitative and qualitative aspects of urban expansion using a globally representative sample of 200 cities. Having the physical extents of a large sample of global cities provides a powerful tool to analyze urbanization trends on a global scale. In addition to monitoring the urban extent of these cities, this dataset includes information on the population, built-up area, walkability, and numerous other variables. The data source also provides data for urban extents circa 1990 and circa 2000.

  
  
This dataset was published by the New York University Urban Expansion Program at the Marron Institute of Urban Management and the Stern School of Business of New York University, in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy.   
  
### Methodology  
  
To create this dataset, the authors first identified cities that had a population of 100,000 or more people. They compiled 2010 population data for cities across the world, using population data from the United Nations Population Division and the [City Population website](http://www.citypopulation.de/). They identified 4,231 global cities that met this criterion.

  
  
The authors then selected the 200 cities included in this dataset with a stratified sampling method, which  was used to ensure that cities of varying sizes, from all regions, and from large and small countries were well-represented. Cities were randomly selected from eight world regions in proportion to the urban population in each region. The eight world regions were
- East Asia and Pacific; 
- Southeast Asia; 
- South and Central Asia; 
- Western Asia and North Africa; 
- Sub-Saharan Africa; 
- Latin America and the Caribbean;
- Europe and Japan; and 
- Land-Rich Developed countries 

  
  
After selecting a representative sample of 200 cities, researchers identified the urban extent of each city. The urban extent was defined as the extent of a city’s built-up area, rather than by its administrative or jurisdictional boundaries.  Each urban extent can cover a large area of land and multiple municipalities, but often share  a single labor market. The geographical extent is typically associated with the name of its largest and most prominent historical center. Researchers created the urban extent data by digitizing and analyzing high-resolution satellite imagery. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.lincolninst.edu/sites/default/files/pubfiles/atlas-of-urban-expansion-2016-volume-1-full.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the average population density of city extent, the fragmentation of the built-up area by open spaces, the compactness of the overall geographic shape, and the shares of infill, extension, leapfrog, and inclusion in the added built-up areas within new urban extent is available from the data provider. This data is available for three time periods: circa 1990, circa 2000, and circa 2014. Data related to blocks and roads is also available. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This dataset was retrieved from AidData GeoQuery. The general steps used to download this dataset are described [here](https://www.aiddata.org/blog/urban-boundaries-for-200-cities-added-to-aiddatas-geoquery-tool), and the specific query used to download the data shown on Resource Watch can be found [here](http://geo.aiddata.org/query/#!/search/atlasofurbanexpansion2016/atlasofurbanexpansion2016_urban_edge_t3).   
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.functions: The percentage of each country's population who have used the internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc.
info.cautions: Operators have traditionally been the main source of telecommunications data, so information on subscriptions has been widely available for most countries. This gives a general idea of access, but a more precise measure is the penetration rate - the share of households with access to telecommunications. During the past few years more information on information and communication technology use has become available from household and business surveys. Also important are data on actual use of telecommunications services. Ideally, statistics on telecommunications (and other information and communications technologies) should be compiled for all three measures: subscriptions, access, and use. The quality of data varies among reporting countries as a result of differences in regulations covering data provision and availability. Discrepancies may also arise in cases where the end of a fiscal year differs from that used by ITU, which is the end of December of every year. A number of countries have fiscal years that end in March or June of every year.

attributes.name: bio.047b Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquitoe Aedes albopictus
Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes albopictus
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmission by one of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible under baseline conditions, as well as in the years 2050 and 2080. The mosquito is *Aedes albopictus*, and it transmits diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the baseline temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change  scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. On Resource Watch, we display the RCP 8.5 which is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century.

  
  
According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. 


  
  
The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows temperature suitability data for one of the other most common-disease-carrying mosquitoes, [*Aedes aegypti*](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio047a-Temperature-Suitability-for-Disease-Carrying-Mosquitoe-Aedes-aegypti).   
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate,  human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data.

  
  
As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for three other climate change scenarios (RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 6.0), as well as results produced by different climate models, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes albopictus
info.technical_title:
Global expansion and redistribution of Aedes-borne
virus transmission risk with climate change
info.functions: The number of months per year the temperature is suitable for disease-carrying mosquito Aedes albopictus
info.cautions: No models can precisely predict the global climate suitability for transmission risk. Models used in this dataset only set an outer spatiotemporal bound on where transmission is thermally plausible, given climate projections. Other environmental, biological, and social factors can also impact disease transmission by mosquitoes. In addition, the relationship between climate change and burdens of diseases carried by mosquitoes is a complex process. Climate change is likely to change the relationship between transmission risk and disease burden at fine scales within those zones of transmission nonlinearly, such that areas with shorter seasons of transmission could still experience increased overall disease burdens, or vice versa.
info.citation: Ryan, S.J., C.J. Carlson, E.A. Mordecai, L.R. Johnson. 2019. “Global Expansion and Redistribution of Aedes-Borne Virus Transmission Risk with Climate Change.” PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 13 (3): e0007213. Accessed through Resource Watch, (date). [www.resourcewatch.org](https://www.resourcewatch.org).

attributes.name: Certified Commodity Crops
attributes.description:
The Certified Commodity Crops Map, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), is the first global data set showing the distribution of commodity crop certification. Crop certification helps consumers purchase more ethical products that come from farms that promote social equality and sustainability. However, these certifications are not well represented in some of the poorest countries of the world or in the tropical rainforests that are at the greatest risk. This map allows users to view the spatial distribution of global crop certification.
The locations of certified farms came from publicly available datasets or by directly contacting standards bodies. Certification data from all major standards and codes of practice were included (4C, Bird-friendly coffee, Bonsucro, Etanol Verde, Fairtrade, ISCC, Rainforest Alliance, Roundtable Responsible Soy, Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices and UTZ). The seven most certified crops (banana, cocoa, coffee, tea, soybean, sugar and palm oil) were mapped.
Coordinates and postal addresses were used to identify point locations of each scheme. Postal addresses were converted to coordinates using ESRI Online World Geocode service. Data cleaning was performed to ensure points were located in their listed country and fell within the crop growing area, identified by a crop cover map.
Some data permissions were granted under the condition that they be aggregated with other standards so that specific certification schemes and crop producers could not be identified. Therefore, data were aggregated at a 30 km x 30 km resolution. Certification data came from the years 2013, 2014 and 2015. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Urban Built-Up Area
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Human Settlement (GHS) built-up dataset provides a global estimation of built-up area between 1975 and 2014. It is available for four time periods: 1975, 1975-1990, 1990-2000, and 2000-2014. Built-up areas represent any urbanized regions containing man-made structures, like buildings. The dataset is based on Landsat imaging and analyzed using a model. The data is available at 30 m, 250 m and 1 km resolution in the source dataset. The 30 m version of the data is displayed here. 
  
  
GHS built-up dataset was released by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (EC JRC). This dataset provides an insight into the human presence on Earth. It is important to understand the pattern of cities' growth. It is projected that 68% of the world’s population will live in urban areas by 2050. This information can help governments create more sustainable urbanization policies and have a more long-term plan for urban growth in the future.  
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was produced by processing 33,202 satellite images using the Symbolic Machine Learning (SML) method. Each year corresponded to a different source of Landsat data, GLS 1975, GLS 1990, GLS 2000, and ad hoc Landsat 8 collection 2013/2014. The image data records collected by different satellite sensors between 1975 and 2014 were classified and automatically selected if they corresponded to a built-up structure. The information was analyzed using the GHS built-up model. The model utilized algorithms to extract patterns and determine the spatial size of the building surface area. It analyzed knowledge from large amounts of spatial data, and the availability of open and free image data input, to identify areas of the planet with high densities of built-up areas. This dataset was an improved version from the 2015 GHS built-up dataset. It used an improved image processing workflow that allowed for the detection of more built-up areas and reduced the amount of false identifications of built-up areas in the final classification. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/data.php).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for water surface and land with no built-up in any epoch are also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cit_033a_urban_builtup_area).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.technical_title: GHS-BUILT
info.functions: Global measure of built-up presence between 1975 and 2014
info.cautions:
There was a lack of image data from the 1975 collection, which led to unstable classification in some geographies. This error in classification was particularly apparent in places with an abundance of vegetation, regardless of being inside or outside urban areas. The1975 results need to be interpreted with caution.
  
  
There was a saturation of information in built-up areas greater than about 10 pixels (300 m). The electromagnetic radiation data from satellite images that was used as the primary source for the built-up area classification prioritized urban structures and had less focus on urban area morphology or texture. Therefore, the classification between built-up and roads that are in close proximity to each other are expected to be rather inconsistent. However, the latest improvement in the learning data set might reduce these errors to some extent.

attributes.name: ocn.027a.rw0 Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas
Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, models human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. When human sewage flows into coastal waters it contributes to increased nitrogen levels and pathogens in coastal systems. This dataset quantifies and maps the flow of nitrogen and pathogen input to the ocean from nearly 135,000 watersheds using a high-resolution geospatial model. The sources of nitrogen inputs are separated by source into treated (sewered systems), septic, and untreated (open defecation) inputs. The dataset provides global rasters of the modeled plume, or extent, of the nitrogen in coastal waters. Nitrogen plume data is shown at ~1 km resolution. 

  
  
Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters. Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management.  

  
  
The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this dataset to inform marine conservation and public health work. The model allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources with traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Nitrogen concentration (grams/yr) was modeled using a high-resolution geospatial model. Population and settlement data were grouped into rural and urban classes. These data were then combined with national-level statistics on protein consumption and the proportion of the population’s access to various types of wastewater treatment facilities. Wastewater treatment types were grouped into three categories - open defecation (untreated), septic tanks (septic), or some level of sewered treatment. The three sewage treatment categories of nitrogen were assigned a nitrogen removal efficiency based on literature. The model assumed that populations with inputs from septic tanks or open defecation that are more than 1km away from surface waters and coastlines do not contribute to effluent totals. 

  
  
The dispersion of the wastewater pollution into the ocean was then modeled from each basin’s pourpoint, which describes the location where freshwater enters the ocean. For each watershed with a pourpoint draining into the ocean, nitrogen inputs were calculated by summing the values for all grid cells falling within the watershed boundary and this value was assigned to the corresponding coastal pourpoint. At each pourpoint, the level of nitrogen was spread into the coastal waters using a plume model based on a logarithmic decay function. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also provides data on nitrogen inputs at the watershed level in [Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/784732cc-8e7e-4dac-be51-d4506ff2ee04) and for the associated coastal “pourpoint” or the location where the watershed empties into the ocean in  [Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5bf349ec-3b14-4021-a7d4-fc4b8104bd74). 
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.   
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/ocn_027a_rw0_nitrogen_plumes/).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

sources.source-description: National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS)

info.technical_title: Global Inputs and Impacts from of Human Sewage in Coastal Ecosystems
info.functions: Modeled annual Nitrogen input from human sewage into coastal areas
info.cautions:
- The model does not fully account for differences in land cover, watershed size, ecosystem processes, sanitation efficiency, and other biogeochemical processes. This may lead to overestimation of impacts in coastal ecosystems with slow-flowing water, and underestimation for areas with rapid flush times.
  
  
- Data on the location of most septic systems and sewer outfalls were modeled not observed and did not include information on septic failure rates or permitted or accidental sewer overflow events. This adds uncertainty to the model, and potentially underestimates the impacts of nitrogen given the high rates of septic tank failure.
  
  
- For treated nitrogen, the model may overestimate actual nitrogen removal rates by treatment plants, leading to underestimation of impacts in the model.
info.citation: Tuholske C, Halpern BS, Blasco G, Villasenor JC, Frazier M, Caylor K (2021) Mapping global inputs and impacts from human sewage in coastal ecosystems. attributes.name: Global Peace Index
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Peace Index (GPI) is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence to assess a nation’s level of peace. This lack of violence is defined as Negative Peace. A higher GPI represents a higher level of violence in a country.

  
  
The Global Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure global peacefulness. Its goal is to create understanding on the effects of violence and help countries develop the means to create peaceful societies. It measures a country’s level of Negative Peace using three domains of peacefulness:

  
  
1. *The extent of Ongoing Domestic and International Conflict:* This investigates the extent to which countries are involved in internal and external conflicts, as well as their role and duration of involvement in conflicts. This is based on six indicators, such as the number and duration of internal conflicts, number of deaths from external organized conflicts, and relationships with neighboring countries.

  
  
2. *The level of Societal Safety and Security:* It evaluates the level of harmony or discord within a nation using ten indicators. These indicators include topics like the level of perceived criminality in society, impact of terrorism, and political instability.

  
  
3. *The degree of Militarisation:* Militarisation refers to a country’s military build-up and access to weapons. This is determined by using seven indicators, such as military expenditure as a percentage of GDP, number of armed services personnel per 100,000 people, and nuclear and heavy weapons capabilities.

  
  
The GPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2008 to 2019 for 163 countries or independent territories covering 99.7% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand the economic value and trends of peace, and how to develop peaceful societies.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Peace Index uses 23 indicators in three domains to quantify the absence of violence or fear of violence. An international panel of independent experts helped to select the indicators in 2007 and reviews them on an annual basis. These 23 indicators were weighted and combined into two categories to create an overall score for GPI out of 100. The total GPI score was then simplified into a value of 1-5, with 5 being the highest amount of violence or fear being present within a country. The two overarching categories were a measure of how peaceful a country is internally and a measure of how peaceful a country is externally.  The value of these two categories out of the total GPI value was 40% for external peace and 60% for internal peace.  The weighting scheme was selected based on the relative importance of each indicator to achieve global peace.

  
  
All scores for each indicator were normalized on a scale of 1-5. Qualitative indicators were banded into five groupings relevant to the indicator. Quantitative indicators were scored continuously  based on relevant data and rounded to the third decimal point. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s team of country analysts scored seven of the eight qualitative indicators and also provided estimates about the gaps in the quantitative data. Scoring for qualitative indicators followed a strict set of guidelines to ensure reliability between values. Quantitative values were taken from a variety of international and government organizations. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/07/GPI-2019web.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_091_global_peace_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.  
  
### Disclaimer

attributes.name: Fire Weather
attributes.description:
The Fire Weather data set is derived from the Fire Weather Index (FWI) System, which was developed by the Canadian Forest Service and is the most widely used fire danger rating system in the world. The Global Fire WEather Database (GFWED) is a global database of daily FWI System calculations, produced by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies. This system combines different weather factors that may influence the start and spread of a vegetation fire and is comprised of three moisture codes and three fire behavior indices. The moisture codes describe the moisture content of three general fuel classes. The fire behavior indices describe the rate of spread, fuel consumption and intensity of a fire if it were to start. 

  
  
 The data inputs for these calculations are measurements of 12:00 local time temperature at 2 m, relative humidity at 2 m and wind speed at 10 m. Daily snow-depth and precipitation were totaled over the previous 24 hours. GFWED includes several different versions of these calculations, each of which uses a different input weather and precipitation data. The version of these calculations shown on Resource Watch uses input data from GEOS-5 for temperature, relative humidity, wind-speed and snow depth; input precipitation comes from the 'Late' version of GPM IMERG Daily Precipitation. Global daily calculations of the FWI System indices using these data inputs are available from 2015 to present with 0.1° resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: wat.033 Agricultural Exposure to Water Stress
attributes.subtitle: WRI

attributes.name: Agricultural Exposure to Water Stress
attributes.description:
This map of baseline water stress in major crop producing areas was created by WRI's Aqueduct program as part of the Water Risk Atlas, an online mapping tool that displays various aspects of water-related risks. The map displays the major crop producing areas for 13 major commodity crops (cocoa, coffee, cotton, maize, oats, oil palm, oranges, canola, rice, rubber, soybeans, sugarcane, and wheat) and 9 crop groups (cereals, fiber crops, fodder crops, fruits, oil crops, legumes, roots and tubers, sugar crops, and tree nuts), and the levels of water stress (low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high) experienced in these major crop-producing areas. Baseline water stress refers to the annual water withdrawals (municipal, industrial, and agricultural) expressed as a percentage of the total annual available flow. Higher values indicate more competition among users. Arid areas with low water use are shown in gray but scored as high stress when calculating aggregated scores. 

Baseline water stress is calculated by dividing water withdrawals (2010) by mean available blue water (1950-2008). Areas with available blue water and water withdrawal less than 0.03 and 0.012/m2 respectively are coded as “arid and low water use." Crop production in each category is computed by overlaying gridded crop production data, which was pulled from 2 articles in Global Biogeochemical Cycle (2008), "Farming the Planet: 1. Geographic Distribution of Global Agricultural Lands in the Year 2000" and "Farming the Planet: 2. Geographic Distribution of Crop Areas, Yields, Physiological Types, and Net Primary Production in the Year 2000." The authors of these studies identified croplands and crop production using a high-resolution satellite-derived land cover data set and agricultural inventory data to derive a global map of croplands. 

PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.description: Ces données présentent les forets communautaires. Elles font partis des dispositifs prévus par la loi forestière de 1994 pour faciliter la participation des communautés locales à la gestion durable et équitable des ressources naturelles, et leur accès au bénéficies socioéconomiques de ces ressources. Elles sont attribuées dans le domaine non permanent et gérées par les communautés et peuvent mesures jusqu’à 5000 hectares. Les données de cette couche sont mises à jour continuellement suivant la disponibilité des nouveaux documents officiels à savoir les conventions provisoires de gestion et plans simples de gestion et les conventions définitives de gestion dont les descriptifs sont faits à base des cartes topographiques ( fond INC) à l'échelle de 1:200 000. les donnees les plus recentes datent de 2013.Néanmoins, il est important de préciser que la qualité de ces données peut varier en fonction des sources. Cette couche ne garantit pas la présence exhaustive de toutes forêts communautaires présentes dans le pays et la localisation de certaines forêts communautaires peut être imprécise.

Les données de cette couche sont mises à jour continuellement suivant la disponibilité des nouveaux documents officiels à savoir les conventions provisoires de gestion et plans simples de gestion et les conventions définitives de gestion dont les descriptifs sont faits à base des cartes topographiques ( fond INC) à l'échelle de 1:200 000. les donnees les plus recentes datent de 2013.Néanmoins, il est important de préciser que la qualité de ces données peut varier en fonction des sources. attributes.name: req.011 Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Modeled 5-day Forecast - March 1-15
Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Modeled 5-day Forecast
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). PM2.5 is an air pollutant made up of fine inhalable particles, with diameters of 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks, or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants and automobiles.  
  
The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/health-and-environmental-effects-particulate-matter-pm), exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing, or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by fine particulate exposure.  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators.  
  
GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model.  
  
To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module.  
  
All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). 
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere is also produced by GEOS-CF. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Seychelles Literacy Rates
attributes.description:
This data set displays the rates of literacy per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics 2010 Population and Housing Census Report. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020. 

There are over 600 enumeration areas on the 3 main islands of Seychelles; this data set focuses on the enumeration areas on Mahé. Enumeration areas are composed of approximately 50-70 dwelling units each. The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households.  	 		

The literacy rates were calculated by dividing the number of literate individuals in an enumeration area by the population of the respective enumeration area and converted to a percentage. This data represents the percentage of the population in each enumeration area that is classified as literate.

attributes.name: cli.003.rw0 Future Precipitation Suitability for Coffee Growth
Future Precipitation Suitability for Coffee Growth
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
These maps show the probability that annual precipitation will be within or outside the range necessary for the growth of coffee (Coffea arabica), as calculated by researchers at World Resources Institute using a combination of historical satellite data and climate simulations of future precipitation. Users can choose to see probabilities of insufficient precipitation, excessive precipitation, or precipitation within coffee’s required range. Because they are probabilities, pixel values range from 0 to 1. Probabilities are available for any location on the globe, for every 10 years from 2020 to 2099. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 0.25 arc degrees, which is approximately 25 kilometers (km) x 25 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. 
 
Like all agricultural crops, coffee can grow only in locations that meet particular climatic requirements. Coffee requires between 750 mm and 4200 mm of precipitation every year ([FAO ECOCROP]( https://gaez.fao.org/pages/ecocrop)). As global climate patterns change, the locations suitable for growing coffee are likely to shift. It is impossible to predict with certainty where coffee will and will not be able to be grown in the coming decades, but we are able to estimate the probability that any location is suitable. In these maps, we focus on suitability related to precipitation, but similar maps can be generated for coffee’s (and other crops’) temperature ranges, humidity ranges, and combinations of these factors. 
 
These maps were generated by the AgriAdapt team at World Resources Institute to support growers, processors, buyers, and investors in making long-term, climate-smart decisions about crops and growing locations.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The probabilities are calculated as Bayesian posterior probabilities that yearlong precipitation falls within or outside the range 750 mm – 4200 mm. The prior probability is taken from historical rainfall as reported in the [ERA5](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/CKB/ERA5%3A+data+documentation) reanalysis of satellite data. The prior is updated using the [NEX-GDDP](https://esgf.nccs.nasa.gov/esgdoc/NEX-GDDP_Tech_Note_v0.pdf) downscaled simulation ensemble as evidence. NEX-GDDP includes several greenhouse gas emission scenarios. These calculations used the highest-emitting scenario, RCP8.5. The probability rasters have a spatial resolution of 0.25 arc degrees (approximately 25 km at the equator). 
 
The full methodology will be published as a WRI Technical Note (Wong and Mackres, forthcoming).   
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Current and Projected Food Insecurity
attributes.description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Bathymetry
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Bathymetry dataset is composed of the GEBCO_2019 Grid, which shows terrain elevation around the world, for both land and the ocean floor. It provides global coverage on a 15 arc-second grid. The data values refer to elevations at the center of grid cells in meters.

  
  
The GEBCO_2019 Grid is the latest global bathymetric product released by the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO) and has been developed through the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO [Seabed 2030 Project](https://seabed2030.gebco.net/). This is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation of Japan and GEBCO. The Seabed 2030 Project aims to bring together all available bathymetric data to produce the definitive map of the world ocean floor and make it available to all.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The grid used Version 1 of the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) 15+ data set as a ‘base’. This dataset is a fusion of land topography with measured and estimated seafloor topography. It is largely based on version 11 of SRTM30+, augmented with the gridded bathymetric data sets developed by the four Seabed 2030 Regional Centers.

  
  
The Regional Centers compiled gridded bathymetric data sets for their areas of responsibility. These regional grids were then provided to the Global Center. For areas outside of the polar regions, these data sets are in the form of 'sparse grids,' meaning only grid cells that contain data were populated. For the polar regions, complete grids were provided due to the complexities of incorporating data held in polar coordinates.

  
  
The majority of the work, for the non-polar regions, was done using the 'remove-restore' procedure. This is a two stage process of computing the difference between the new data sets created by regional centers and the 'base' grid SRTM15+. The difference between the datasets was gridded and then added back to the existing 'base' grid. The aim was to achieve a smooth transition between the 'new' and 'base' data sets with minimum disturbance of the existing base data set. The polar and Red Sea datasets were supplied in the form of complete grids and were created using feather blending techniques from GlobalMapper software version 11.0.
  
  
The compilation of the GEBCO_2019 Grid from these regional data grids, with some additional source data sets, was carried out at the Global Center, with the aim of producing a seamless global terrain model. The global grid consists of 86,400 rows and 43,200 columns, giving 3,732,480,000 data points. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the Type Identifier Grid (TID) is available from the data provider. The TID identifies the type of source data that the corresponding grid cells in the GEBCO Grid are based on.  For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding & Sea Level Rise (m)
attributes.description:
The Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding and Sea-Level Rise data set is prepared by Climate Central. These layers are relative to local high tide lines (mean higher high water, or MHHW). Map areas below the selected water level are displayed in blue, indicating vulnerability to flooding from combined sea-level rise, storm surge, and tides, or to permanent submergence by long-term sea-level rise. Elevation data used for parts of this map within the United States come almost entirely from ~5 m horizontal resolution digital elevation models curated and distributed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in its Coastal Lidar collection, derived from high-accuracy laser-rangefinding measurements. Areas outside the United States use elevation data on a roughly 90 m horizontal resolution grid derived from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM). Local high tide level is determined using 2 data sources as well: the VDatum tidal model for the contiguous United States and a global tidal model supplied by Mark Merrifield of the University of Hawaii for the rest of the world.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding & Sea Level Rise (m)
info.technical_title: Projections of SLR linked to Climate Scenarios
info.functions: Identify areas vulnerable to flooding at a number of different water heights, potentially caused in the near- and long- term by a combination of sea-level rise, storm surge, tides, or tsunamis
info.cautions: The SRTM provides surface, rather than bare-earth, elevations, causing it to commonly overestimate elevation, especially in areas with dense and tall buildings or vegetation. While the SRTM contains significant error in both directions, depending on location, the map more often underportrays areas that could be submerged at each water level, and exposure is usually greater than shown (Kulp and Strauss 2016). The SRTM does not cover latitudes above 60°N or below 56°S, meaning that sparsely populated parts of Arctic Circle nations are not assessed here. Areas of this map in Alaska use elevation data on a roughly 60 m horizontal resolution grid supplied by the U.S. Geological Survey. These data are referenced to a vertical reference frame from 1929, based on historic sea levels, and with no established conversion to modern reference frames. The data also do not take into account subsequent land uplift and subsidence, widespread in the state. As a consequence, low confidence should be placed in Alaska map portions. This data set does not indicate where certain areas of low-elevation land are protected from sea-level rise by local topographical features, such as being surrounded by higher land that will not allow rising seas to seep through. Similarly, these data do not indicate whether an area of land is protected from sea-level rise through built infrastructural mitigations such as levees, seawalls, or other structures. Analysis does not consider erosion, marsh migration, porous bedrock geology, channels, holes, or passages for drainage, or other connectivity features not revealed in the elevation data.

Urban Land Use (Areal) – India
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – India dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for urban spaces in India. Maps are available for the years 2016 and 2019. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The final product has a resolution of 5 meters (m).
  
  

The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. Example uses might be measuring the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identifying what types of land use have been affected by disasters. There is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions.

attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the total primary energy consumption in 230 countries from 1980 to 2017. Primary energy is energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form. This dataset is published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). EIA defines primary energy consumption to include coal, petroleum, dry natural gas, nuclear electricity, hydroelectricity geothermal, solar, wind, wood, biomass, and [other sources](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=Primary%20energy%20consumption).
  
  

Energy consumption is a key indicator of the environmental impact and input costs of economic activity. The intensity of energy consumption and the sources of energy are among the key indicators of sustainable energy, as defined by Sustainable Development Goal 7.  
  
### Methodology  
  
EIA collected and analyzed consumption data from multiple external sources. The estimates in this dataset are based on a time series analysis, and the performance of the model was evaluated with hold‐out validation.
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.eia.gov/beta/international/images/International_Energy_Statistics_Estimation_for_Lagged_Data.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information

attributes.name: Daily Nighttime Lights
attributes.description:
Nighttime Imagery (Day/Night Band, Enhanced Near Constant Contrast)  is available from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the joint NASA/NOAA Suomi National Polar orbiting Partnership (SNPP) satellite. The VIIRS Nighttime Imagery layer shows the earth’s surface and atmosphere using a sensor designed to capture low-light emission sources, under varying illumination conditions. It is displayed as a grey-scale image.  
  
  Sources of illumination include both natural and anthropogenic sources of light emissions. Lunar reflection can be used to highlight the location and features of clouds and other terrestrial features such as sea ice and snow cover when there is partial to full moon conditions. When there is no moonlight, natural and anthropogenic night time light emissions are highlighted such as city lights, lightning, auroras, fires, gas flares, and fishing fleets.   
  
  The VIIRS sensor collects imagery as it orbits the Earth every 100 minutes. Passing over the poles 14 times per day, it crosses the equator at at 1:30am local time, photographing the entire world each day.  The sensor resolution is 750 m at nadir and the imagery resolution is 500 m.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information

This data set displays the population density per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics’ preliminary data from the 2020 Population and Housing Census. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020.

The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households.  	

Population density was calculated by dividing the total number of individuals in an enumeration area by the area in square kilometers of the respective enumeration area.

Seychelles Geologic Events
attributes.description:
This dataset displays a set of geologic events on the Seychellois island of Mahé from 1862 through 2011. An assessment of area-specific risk for landslides, flooding, and rockfalls was conducted in 2011 as part of the Sustainable Land Management (SLM) project. The SLM report, Compilation of Information in View of Developing a Geological Risk Map of the Islands of Mahé, Praslin, and La Digue, was shared with the researchers by the Seychellois Department of Risk and Disaster Management and provided the underlying data of this map. Historical data including the event type, date, location, and cause of each geologic event was extracted from the report to create these data points. 
As defined in the source document, landslides are the downslope movement of soil, rock, and organic materials under the effects of gravity. Landslides depicted in this layer represent mass movements in which the material on a zone of weakness is separated from the more stable underlying material. 

Rockfalls are sudden and rapid processes by which a rock detaches from a slope and descends by falling, bouncing, or rolling. They typically occur along cliffs or steep slopes and result in the displacement of large rocks, sometimes landing on roads or built structures. Rockfalls are strongly influenced by gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial weather such as regular intervals of rain. 

Debris falls are the processes by which a combination of soil, rock, mud, and organic material detaches from a steep slope and descends by falling, bouncing, or rolling as a conglomerate. They typically occur suddenly along cliffs or steep slopes, resulting in displaced materials that can land on roads or built structures. Debris falls are strongly influenced by gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial weather such as regular intervals of rain. 
Debris flow (commonly called a mudslide) is the process by which masses of loose soil, fragmented rocks, mud, organic matter, and water moves down a slope under the influence of gravity. While a debris flow mobilizes as a conglomerate, the components move independently. Source areas of debris flows are typically adorned with steep gullies. Debris flows deposit materials in fan-like shapes at the foot of the slope or accumulate where an obstruction - like a built structure - is encountered. Debris flows are commonly caused by intense surface water flow due to heavy rain that erodes material on a slope.

Slope failures are abrupt processes in which a very steep slope collapses due to weakened self-retainability, or the ability to uphold materials. Slope failures typically occur along slopes that are steeper than landslides and are characterized by smaller-scale movement than landslides. Materials displaced as a result of slope failure accumulate at the bottom of the slope. Slope failures are commonly triggered by heavy rain or earthquakes.

attributes.name: Inflation
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Inflation dataset shows national annual rates of inflation for each year from 1960-2019. Inflation reflects the annual percentage change in cost to the average consumer of acquiring specific goods and services. The dataset calculates inflation using the consumer price index (CPI), which is a weighted average of prices of a basket of consumer goods and services that can be measured and compared yearly. The dataset includes all countries that have CPI data available and has a national spatial resolution. It uses the units of percent change (% change) to compare how consumer prices have changed compared to previous years.

  
  
The dataset is created by The World Bank with data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Inflation affects the purchasing power of a currency, so when inflation increases, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services. Understanding and monitoring national inflation rates is important for governments and financial institutions in creating economic policies that reflect the state of their economy.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset was created by comparing CPI between years for each country. The CPI and inflation rate for each country was calculated using the Laspeyres formula. When a large range of goods and services are used in the formula it can be used to measure changes in a country’s cost of living. The Laspeyres formula was calculated by working out the cost of a group of commodities at the target year, dividing this by the cost of the same group of commodities at the previous year prices, and then multiplying by 100. The Laspeyres formula uses a base value of 100, so a value of 102 actually means there was an inflation rate of 2%. CPI data was taken from the International Monetary Fund, International Financial Statistics and data files.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

- The laspeyres formula tends to overstate yearly price increases, so it tends to overestimate price levels and inflation.

attributes.name: Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20)
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset shows the percentage of the population living below a $3.20 a day poverty line in 2011 international prices. The $3.20 poverty line is derived from typical national poverty lines in countries classified as Lower Middle Income. The dataset is created by comparing the $3.20 poverty line to income and consumption data from each country. Income and consumption data allows researchers to determine the cost of living and the cost of goods and services in each country based on 2011 pricing. This is used to convert the $3.20 poverty line into local currencies and poverty rates. The dataset is published for low- and middle-income countries, countries eligible to receive World Bank loans, and recently graduated countries only. It is available for all years from 1967-present and has a national spatial resolution. 

  
  
The dataset was created by the World Bank as part of its internationally comparable poverty monitoring database. The database serves to monitor poverty rates for all countries and utilizes different poverty rates for different country income classifications. The World Bank Group is committed to reducing extreme poverty to 3 percent or less, globally, by 2030. Monitoring poverty is important on the global development agenda as well as on the national development agenda of many countries.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Population below Income Poverty Line ($3.20) dataset was created as part of the World Bank’s Poverty Measures of the Developing World database to calculate the poverty headcount ratio per country at a $3.20 a day poverty line. The poverty headcount ratio is the proportion of a population that lives below the poverty line. First, researchers determined the international poverty line to create a common standard of what “poverty” is. This was first done in the 1980’s by looking at academic papers on the economies of 22 developing countries and a poverty line of $1 a day was created. Since then new and updated international poverty lines have been created and as of 2015 the World Bank has used an international poverty line of $1.90 a day at 2011 purchasing power parity (PPP). This was created by averaging the national poverty lines of 15 of the poorest countries ranked by per capita consumption. The dataset shown here uses a more liberal poverty line of $3.20, which is based on low- and middle- income countries. It is based on 2011 PPP, which means the monetary value is representative of the cost of specific goods in each country as of 2011 and highlights the differences in absolute purchasing power between economies.
  
  
International poverty lines cannot be directly compared with poverty measured at national poverty lines in local currency, which reflect economy-specific decisions of poverty. To make them comparable and determine the rate of poverty in a country the international poverty line was applied to each country individually. To do this, income and consumption data from household surveys across 164 countries in six regions and 25 other high income countries were used to determine household living standards. The poverty line at 2011 PPP was converted into local currencies in 2011 prices and then converted to the prices of goods at the time of the relevant nationally representative household survey using the best available Consumer Price Index (CPI). CPI is a measure of the cost of consumer goods and services at a given time. Then the poverty rate was calculated by determining how much of the country's population fell below the $3.20 2011 PPP poverty line. The population living below the poverty line was then divided by the country’s total population and multiplied by 100 to create the final dataset. Nationally representative household surveys were conducted by national statistical offices or by private agencies under the supervision of government or international agencies and obtained from government statistical offices and World Bank Group operational departments. CPI data was primarily taken from the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) International Financial Statistics.
  
  
To make national poverty rates comparable between countries they were calculated and shown for individual years, known as reference years. This required interpolating and extrapolating data for countries that lacked survey data for each year. This was done by adjusting the mean income or expenditure observed in a survey year by a country’s growth factor to estimate the unknown survey data in the reference year. 
  
  
For the full documentation, please see this [methodology document](http://iresearch.worldbank.org/PovcalNet/methodology.aspx) or click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.  
  
### Disclaimer

info.name: Population Below Income Poverty Line ($3.20)
info.technical_title: Poverty Headcount Ratio at $3.20 a day (2011 PPP) (% of Population)
info.functions: The percentage of the population living in poverty, defined as those living on less than $3.20 a day in 2011 international prices.
info.cautions:
- An important step in the process of compiling global poverty estimates is the conversion of the International Poverty Line into respective national currency units. Since PPP rates were designed for comparing national accounts aggregates, they were not intended for making international poverty comparisons. PPPs are based on prices of goods and services that may not be representative of the consumption baskets of the poor, so they may not fully reflect the relative price level faced by very poor consumers. As a result, there is no certainty that an international poverty line measures exactly the same degree of deprivation across economies. Similarly, the poverty line may need to be adjusted for different locations (such as urban and rural areas) within the economy, if prices or access to goods and services differs. However, for most economies, this information is not available.
 
- There are also problems with comparability of surveys, both over time and across economies. The surveys underlying the welfare distributions are carried out by national statistical offices, central banks, or other national agencies, so they are designed to serve the specific needs and interests of each particular economy. Household survey questionnaires can differ widely, and similar surveys may not be strictly comparable because of differences in quality. 
 
- Poverty rates for a region are only reported when the available surveys cover at least 40 percent of the population in that region.

- As a result of revisions in PPP exchange rates, poverty rates for individual countries cannot be compared with poverty rates reported in earlier editions.

- Poverty rates for a region are only reported when the available surveys cover at least 40 percent of the population in that region.

### Overview  
  
This dataset shows countries experiencing disaster events that are actively being monitored by ReliefWeb on May 11 2020. These disaster events include floods, droughts, severe local storms, tropical cyclones, storm surges, tsunamis, earthquakes, wildfires, cold waves, heat waves, volcanic activity, landslides, mudslides, snow avalanches, epidemics, insect infestations, and technological disasters.
  
  

ReliefWeb is the leading humanitarian information source on global crises and disasters. ReliefWeb continuously collects the latest information on ongoing crises and monitors for emerging situations. By providing reliable and timely information, they enable humanitarian workers to make informed decisions and plan effective responses.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
ReliefWeb's editorial team monitors and collects information from more than 4,000 key sources, including humanitarian agencies at the international and local levels, governments, think tanks and research institutions, and the media. From this information, ReliefWeb editors identify and select the content that is most relevant to global humanitarian workers. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: Food Price Spikes
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) dataset tracks the current prices of key staple food commodities and compares them to expected prices, which are calculated based on seasonal trends. An ALPS value is assigned to a given commodity at a particular market based on how much its current price differs from the expected price. This value is used to categorize a commodity’s price into one of four categories: normal, stress, alert, or crisis.
  
  

Food prices on a local market often correlated with food security crises. Food price spikes can have devastating impacts for rural households in developing countries since they spend a large percentage of income on food. ALPS serves three main purposes for decision-making. First, it can serve as a price monitoring tool that allows users to identify price abnormalities. Second, ALPS can generate early warning information that enables users to prepare and act to reduce harm to households most vulnerable to food price fluctuations. Third, ALPS can trigger contingency planning by anticipating food price crises. 
  
  

The ALPS dataset is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP) and monitors markets spanning more than 60 countries. The time period over which prices have been tracked varies by location, but certain markets have food price data as early as 1994. The data is updated monthly for markets that are actively being monitored.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Seasonal price trends were determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) Food and Commodity Price dataset. This dataset was collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. 
  
  

The ALPS indicator level was calculated in four steps:
- **Estimation of seasonal price trends**: The seasonal price trend was calculated using a linear regression of market price data over the entire period for which data was available. Both the long-term trend and monthly fluctuations, related to the production or demand of a commodity, were included in the regression.
  
  
- **Calculation of the difference between market price and estimated price**: The difference between the observed price and the expected price based on seasonal trends was calculated for each month.
  
  
- **Calculation of the ALPS indicator considering price volatility**: Each month’s difference was divided by the standard deviation of the differences over all of the recorded months, producing the value of the ALPS indicator.
  
  
- **Categorization of the ALPS indicator**: Based on the ALPS indicator value, markets were assigned to one of four situations:  (1) Normal: ALPS < 0.25; (2) Stress: 0.25 ≤ ALPS < 1; (3) Alert: 1 ≤ ALPS < 2; (4) Crisis: ALPS ≥ 2.
  
  

For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Food Price Spikes
info.technical_title: Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS)
info.functions: Deviation of key staple food commodity prices from seasonal trends
info.cautions:
These alerts are a result of a statistical process that compares current prices to seasonal trends in prices. It does not account explicitly for other factors in the general economy, such as general price inflation rates, that may impact how seriously fluctuations in key staple food prices affect local buying power and food security. The linear regression used to calculate the seasonal trends and variability in prices assumes that the time series of prices is stationary for each market, i.e., that the nature of the trend doesn't vary over time for each market. The general economic forces affecting prices, such as population growth and inflation, are implicitly represented by the coefficient of the trend term in the linear regression. Under the assumption of stationarity, these forces are assumed to be constant for each market, but this may not be realistic. 
  
  

When using and interpreting ALPS dataset in the context of market and food security analysis, it is important to note that the indicator is more meaningful when used for the most consumed food commodities in the country. Locally produced staples food commodities should also get priority attention, and finally analysts can also consider imported commodities.

attributes.name: Current and Projected Food Insecurity
attributes.description:
The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
