The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: ocn.027c.rw0 Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean
Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Watersheds that Transport Wastewater to Coastal Ocean dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, maps human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. This dataset displays the size and shape of nearly 135,000 watersheds across the globe that contribute to nitrogen and pathogen input from wastewater to the coastal ocean. Nitrogen concentration in each watershed is measured in grams/year.

  
  
Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue, because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters. Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management.  

  
  
The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this map of pourpoints, along with a model of nitrogen dispersion into the ocean, to inform marine conservation and public health work. The data allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources and traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
High-resolution watershed vector data and pourpoints were used with an automated flow-accumulation process to determine the boundaries for ~135,000 global basins that drain into the ocean. Population and settlement data for each basin were used to estimate the levels of nitrogen and pathogen inputs to coastal waters. Nitrogen concentrations in grams per year (g/yr) were modeled from data on three types of wastewater (treated, septic, and open defecation) and the estimated amount of nitrogen removed by each treatment type. The inputs to coastal waters were determined by totaling the estimates that fell within the watershed boundary. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also provides data on the location of ‘pourpoints’, the location at which water drains into the ocean, in [Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5bf349ec-3b14-4021-a7d4-fc4b8104bd74) and the dispersion of nitrogen into the coastal ocean at each pourpoint in [Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/11804f04-d9c7-47b9-8d27-27ce6ed6c042).
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.   
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github]((https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/ocn_027c_rw0_wastewater_watersheds/).

info.cautions:
- The model does not fully account for differences in land cover, watershed size, ecosystem processes, sanitation efficiency, and other biogeochemical processes. This may lead to overestimation of impacts in coastal ecosystems with slow-flowing water, and underestimation for areas with rapid flush times.
  
  
- Data on the location of most septic systems and sewer outfalls were modeled not observed and did not include information on septic failure rates or permitted or accidental sewer overflow events. This adds uncertainty to the model, and potentially underestimates the impacts of nitrogen given the high rates of septic tank failure.
  
  
- For treated nitrogen, the model may overestimate actual nitrogen removal rates by treatment plants, leading to underestimation of impacts in the model.

attributes.name: [Archived] Gender Development Index
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](cf069d6d-27b0-4282-8ff3-ee04d90e841d) as a replacement.**_
  
The Gender Development Index (GDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), measures gender gaps in human development achievements by accounting for disparities between women and men in 3 basic dimensions of human development using the same component indicators as in the Human Development Index (HDI). The HDI is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The GDI is the ratio of the HDIs calculated separately for females and males using the same methodology as in the HDI. It is a direct measure of gender gap, showing the female HDI as a percentage of the male HDI. The GDI is calculated for 161 countries in 2015 and shows how much women are lagging behind their male counterparts in each dimension of human development. It facilitates understanding of the real gender gap in human development achievements and is useful in designing policy tools to close the gap. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: cit.038.nrt Air Quality - Modeled Forecast - WACCM (PM2.5)
Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Modeled Next-day Forecast
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). PM2.5 is an air pollutant made up of fine inhalable particles, with diameters of 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants and automobiles.  
  
The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/health-and-environmental-effects-particulate-matter-pm), exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by fine particulate exposure.  
  
WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted PM2.5 concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps.   
  
WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution.  
  
### Methodology  
  
WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_038_waccm_atmospheric_chemistry_model).

The Energy Facility Emissions data set, published by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), provides greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions data for large facilities and industrial sources that emit over 25,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) per year in the United States. The EPA collects annual reporting of GHG data from these large facilities and publishes the data through the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP). The data set includes facility names, locations, fuel types, industry sectors and subsectors, annual facility emission thresholds, and greenhouse gas types. Users can search for national, state, local, sector, and facility-specific data. All reports submitted to EPA are evaluated by electronic validation and verification checks. This data set reflects 85-90% of total U.S. emissions and spans 2010-2016. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Sea Surface Temperature Variability
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset describes historical variations in sea surface temperature wherever coral reefs are present. Sea surface temperature (SST) is water temperature close to the ocean's surface. This changes everywhere within and between years, and the pattern and range of those fluctuations differ from place to place. This dataset characterizes those spatially distinct patterns at coral reef sites around the globe, by capturing the average variation in temperature from year to year in each 5 km grid cell, as well as the average variation in temperature from summer to summer (i.e., from the warmest month in each year to the next).

  
  
SST and its fluctuations are critical to ecosystem dynamics and health, as many marine organisms can thrive only within certain temperature ranges. In particular, research indicates that thermal history is among the most important factors influencing coral reef resilience—i.e., ability to withstand heat stress events. Accordingly, with support from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) [Coral Reef Conservation Program](http://coralreef.noaa.gov/), [Coral Reef Watch (CRW)] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php) developed a variety of thermal history metrics for coral reef management, initially released in July 2014. The metrics were derived from CRW's Version 3.1 [CoralTemp daily global 5 km (1/20°) satellite SST data product] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), for the period 1985-2018. 

  
  
Historical SST variability has been related to the level of sensitivity of corals to heat stress, in that higher variability can confer lower sensitivity. Less-sensitive corals and reef sites are less impacted when exposed to particular heat stress levels. Annual variability speaks to the variability between years, which can modify the impact of heat stress events and the susceptibility of corals and reef sites to future events. Similarly, sites with high summer temperature variability can have less sensitivity to coral bleaching.

  
  
Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Variability products are derived from the Version 3.1 [CoralTemp](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php) daily global 5km satellite SST data product.

  
  
For the Annual Variability metric, the average temperature was determined for each year in the time-series (1985-2018). The warmest month was identified separately on the basis of a 28-year (1985-2012) record. The average temperature for the relevant period of time—either the entire year or the warmest month—is calculated for each year in the time-series (1985-2018); the variability shown is the standard deviation of these values after the removal of any linear trend.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data about heat stress frequency are also available for display here, while heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_009_sea_surface_temperature_variability).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Station Measurements
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for sulfur dioxide (SO₂). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) is a colorless air pollutant with a strong odor. The main sources of sulfur dioxide emissions are from fossil fuel combustion and natural volcanic activity. Additionally, it can react in the atmosphere to form other harmful compounds, like sulfuric acid, and causes acid rain.  It can be a threat to human health, animal health, and plant life. Sulfur dioxide irritates the skin and mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, throat, and lungs. High concentrations of SO₂ can cause inflammation and irritation of the respiratory system, especially during heavy physical activity. The resulting symptoms can include pain when taking a deep breath, coughing, throat irritation, and breathing difficulties. High concentrations of SO₂ can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups. People with preexisting respiratory issues and children are most affected by SO₂ exposure.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25),  [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The sulfur dioxide station measurements dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)]https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)]https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Watersheds
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The HydroBASINS dataset depicts watershed boundaries and sub-basin delineations at a global scale.  A watershed is an area of land that drains all surface and groundwater to a common body of water. The boundaries of watersheds provide important geospatial units for many applications, but at a global
scale there is a lack of high-quality sources for watershed mapping and analysis. The HydroBasins dataset is part of the HydroSHEDS database ([Hydrological data and maps based on SHuttle Elevation Derivatives](http://www.hydrosheds.org)) which provides hydrographic data layers that allow for the derivation of watershed boundaries for any given location based on the near-global, high-resolution [Shuttle Radar Topology Mission](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/srtm/) digital elevation model.

  
  
The goal of this product is to provide a seamless global coverage of consistently sized and hierarchically nested sub-basins at different scales (from tens to millions of square kilometers), supported by a coding scheme that allows for analysis of watershed topology such as up- and downstream connectivity. The HydroSHEDS database generates key data layers to support regional and global watershed analyses, hydrological modeling, and freshwater conservation planning at a quality, resolution and extent that has previously been unachievable.

  
  
Watersheds in this database are delineated at 15 arc-second resolution with a hierarchical sub-basin breakdown. The HydroBASINS product was created in 2013. It was developed on behalf of the World Wildlife Fund US (WWF), with support from and in collaboration with the [EU BioFresh] (http://www.freshwaterbiodiversity.eu/contact/) project, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and McGill University.  
  
### Methodology  
  
All HydroBASINS layers were derived from World Wildlife Fund’s [HydroSHEDS data](http://www.hydrosheds.org) based on a grid resolution of 15 arc-seconds (approximately 500 m x 500 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.). 

  
  
An important characteristic of any sub-basin delineation is the sub-basin breakdown, i.e. the decision of when and how to subdivide a larger basin into multiple tributary basins. Standard GIS tools offer the possibility to break out sub-watersheds at any confluence where the inflowing branches (i.e., a tributary and its main stem) exceed a certain size threshold, typically measured by the number of upstream pixels or the upstream catchment area. HydroBASINS divides a basin into two sub-basins at every location where two river branches meet which each have an individual upstream area of at least 100 km².

  
  
A second critical feature of sub-basin delineations is the way the sub-basins are grouped or coded to allow for the breakout of nested sub-basins at different scales, or to navigate within the sub-basin network from up- to downstream. One of the easiest methods for navigation is to provide the ID of the next downstream object, which allows for moving from object to object in order to traverse the network. As for nesting and topological concepts, the ‘Pfafstetter’ coding system is frequently used due to its relative simplicity and ease of application. The basic principle of the Pfafstetter coding is that a larger basin is sequentially subdivided into 9 smaller units (the 4 largest tributaries, coded with even numbers, and the 5 inter-basins, coded with odd numbers). Thus, the next finer resolution of a sub-basin delineation is achieved at the next Pfafstetter level by adding one digit to the code of the previous level. A more detailed description of the Pfafstetter coding is provided in literature (e.g., [Verdin and Verdin 1999](https://www.bowdoin.edu/~ltoma/teaching/cs3225-GIS/fall16/Project-watershed/papers-watershed/1999-delineate-verdin.pdf)). 

  
  
The HydroBASINS product provides levels 1 to 12 globally. Level 1 distinguishes 9 continents. Level 2 splits each continent into up to 9 large sub-units. Level 3 corresponds to the largest river basins for each continent. From Level 4 onwards, the breakdown follows the Pfafstetter concept.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.hydrosheds.org/images/inpages/HydroBASINS_TechDoc_v1c.pdf)
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Delineations for all Pfafstetter levels (1-12) by region can be downloaded from the the source. A version of this dataset with inserted lakes as well as data for void-filled elevation, hydrologically conditioned elevation, drainage directions, flow accumulation, river networks, basin outlines, lake shorelines, and other hydro-environmental variables is also available from the data provider.
  
  
 For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_068_rw0_watersheds).
  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

info.name: Watersheds
info.technical_title: HydroBASINS, version 1.c
info.functions: Watershed and sub-basin boundaries
info.cautions:
- The quality of HydroSHEDS mostly depends on the characteristics of the SRTM-based elevation model. Being a radar product, SRTM elevation values are influenced by vegetation and other surface features which affect hydrographic derivatives. Regions prone to errors in HydroSHEDS can be found on the [source website](https://www.hydrosheds.org/page/development).
  
  
- The quality of the HydroSHEDS data is significantly lower for regions above 60 degrees northern latitude as there is no underlying SRTM elevation data available and thus a coarser scale DEM has been inserted by the authors ((HYDRO1k provided by USGS)[http://gcmd.nasa.gov/records/GCMD_HYDRO1k.html].)
  
  
- Sub-basins can grow to sizes much larger than the 100 km² threshold if there is no tributary joining the main stem for a long distance. This inconsistency due to “oversized” sub-basins has been addressed and reduced in HydroBASINS by forcing additional subdivisions for every sub-basin larger than 250 km². These polygons are split into appropriately sized sub-basins by introducing break points along their main stem rivers.

attributes.name: loc.mcaqf.001c.rw0 Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃) Forecast
Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃) Forecast
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City, specifically its pollutant's forecasting section. This dataset represents the forecasted density of ozone in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Ozone density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA).

  
  
Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that is harmful to humans and damages crops and vegetation. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/ground-level-ozone-pollution/health-effects-ozone-pollution), ozone irritates respiratory systems and can damage cells that line your lungs. Ozone may also aggravate chronic lung diseases such as bronchitis and may cause permanent lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults. Ozone is one of the main causes of air quality deterioration in the MCMA, especially in the south and downtown areas of the city. As the [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)] (http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf) mentions, despite the reduction of  maximum concentrations of the pollutant during recent years, its levels still exceed the limits established by Mexican regulations, as well as those recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) and EPA. Showcasing the spatial distribution of ozone in the MCMA provides insights about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models. The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles.

  
  
The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset is comprised of the following models:
  
  
Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)] (https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates  temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators.among others.
  
  
Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate O₃  levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution.
  
  
Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)](https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e39f5910-a9b8-4ef1-b4b4-f6b141b15541), [Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/918ba6bc-69ed-44fb-9b29-5fb445fdfef6),[Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/59790e64-d95d-43fa-a124-5c7eb1cb4456), and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e)

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source also includes the outputs for their weather model as well as the measurements of the Mexico City Weather Monitoring System (SIMAT) using their air quality index. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/loc_mcaqf_mexico_city_aq_forecast).

attributes.name: Anthropogenic Biomes
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Anthropogenic Biomes dataset illustrate human transformation and use of the terrestrial biosphere over the past 12,000 years at 73 time points between 10,000 BCE and 2015 CE. Anthromes (Anthropogenic Biomes) represent the globally significant patterns of Earth’s ecology created and sustained by human populations and their use of land, including urban, village, cropland, rangeland and semi-natural anthromes, together with wildlands without evidence of human populations or land use. Anthromes were mapped using gridded global estimates of human population density and land use from the History of the Global Environment database [(HYDE version 3.2)](https://doi.org/10.17026/dans-25g-gez3). The dataset has global coverage from 10,000 BC to 2015 AD at a resolution of 5 arc minutes (about 10 km).

  
  
Much attention has focused on the role of recent global changes in human populations and their use of land in transforming climate, ecosystems, biodiversity, and the functioning of the Earth system as a whole, as part of a planetary transition to the Anthropocene. Yet humans have been transforming landscapes around the world for thousands of years, from hunter-gatherer burning to clear land, to the emergence and spread of agriculture, to the rise of large-scale urban industrial societies. To understand the causes and consequences of Earth’s transformation by human societies, the full, continuous trajectory of these anthropogenic transformations of the terrestrial biosphere must be examined from their first beginnings to the present day. As with prior anthrome datasets,  the  Anthropogenic Biomes dataset offers many opportunities to investigate the global consequences of long-term changes in the global reshaping of ecology by human societies.The many other assessments of Earth’s ecological and social patterns, processes, and dynamics that have utilized prior anthrome datasets are also clear targets for new and improved investigations using this dataset, including, for example, studies of biogeography and biodiversity, primary productivity, fire, conservation, disease and ecological research itself.

  
  
The Anthropogenic Biomes dataset was developed by the [Anthroecology Lab](https://anthroecology.org/) working group, part of the Department of Geography & Environmental Systems at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC). The Anthroecology Lab explores the ecology of populated landscapes at local, regional and global scales towards the goal of making ecosystem management more sustainable.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The rule-based mapping approach of [Anthromes 2.0](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2010.00540.x) utilized 5 arc minute gridded global data for population density and percent cover by crops, pastures and urban areas from [HYDE 3.1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2010.00587.x) together with global data for potential vegetation cover, irrigation and rice. To classify and map anthromes from 10,000 BCE to 2015 CE, the HYDE 3.2 dataset was used, as it now provides all necessary input data for anthromes classification over this entire interval in a standard open-access dataset. The Anthropogenic Biomes dataset covers all of Earth’s land surface with 20 anthrome classes,by including an anthrome class for uninhabited ice-covered land areas. These 20 detailed classes are grouped into six anthrome levels: Dense settlements, Villages, Croplands, Rangelands, Seminatural lands and Wildlands. 

  
  
The use of HYDE 3.2 data inputs, and the goal of including Earth’s entire terrestrial surface in the maps, not just ice-free land, required slight adjustments to the rule-based classification of Anthromes 2.0, leading to an updated classification algorithm and classification legend: the Anthromes 2.1 classification. The HYDE 3.2 “grazing” area variable was used in the same way as the original, “pasture” variable of HYDE 3.1, to which it is equivalent. In contrast with the 19 original anthrome classes covering Earth’s ice-free land in the Anthromes 2.0 classification. Anthromes 2.1 covers all of Earth’s land surface with 20 anthrome classes, by including an anthrome class for uninhabited ice-covered land areas. Taken together, HYDE 3.2 now provides all data needed to compute anthromes classes without reference to other global map layers, therefore avoiding potential artifacts and errors introduced by differences across datasets in land/sea masks, classification definitions and spatial resolutions.

  
  
Differences between anthrome maps caused by the change in input data from HYDE 3.1 plus additional data inputs, to the use of HYDE 3.2 exclusively, were assessed by comparing maps directly using statistical measures of association, by comparing land area tabulations for anthrome classes in comparable time periods, and by comparing maps using a GIS to highlight differences in data inputs and anthrome classification across the planet. Land areas were computed for Anthromes 2.0 classes using the original land area data layer for this dataset and for Anthromes 12K using the HYDE 3.2 land area data layer.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-445X/9/5/129)
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source shows information for over 73 time steps from 10,000 BC to 2015 AD; as well as a [Discrete Global Grid version](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/E3H3AK) of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/edit/soc_108_anthropogenic_biomes).

attributes.name: Gridded Carbon Footprint
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Gridded Carbon Footprint dataset shows a gridded estimate of absolute and per capita carbon emissions in the year 2013 for 189 countries. The results were produced by the Gridded Global Model of Carbon Footprints (GGMCF) model at a spatial resolution of 250 meters. GGMCF is based on previously available data for carbon footprint (CF), population, and household spending. The model uses urban vs. rural consumption patterns and purchasing power as the main indicators of per capita footprint. Higher purchasing power generally increases the chance of participating in activities that lead to more carbon emissions.
  
  
The dataset was created by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) in collaboration with Shinshu University, Yale, and Lund University. Most cities, towns, and rural areas around the world have no carbon footprint data. This dataset provides the first internationally comparable CF estimates for many regions of the world. The results presented here can help develop strategies to reduce carbon footprint. Additionally, this dataset can be used by national governments to locate small regions with disproportionally high emissions rates.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset was created in four distinct steps:

  
  
1. National CFs of consumption (CFn) data were taken from the Eora multi-region input-output (MRIO) database for the year 2015. This data included 189 countries and accounted for close to 100% of global CO₂ emission.

  
  
2. For the EU, UK, USA, Japan, and China, existing subnational CF models were available from a variety of publications. These models were used to separate national CF of consumption data into subnational/regional data CFr. The size of regions ranged from ZIP codes to provinces. In steps 3 and 4 these subnational regions are treated the same as countries. Regions included the disaggregated subnational regions along with countries that are not disaggregated.

  
  
3. Within each region, the CFr was further disaggregated into urban and rural residents utilizing urban vs. rural population data and urban vs. rural expenditure pattern data from the World Bank, Eurostat, and US BEA. This data included 113 countries and accounted for 81% of global CO₂ production for the year 2015.

  
  
4. The data was subsequently disaggregated to produce CFs of grid cells using gridded population maps and gridded income data. First, the urban and rural grid cells were identified using the Global Human Settlement Layer Settlement Model Grid (GHS-SMOD). Then the CF for each region was disaggregated across the grid cells based on the combined purchasing power of the population living within each grid cell. Carbon footprints are usually directly related to income and purchasing power. The population in each cell was multiplied by the mean purchasing power at that location to calculate the overall purchasing power per grid cell.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aac72a#erlaac72at1).

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on carbon footprints for the top 500 cities in absolute and per capita values are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.   
  
### Disclaimer

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](926e6be3-8699-4a0c-8214-b8c05b7e0083) as a replacement.**_
  
The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: loc.mcaqf.001e Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Forecast
Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Forecast
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality in Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density for sulfur dioxide in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Sulfur Dioxide density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA).

  
  
SO₂ is a colorless air pollutant with a strong odor. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)] (https://www.epa.gov/so2-pollution/sulfur-dioxide-basics) the largest source of SO₂ in the atmosphere is the burning of fossil fuels by power plants and other industrial facilities. Smaller sources of SO₂ emissions include the following: industrial processes such as extracting metal from ore; natural sources such as volcanoes; and locomotives, ships and other vehicles and heavy equipment that burn fuel with a high sulfur content. SO₂ is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health, it can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of SO₂ can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks and existing heart disease. According to the [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)] (http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), SO₂ is one of the criteria pollutants whose concentrations decreased during the 1990’s and have continued to decline since then. Furthermore, its maximum concentrations have been kept below the limits indicated by Mexican regulations. The highest concentrations of SO₂ were observed in the north of the MCMA, which is mostly due to the emissions of an oil processing plant located in the municipality of Tula. Showcasing the spatial distribution of SO₂ in the MCMA will provide insight about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models. The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles.

  
  
The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset is comprised of the following models:
  
  
Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)] (https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates  temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators.among others.
  
  
Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate SO₂ levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution.
  
  
Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ) (https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e39f5910-a9b8-4ef1-b4b4-f6b141b15541), [nitrogen dioxide (Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/918ba6bc-69ed-44fb-9b29-5fb445fdfef6),[Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/00d6bae1-e105-4165-8230-ee73a8128538) and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e)

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source also includes the outputs for their weather model as well as the measurements of the Mexico City Weather Monitoring System (SIMAT) using their air quality index. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/loc_mcaqf_mexico_city_aq_forecast).

attributes.name: Certified Commodity Crops
attributes.description:
The Certified Commodity Crops Map, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), is the first global data set showing the distribution of commodity crop certification. Crop certification helps consumers purchase more ethical products that come from farms that promote social equality and sustainability. However, these certifications are not well represented in some of the poorest countries of the world or in the tropical rainforests that are at the greatest risk. This map allows users to view the spatial distribution of global crop certification.  
  
The locations of certified farms came from publicly available datasets or by directly contacting standards bodies. Certification data from all major standards and codes of practice were included (4C, Bird-friendly coffee, Bonsucro, Etanol Verde, Fairtrade, ISCC, Rainforest Alliance, Roundtable Responsible Soy, Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices and UTZ). The seven most certified crops (banana, cocoa, coffee, tea, soybean, sugar and palm oil) were mapped.  
  
Coordinates and postal addresses were used to identify point locations of each scheme. Postal addresses were converted to coordinates using ESRI Online World Geocode service. Data cleaning was performed to ensure points were located in their listed country and fell within the crop growing area, identified by a crop cover map.  
  
Some data permissions were granted under the condition that they be aggregated with other standards so that specific certification schemes and crop producers could not be identified. Therefore, data were aggregated at a 30 km x 30 km resolution. Certification data came from the years 2013, 2014 and 2015.  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information

info.cautions: Not all certification schemes were willing or able to provide data. Cotton certification data did not have usable spatial data, so this major commodity crop had to be excluded. A few issues arose when locating certified farms. From certificates that were located with an address, rather than spatial coordinates, only 23% were able to be to be converted to point coordinates. Some certificate coordinates were associated with an administrative office in place of the actual farm. A selection of certification standards included group certificates, in which multiple farms were represented by a single certificate and coordinate. Lastly, certain farms held multiple certificates for a single farm; however, these certificates were treated as unique due to the inability to tell if the certificates were for the same farm. After data cleaning was performed, 93% of data were able to meet the data validation requirements of this study.

attributes.name: Gridded Livestock
attributes.description:
The Gridded Livestock of the World Version 3, produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the University of Oxford, shows the distribution of eight livestock animal densities in animals per square kilometer at a spatial resolution of 5 arcminutes. The animals include cattle, water buffalo, horse, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and ducks.   
  

The Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW) created two versions of their data for two different methods of distributing livestock census weighting: area weighting and dasymetric weighting. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data, and the metadata refers to this methodology. More information can be found in the Cautions section.    
  

The total livestock census numbers for administrated levels are found by mining agricultural yearbooks or through direct contacts with ministries or statistical bureau. The livestock numbers are then distributed within census polygons according to weights established by a Random Forest model using high resolution spatial covariates including population, vegetation health, and climate. 
In compiling subnational census counts, priority is given to censuses that most closely match the reference year, 2010, and those with the highest level of spatial detail. This results in a global mosaic of data from different spatial resolutions and different years. Both the spatial resolution and year of census data depend on the country and species in question. See cautions section and source publication for more information.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Gridded Livestock
info.technical_title: Gridded Livestock of the World 2010 (GLW 3)
info.functions: Global distributions of cattle, water buffalo, sheep, goats, horses, pigs, chickens and ducks per square km at the equator in 2010
info.cautions:
Two versions of each species distribution are produced. In the first version, livestock numbers are disaggregated within census polygons according to weights established by statistical models using high resolution spatial covariates (dasymetric weighting). In the second version, animal numbers are distributed homogeneously with equal densities within their census polygons (areal weighting) to provide spatial data layers free of any assumptions linking them to other spatial variables. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting product. The dasymetric version is recommended for applications where spatial detail matters more than concerns about circularity in the analytical workflow in relation to spatial predictor covariates. However, the authors warn potential users against over-interpretation of spatial accuracy of the dasymetric product. When circularity concerns are more important than detailed spatial resolution, it is recommended that the area weighted versions be used. Users can find both versions of the data on the source website, and again Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data divided by the area per pixel, resulting in animal densities or animals per square kilometer.   Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.   
  

Due to the nature of the livestock subnational census statistics, the age and spatial resolution of the census statistics vary by age and by livestock animal. The oldest subnational census data are for the Democratic Republic of the Congo (1994), whilst some countries, for example Turkey, have very recent data (2014). The average spatial resolution (ASR) varies from country to country, with countries such as Italy and Thailand having very detailed subnational data (ASR<10 km2 and a mean area<100 km2), and countries such as Russia or South Africa with very coarse subnational census data (ASR > 250 km2 and mean area > 62 500 km2). 
Decisions regarding the use of this version of GLW over smaller spatial extents should be taken in relation to the ASR of the underlying census data. For example, analyses of GLW data in Brazil, Spain or Thailand would be appropriate because their respective ASRs are small relative to the size of the country. In contrast, we would discourage the country-level use of GLW data in countries such as Russia or Mali, because the ASR values are particularly high (>250 km2).

attributes.name: foo.046b Food Footprint in Calories WRR update
Environmental Impact by Food Type (Calories)
attributes.description:
The Environmental Impact by Food Type (Calories) data set, produced by World Resources Institute in its 2018 World Resources Report: _Creating a Sustainable Food Future_, illustrates the variations in impact of various food products on land use, freshwater use, and greenhouse gas emissions per million kilocalories consumed. Land use is separated into cropland use and pasture land use. Freshwater use is specified as either from rainwater or irrigation. Greenhouse gas emissions are categorized as occurring during land-use change (e.g., converting forested land to pasture or cropland) or during agricultural production. The impact is measured by the hectares used, thousand cubic meters of freshwater used, or tons of carbon dioxide equivalent produced per million of kilocalories consumed. Both plant-based and animal-based food products are examined in this data set. The plant-based products examined are sugar, rice, rapeseed and mustard seed oil, palm oil, maize, roots and tubers, wheat, soybean oil, fruits and vegetables, sunflower seed oil, and pulses; the animal-based products are pork, eggs, fish (farmed, includes all aquatic animal products), poultry, dairy, beef, and sheep and goat meat. The data set clearly illustrates that animal products overwhelmingly use more land and water, and produce greater quantities of greenhouse gas emissions, than plant-based products. The data used in this data set are global means for land use, water use, and GHG emissions and were derived from the GlobAgri-WRR model (land use and greenhouse gas emissions), authors’ calculations from Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012) (freshwater consumption), and Waite et al. (2014) (farmed fish freshwater consumption). Freshwater use for farmed fish products is shown as rainwater and irrigation combined. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates are based on a marginal analysis (i.e., additional agricultural land use and emissions per additional million calories or ton of protein consumed). Based on the approach taken by the European Union for estimating emissions from land-use change for biofuels, land-use change impacts are amortized over a period of 20 years and then shown as annual impacts. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates for beef production are based on dedicated beef production, not beef that is a coproduct of dairy. Tons of harvested products were converted to quantities of calories and protein using the global average edible calorie and protein contents of food types as reported in the Food and Agriculture Organization's FAOSTAT (2017). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Costa Rica Current Coffee Suitability
attributes.description:
This data set shows current coffee suitability. It was created using multiple environmental variables as part of a study that attempts to utilize data from four Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPC) emissions scenarios to determine the impact of climate change on coffee cultivation in coffee growing regions of Costa Rica. The study was done using georeferenced points obtained from Instituto del Café de Costa Rica (ICAFE), and using the MaxEnt model to simulate the adaptability of coffee production. 

Environmental layers taken into account comprise 19 bioclimatic variables from the Worldclim database. Developed by Hijmans et al. 2005, thousands of data points from meteorological stations around the world were collected for the time period of 1960 to 1990, using an interpolation to create environmental layers (rasters) of average temperature with 24,542 locations, minimum and maximum temperatures with 14,835 locations, and precipitation with 47,554 locations. These were all calculated by month, with a resolution of 1 square km. Bioclimatic variables were derived from monthly temperature and precipitation values with the goal of generating biologically significant variables related to crop development.

attributes.name: Global Land Cover (UNLCCS Classification)
attributes.description:
The Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover (LC) project of the European Space Agency (ESA) delivers consistent global LC maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2015. Each pixel value corresponds to the label of a land cover class defined based on the UN Land Cover Classification System (LCCS). This unique data set was produced thanks to the reprocessing and the interpretation of 5 different satellite missions.   
  
Baseline LC maps are generated thanks to the entire MERIS FR and RR archive from 2003 through 2012. Independently from this baseline, LC changes are detected at 1 km based on the AVHRR time series between 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT time series between 1999 and 2013, and PROBA-V data for years 2013, 2014, and 2015. When MERIS FR or PROBA-V time series are available, changes detected at 1 km are remapped at 300 m. The last step consists in back- and updating the 10-year baseline LC map to produce the 24 annual LC maps from 1992 to 2015. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. attributes.name: Potential Evapotranspiration
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset details global potential evapotranspiration of a reference crop at 30 arc-seconds resolution (approximately 1km at the equator) for the 1970-2000 period. 

  
  
Evapotranspiration is the simultaneous process of evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation is the process in which liquid water is converted to water vapor. Transpiration is when plants take up water with their roots and release water vapor to the atmosphere through stomata in their leaves. The unit for evapotranspiration is total millimeters (mm) per year. A higher value in mm suggests more water is lost from that cropped surface. 

  
  
Potential evapotranspiration measures the ability of the atmosphere to remove water through evapotranspiration. In this dataset crop evapotranspiration (ET₀) is used as a measure of the evapotranspiration rate from a referenced and standardized vegetated surface (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nation ([FAO](http://www.fao.org/3/X0490E/x0490e04.htm)). This concept of ET₀ is useful to study evaporative demand of the atmosphere in relation to climatic factors and independently of crop type, crop development, and management practices. 

  
  
This dataset was developed by Antonio Trabucco and Robert Zomer with the support of the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI). The dataset can be used to support studies on sustainable development, poverty alleviation, and climate change adaptation. It is particularly relevant to crop and yield modeling and studying the impacts of climate change on future crop production. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The widely-used standard equation to estimate potential evapotranspiration is the FAO Penman-Monteith equation (FAO-PM). Researchers used the FAO-PM equation in combination with data on multiple climate variables to produce an estimated ET₀ for a reference crop (well-watered grass at 12 cm of height). A reference crop was used to ensure the final results provided ET₀ information solely based on climate information of a region.  Climate data was collected from [WorldClim 2.0 dataset](http://worldclim.org/version2). The World Clim 2.0 dataset includes monthly data on temperature, solar radiation, wind speed and water vapor pressure. 
  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://figshare.com/articles/Global_Aridity_Index_and_Potential_Evapotranspiration_ET0_Climate_Database_v2/7504448/3).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [aridity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cli030-Land-Aridity) data from the data provider.   
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly averaged potential evapotranspiration is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.

attributes.name: Human Settlement Grid
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the global spatial distribution of settlement classifications related to the land area’s degree of urbanization. It is created with a combination of data on population and built-up density. The data covers 1975, 1990, 2000, and 2015 with a 1 kilometer (km) resolution, and was created by the European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC).

  
  
This dataset classifies land into seven classifications that range from urban city to low-density rural areas. Cells that contain over 50% water or are completely unpopulated are excluded. The classifications are presented in grid-level terms with the associated municipal level terms. For example, grid-level term *urban center* corresponds with municipal level term *city*. 

  
  
This dataset is part of a larger project called the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHS), which produces global spatial information and analytics to describe human presence on earth. GHS is used as a base measurement to support multiple projects, like the Geo Human Planet Initiative (HPI) and the European Union’s 2030 Development Agenda.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The final dataset was created using the information on population density, the share of built-up area, and the number of contiguous grid cells sharing similar settlement classifications. This dataset is derived from a combination of two input datasets: Landsat image data processing (GHS-BUILT) and GHS population density dataset (GHS-POP). GHS-BUILT shows built-up density and is based on remote sensing image data from the Global Land Survey’s (GLS) Landsat image database. GHS-POP depicts the residential density and distribution of population based on the Center for International Earth Science Information Network’s (CIESIN) Gridded Population of the World, version 4.10 (GPWv4.10). Land data was extracted from the [Global ADMinstrative Map 2.8](https://gadm.org/data.html) and the [Global Surface Water Occurrence](https://global-surface-water.appspot.com/download). Name data was collected OpenStreetMaps and filtered by EUROSTAT.

  
  
GHS-POP and GHS-BUILT were combined to create the final product on settlement classifications presented at a spatial resolution of 1 km. The final dataset has grid cells classified into seven settlement classifications ranging from city (urban centers)  to very low-density areas (rural land). 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/documents/GHSL_Data_Package_2019.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information

attributes.name: foo.057 Crop Allocation to Food, Feed, Nonfood
Crop Allocation to Food, Feed, Nonfood
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Crop Allocation to Food, Feed, Nonfood dataset shows how crops are used around the world. The dataset also shows calorie production per what fraction of global crop production actually becomes food. This data shows how many kilocalories of food, feed, and nonfood are produced by 41 crops combined. Food includes all kilocalories used for human consumption, feed includes those used for animal feed, and nonfood includes those used for biofuels and other industrial uses. Worldwide demand for crops is increasing rapidly due to global population growth, increased biofuel production, and changing dietary preferences. Meeting these growing demands will be a substantial challenge that will tax the capability of the food system and prompt calls to dramatically boost global crop production. However, to increase food availability, we may also consider how the world’s crops are allocated to different uses and whether it is possible to feed more people with current levels of crop production.
 
  
  
This data was developed by researchers at the University of Minnesota. It reflects the production and use of 41 crops combined, circa 2000. The spatial resolution of the data is five arc minutes by five arc minutes (~10 km x 10 km at the equator).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Crop-specific uses for 41 crops were estimated based on the Food Balance Sheets (FAOstat.org) produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), which provide national-level statistics. This data uses a global compilation of census data and satellite images to depict geographic patterns of crop area and yields across the world on a 5′ × 5′ latitude–longitude grid (equivalent to roughly 9 km × 9 km on the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/8/3/034015/meta).

attributes.name: Crop Nutrient Balance
attributes.description:
The Crop Nutrient Balance data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE) and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). This map shows the excess or deficit of elemental nitrogen and phosphorus globally at a 5 arc minute resolution. These data represent the year 2000 but were calculated from input data sets ranging from 1994-2001. The addition of these nutrients to croplands has led to widespread increases in agricultural productivity; however, this act has also increased nutrient pollution, especially in bodies of water. Converting atmospheric nitrogen and mining phosphorus also incur energy costs. The excess or deficit of nutrients is calculated using a simple mass balance. Inputs for nitrogen include chemical fertilizer, manure, nitrogen deposition and nitrogen fixation by legumes, which is scaled by yields. Phosphorus inputs include chemical fertilizer and manure. Nutrient removal from harvest is calculated as the product of yield, dry fraction and nutrient density. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. attributes.description: The Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group monthly climate normals are baseline data sets describing average monthly conditions over the most recent three full decades. The most recent PRISM normals are for the period 1981-2010. Spatial climate data sets for mean monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature were developed for the conterminous United States. These 30-arcsec (∼800-m) grids are the official spatial climate data sets of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The PRISM interpolation method was used to develop data sets that reflected, as closely as possible, the current state of knowledge of spatial climate patterns in the United States. PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each digital elevation model (DEM) grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell. Factors considered are location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position, and orographic effectiveness of the terrain. Surface stations used in the analysis numbered nearly 13,000 for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature. Station data were spatially quality controlled, and short-period-of-record averages adjusted to better reflect the 1981–2010 period.
