attributes.name: bio.012 Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels_replacement
Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset shows the species richness and number of threatened species for amphibians and mammals. Species richness is defined by the number of mammal or amphibian species present in a given area. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) [Red List](https://www.iucnredlist.org/about/background-history) defines a [threatened species](https://www.iucn.org/resources/conservation-tools/iucn-red-list-threatened-species) as one that is threatened with global extinction (critically endangered, endangered, or vulnerable). The Red List is the world’s most comprehensive list of species status and extinction risk, with assessments for over 120,000 species. The data shown here evaluated 5,198 amphibian species and 5,488 mammalian species in 2013. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 kilometer (km) x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

  
  
Biodiversity – the variety of life on earth – is essential to a healthy and stable environment. Biodiversity conservation is critical for food supply, fighting climate change, and providing natural resources for humans. However, human activities such as pollution, farming and deforestation have negatively impacted biodiversity, causing the loss of species and their habitats. Amphibians are facing the highest rates of decline: almost 50% of amphibian species are threatened, primarily in South America and Southeast Asia. Similarly, almost 50% of mammal species are in decline and 20% are threatened. Marine mammals are among the most threatened species. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset is an important tool for wildlife conservation efforts. Understanding the magnitude and geographic focus of threatened species is important for making policy decisions and allocating conservation resources. Additionally, this dataset can be used for biodiversity modeling studies and understanding human interactions with the environment. 

  
  
Founded in 1948, the [International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN)](https://www.iucn.org/about) comprises more than 1,400 governmental and civil member organizations. Its mission is to influence, encourage and assist conservation of natural diversity, and ensure that the use of any natural resources is equitable and sustainable. The IUCN provides the Red List as a tool to inform conservation decisions and protect the natural resources necessary for human life. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Level dataset was aggregated by [Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN)](http://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/) using data from the IUCN Red List. CIESIN specializes in online data management and spatial data integration for interdisciplinary research related to human interactions with the environment.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset was created from species distribution shapefiles from the IUCN Red List. The shapefile data is from 2013 and has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 km at the equator). The number in each grid cell represents the number of species present or the number of species threatened within that cell. 

  
  
CIESIN created the richness and threat level rasters by converting the shapefiles to GeoTIFF rasters based on attributes from the IUCN data. Amphibian and mammalian richness maps were created by aggregating individual species maps with the **Extant** class attribute. This attribute refers to species that are currently surviving in the wild. Threat level maps were created in the same way using the **All Threats** IUCN threat category. The All Threats category includes species classified as Critically Endangered (extremely high risk of extinction in the wild), Endangered (very high risk of extinction in the wild ) or Vulnerable (high risk of extinction in the wild). Species within these categories are undergoing reversible declines in population, geographic extent, habitat, and mature individuals. Red List species assessments follow a specific set of guidelines and undergo review before publication. More information about the Red List assessment process can be found [here](https://www.iucnredlist.org/assessment/process). 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.

attributes.name: Terrestrial Human Footprint
attributes.description:
The global human footprint map, created by Venter et al. (2016), used the human footprint framework to compile remotely sensed and bottom-up survey information on 8 variables measuring the direct and indirect human pressures on the environment in 1993 and 2009. The study included data on (1) extent of built environments, (2) crop land, (3) pasture land, (4) human population density, (5) nighttime lights, (6) railways, (7) roads, and (8) navigable waterways. These pressures were weighted according to estimates of their relative levels of human pressure and then summed together to create the standardized human footprint for all non-Antarctic land areas at 1 km resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: bio.008 Cumulative Climate Impacts on Marine Ecosystems_replacement
Cumulative Climate Impacts on Marine Ecosystems
attributes.description:
This cumulative impact index ranging from ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change) for the impact of climate change on oceans was calculated using sea surface temperature (SST), ocean productivity measured by chlorophyll (CHL), and ocean circulation by Ramirez et al. (2017). The data to calculate were from the longest time series of remote-sensing records (annual composites) on SST (1980-2014), CHL (1979-2014), and marine currents (1980-2014) available to provide finest-scale measurements of the impacts of climate change on the marine environment globally.   
  
Pixel basis, least-squares linear regression of annual information from SST, CHL, and the eastern and northern components of water speed were used for deriving the significance of temporal trends and its magnitudes (slopes; that is, annual changes in target features) over the past 3 decades. CHL data were sourced online as annual composites, whereas data on SST and marine currents were obtained on a monthly basis and averaged yearly to generate a linear relationship to extract slopes. This calculation was repeated for every pixel of the globe. These magnitudes were combined to obtain the spatially explicit Cumulative Impact Index.   
  
Different layers were first resampled following a bilinear interpolation procedure to match the spatial resolution of the coarsest SST product (that is, 1° grid). Absolute values for the slopes of obtained trends (a proxy to the magnitude of environmental changes) were then standardized to the maximum value to make all variables comparable. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value. In this way, researchers obtained a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change), thereby providing information about spatial heterogeneity in the magnitude of environmental changes and highlighting those marine areas that have undergone the largest changes in their environmental conditions. attributes.name: Urban Expansion Probabilities
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050. It separates the data into five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs), at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. SSPs represent how different policy and societal choices will affect greenhouse gas emissions. The five scenarios used in this analysis are labeled as: 
- SSP1: Sustainability – Taking the Green Road (low challenges to mitigation and adaptation)
- SSP2: Middle of the Road (medium challenges to mitigation and adaptation)
- SSP3: Regional Rivalry – A Rocky Road (high challenges to mitigation and adaptation)
- SSP4: Inequality – A Road Divided (low challenges to mitigation, high challenges to adaptation)
- SSP5: Fossil-fueled Development – Taking the Highway (high challenges to mitigation, low challenges to adaptation)

  
  
The dataset was created with information from a combination of five sources based on current urban land extent, population rates, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) information, and SSP scenarios. 
                
  
  
It is important to understand urban expansion because it can cause implications for warming, water scarcity, land use, and other environmental and social challenges. This dataset can be combined with other socioeconomic data to further examine the impacts of urban expansion. For instance, the dataset authors predicted urban expansion-induced warning in cities and suggested that it will increase extreme heat risks for about half of the future urban population. This will primarily affect communities in the tropical Global South that lack the adaptive capacity to meet environmental change. Policymakers can use this dataset to restrict or redistribute urban expansion and design strategies needed to mitigate Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) to reduce their negative impacts on human health, urban ecosystems, energy systems, and infrastructure.         

  
  
This dataset was published by Seto Lab, based at Yale School of the Environment.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers created this dataset using the URBANMOD-ZIPE model. The URBANMOD-ZIPE model was based on a 2012 global urban land change model, URBANMOD, and used to forecast pixels of urban expansion probabilities. The input data sources used for the updated model were:
  
  
1. urban land extent from the Global Human Settlement grid
  
  
2. urban population from the United Nations
  
  
3. Gross Domestic Product from the World Bank
  
  
4. future scenarios of the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis

  
  
There were two phases to the model. Phase 1 predicted the quantities of urban land by 2050. This was done using a fixed effect panel regression model to relate urban land per capita to GDP per capita. Phase 2 utilized a land change model to allocate new urban lands to map pixels using slope, distance to roads, population density, and land covers as the drivers of land change. The final dataset was produced in raster format at a spatial resolution of 5 km.


  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ab4b71).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
Resource Watch has previously shown this data for urban expansion probabilities for 2030. This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed and the global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050 is now available. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit005-Urban-Expansion-Probabilities_replacement).  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.

info.cautions: The dataset assumes that historical patterns of urban land expansion will continue in the future. However, in the past we have seen these patterns altered by government policy. For instance, the urban registration system (hukou) in China limited the growth of the country’s larger cities. In the United States, lower fuel taxes, subsidies for highways, and zoning laws limited high-rise development and have led to more urban sprawls. Since policy interventions were not explicitly incorporated in the model, these probability forecasts cannot capture the full range of uncertainty in future urban land expansion.

attributes.name: Gridded Livestock
attributes.description:
The Gridded Livestock of the World Version 3, produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the University of Oxford, shows the distribution of eight livestock animal densities in animals per square kilometer at a spatial resolution of 5 arcminutes. The animals include cattle, water buffalo, horse, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and ducks. 

The Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW) created two versions of their data for two different methods of distributing livestock census weighting: area weighting and dasymetric weighting. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data, and the metadata refers to this methodology. More information can be found in the Cautions section. 

The total livestock census numbers for administrated levels are found by mining agricultural yearbooks or through direct contacts with ministries or statistical bureau. The livestock numbers are then distributed within census polygons according to weights established by a Random Forest model using high resolution spatial covariates including population, vegetation health, and climate.
 
In compiling subnational census counts, priority is given to censuses that most closely match the reference year, 2010, and those with the highest level of spatial detail. This results in a global mosaic of data from different spatial resolutions and different years. Both the spatial resolution and year of census data depend on the country and species in question. See cautions section and source publication for more information.  

PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: GLAD Deforestation Alerts
attributes.description:
This dataset, created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland and supported by Global Forest Watch, is the first Landsat-based alert system for tree cover loss. While most existing loss alert products use 250 m resolution MODIS imagery, these alerts have a 30 m resolution and thus can detect loss at a much finer spatial scale. The alerts are currently operational in the tropics. New Landsat 7 and 8 images are downloaded as they are posted online at USGS EROS, assessed for cloud cover or poor data quality, and compared to the 4 previous years of Landsat-derived metrics (including ranks, means, and regressions of red, near infrared, and shortwave infrared bands, and ranks of NDVI, NBR, and NDWI). The metrics and the latest Landsat image are run through decision trees to calculate a median probability of forest disturbance. Pixels with probability > 50% are reported as tree cover loss alerts. For more information on methodology, see the paper in Environmental Research Letters. Alerts remain unconfirmed until 2 or more loss observations occur out of 4 observations or within 180 days. Alerts that remain unconfirmed after subsequent observations are removed from the data set. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

info.technical_title: Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) Alert
info.functions: Areas of likely tree cover loss in near-real time
info.cautions:
- While Landsat 7 and 8 satellites together have a revisit period of 8 days, cloud cover can significantly limit the availability of imagery, particularly in the wet season. Alert dates represent the instance of detection, though tree cover loss could have taken place earlier, possibly weeks earlier, due to persistent cloud cover. 
- Forest cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 m in height with greater than 30% canopy cover and may take the form of natural forests or plantations. An alert indicates a canopy loss in excess of 50% cover and can be due to factors other than deforestation.

attributes.name: Solar Energy Potential
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Solar Energy Potential dataset is made up of two layers: average daily global horizontal irradiation (GHI) and average daily photovoltaic power potential. GHI is the sum of direct and diffuse radiation received on a horizontal plane presented in the units kilowatt hour per square meter (kWh/m²). Radiation is energy that moves from one place to another and in this dataset it refers to energy released by the sun traveling to Earth. Irradiance refers to the average amount of radiation received in a given area on Earth.  Photovoltaic power potential, or Potential photovoltaic electricity
Production (PVOUT), is the estimated amount of energy converted by a photovoltaic system into electricity presented in kilowatt-hour per kilowatt peak of the photovoltaic system (kWh/kWp) according to the geographical conditions of a site and configuration of the photovoltaic system. GHI acts as an important base measurement to help determine regions that receive enough sunlight and is used to assess an area for flat-plate photovoltaic and solar heating technologies. PVOUT works to calculate the actual effectiveness of a solar energy project in the region based on local conditions.

  
  
The datasets were created using geostationary satellite imagery and meteorological models, including SolarGIS’s global solar model (v2.1). Satellite imagery data comes from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), North American Space Agency (NASA), European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMESTAT), and Japan Meteorological Administration (JMA).

  
  
The final averages presented in these datasets were created using yearly and daily averages taken between 1994/1999/2007 and 2018, depending on region of the world. The GHI dataset is presented on Resource Watch at a spatial resolution of 250 meters and PVOUT 1 kilometer. 

  
  
These datasets are taken from SolarGIS’s Global Solar Atlas, which is funded by the World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). The Global Solar Atlas was created to help companies and governments improve the efficiency of photovoltaic projects. Increasing sustainable energy production, like solar, is a crucial step in reducing the world’s reliance on fossil fuels.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The average daily global horizontal irradiation (GHI) and average daily photovoltaic power potential layers were created using SolarGIS’s global solar model (v2.1). The model utilizes data from geostationary satellites and metrological models. First, clear-sky irradiance values were calculated using the position of the sun on earth at a given time. The irradiance values used in the calculations assumed that there were no clouds present in the sky. This determined the sun’s irradiance that reached earth based on the effect of altitude, concentration of aerosols (particles coming from different sources, natural and human), water vapor, and ozone. Then data from geostationary meteorological satellites was input to determine cloud cover during the same time period. These two data sources were coupled to provide the global horizontal irradiation values.

  
  
The photovoltaic power potential was calculated by combining the horizontal irradiation dataset with data on surface air temperature and a simulation of photovoltaic power cells. First, the horizontal irradiation dataset was converted into irradiation at optimum tilt to provide ideal conditions for power potential on a photovoltaic cell. Optimum tilt refers to the most efficient angle for a surface to be at to receive the highest amount of the sun’s radiation. Surface air temperature data was collected from meteorological stations when available and otherwise from meteorological models. Data from models was disaggregated by SolarGIS to increase their spatial resolution. The photovoltaic power cell simulation used was the Single-diode equivalent circuit simulation.


  
  
To create a daily average value of GHI and PVOUT, data was averaged between 1994 and 2018 for Europe/Africa, 1999 and 2018 for North America/South America/Central Asia, and 2007 and 2018 for East Asia. GHI data was presented in kWh/m² at a spatial resolution of 9 arcsec (250 m). PVOUT data was in kWh/kWp with a spatial resolution of 30 arcsec (1 km).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for diffuse horizontal irradiation, direct normal irradiation, terrain elevation above sea level, global irradiation for optimally tilted surfaces, optimum tilt to maximize yearly yield, and air temperature at 2 m above ground level is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved and pre-processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ene_031a_solar_irradiance).  
  
### Disclaimer

attributes.name: Landslide Susceptibility
attributes.description:
This Global Landslide Susceptibility Map, created by scientists at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and published in 2017 at 1 km resolution, improves upon past landslide susceptibility maps by incorporating the most up-to-date data. NASA scientists evaluated landslide susceptibility on slope from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and forest loss from a Landsat-based record of forest change compiled by a University of Maryland team. They also included data on key factors including the presence of roads from OpenStreetMap, the strength of bedrock and soils, and the locations of faults from the Geological Map of the World, 3rd ed., by Philippe Bouysse (2009). They generated the map using a heuristic fuzzy approach that generated the possibility of landslides and validated it through landslide inventories. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Landslide Susceptibility
info.technical_title: Global Landslide Susceptibility Map
info.functions: Global map of susceptibility to landslides
info.cautions: A disadvantage of a heuristic fuzzy approach to the creation of the map is that the output is a “possibility,” which is not strictly comparable to the probabilities generated by classical statistics; several features of the map thus may limit its use. First, the resolution of the map is approximately 1 km, and terrain varies significantly within many pixels. The choice to aggregate slope by computing the maximum value means that some pixels may contain a very small area of steep terrain, while the remainder is not susceptible to landslides. Second, the use of biased and incomplete landslide inventories to evaluate the susceptibility map makes the results more difficult to interpret. Third, the Geological Map of the World is only appropriate for use over very large areas. At local and national scales, more detailed information is often available, but it varies in quality, format, and cost. Fourth, this map models all mass movements with the same treatment. The real world is more complex, and factors that drive rock toppling in Canada are not the same as those which can cause debris flows in New Guinea. Fifth, this map does not provide an explicit hazard level in the form of an annual probability of slope failure. Therefore it is very likely that landslides will occur at some date in all of the very highly susceptible locations, but the size, frequency, and timing of those events are not known. These limitations suggest that the global susceptibility map is best used for a few purposes: situational awareness of global landslide hotspots and potential occurrence, the development of global decision support systems, and prioritization of future landslide research. It is not appropriate for decisions about infrastructure design, building code legislation, or local land use planning.

info.name: Landslide Susceptibility
info.description:
This Global Landslide Susceptibility Map, created by scientists at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and published in 2017 at 1 km resolution, improves upon past landslide susceptibility maps by incorporating the most up-to-date data. NASA scientists evaluated landslide susceptibility on slope from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and forest loss from a Landsat-based record of forest change compiled by a University of Maryland team. They also included data on key factors including the presence of roads from OpenStreetMap, the strength of bedrock and soils, and the locations of faults from the Geological Map of the World, 3rd ed., by Philippe Bouysse (2009). They generated the map using a heuristic fuzzy approach that generated the possibility of landslides and validated it through landslide inventories. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

info.cautions: A disadvantage of a heuristic fuzzy approach to the creation of the map is that the output is a “possibility,” which is not strictly comparable to the probabilities generated by classical statistics; several features of the map thus may limit its use. First, the resolution of the map is approximately 1 km, and terrain varies significantly within many pixels. The choice to aggregate slope by computing the maximum value means that some pixels may contain a very small area of steep terrain, while the remainder is not susceptible to landslides. Second, the use of biased and incomplete landslide inventories to evaluate the susceptibility map makes the results more difficult to interpret. Third, the Geological Map of the World is only appropriate for use over very large areas. At local and national scales, more detailed information is often available, but it varies in quality, format, and cost. Fourth, this map models all mass movements with the same treatment. info.name: Susceptibilidad a deslizamientos de tierra
info.description:
Este Mapa Global de Susceptibilidad a Deslizamientos de Tierra, creado por científicos de la Administración Nacional de Aeronáutica y del Espacio (NASA) y publicado en 2017 a una resolución de 1 km, mejora los mapas de susceptibilidad a deslizamientos de tierra anteriores al incorporar los datos más actualizados. Científicos de la NASA evaluaron la susceptibilidad a los deslizamientos de tierra en la pendiente de la Misión de Topografía del Radar del Transbordador y la pérdida de bosques de un registro de cambio forestal basado en Landsat compilado por un equipo de la Universidad de Maryland. También incluyeron datos sobre factores clave como la presencia de carreteras de OpenStreetMap, la resistencia del lecho rocoso y los suelos, y las ubicaciones de las fallas del Mapa Geológico del Mundo, 3ª ed., por Philippe Bouysse (2009). Generaron el mapa utilizando un enfoque difuso heurístico que generó la posibilidad de deslizamientos de tierra y lo validó a través de inventarios de deslizamientos. Resource Watch muestra solo un subconjunto del conjunto de datos. Para acceder al conjunto de datos completo e información adicional, consulte el vínculo Más información.

info.technical_title: Mapa Global de Susceptibilidad a Deslizamientos de Tierra
info.functions: Mapa global de susceptibilidad a deslizamientos de tierra
info.cautions: Una desventaja de un enfoque difuso heurístico para la creación del mapa es que la salida es una "posibilidad", que no es estrictamente comparable a las probabilidades generadas por la estadística clásica; por lo tanto, varias características del mapa pueden limitar su uso. Primero, la resolución del mapa es de aproximadamente 1 km, y el terreno varía significativamente dentro de muchos píxeles. La elección de agregar la pendiente calculando el valor máximo significa que algunos píxeles pueden contener un área muy pequeña de terreno escarpado, mientras que el resto no es susceptible a deslizamientos de tierra. En segundo lugar, el uso de inventarios de deslizamientos de tierra sesgados e incompletos para evaluar el mapa de susceptibilidad hace que los resultados sean más difíciles de interpretar. En tercer lugar, el Mapa Geológico del Mundo sólo es apropiado para su uso en áreas muy grandes. A escala local y nacional, a menudo se dispone de información más detallada, pero varía en calidad, formato y costo. Cuarto, este mapa modela todos los movimientos de masas con el mismo tratamiento. El mundo real es más complejo, y los factores que impulsan el derribo de rocas en Canadá no son los mismos que los que pueden causar flujos de escombros en Nueva Guinea. En quinto lugar, este mapa no proporciona un nivel de peligro explícito en forma de una probabilidad anual de falla de la pendiente. Por lo tanto, es muy probable que los deslizamientos de tierra ocurran en alguna fecha en todos los lugares muy susceptibles, pero no se conoce el tamaño, la frecuencia y el momento de esos eventos. Estas limitaciones sugieren que el mapa de susceptibilidad global se utiliza mejor para algunos propósitos: conciencia situacional de los puntos críticos de deslizamiento de tierra globales y la posible ocurrencia, el desarrollo de sistemas globales de apoyo a la toma de decisiones y la priorización de futuras investigaciones sobre deslizamientos de tierra. No es apropiado para decisiones sobre el diseño de infraestructura, la legislación del código de construcción o la planificación local del uso de la tierra.

info.name: மண்சரிவு ஏற்படக்கூடிய தன்மை
info.description:
தேசிய வானூர்தியியல் மற்றும் விண்வெளி நிர்வாகத்தின் (நாசா) விஞ்ஞானிகளால் உருவாக்கப்பட்டு 2017 ஆம் ஆண்டில் 1 கி.மீ தீர்மானத்தில் வெளியிடப்பட்ட இந்த உலகளாவிய நிலச்சரிவு உணர்திறன் வரைபடம், மிகவும் புதுப்பித்த தரவுகளை உள்ளடக்குவதன் மூலம் கடந்த கால நிலச்சரிவு உணர்திறன் வரைபடங்களை மேம்படுத்துகிறது. நாசா விஞ்ஞானிகள் மேரிலாந்து பல்கலைக்கழக குழுவால் தொகுக்கப்பட்ட லேன்ட்சாட் அடிப்படையிலான வன மாற்றம் குறித்த பதிவுகளிலிருந்து ஷட்டில் ரேடார் இடவியல் மிஷனிலிருந்து சரிவில் நிலச்சரிவு மற்றும் வன இழப்பு ஆகியவற்றை மதிப்பீடு செய்தனர். ஓபன்ஸ்ட்ரீட்மேப்பில் இருந்து சாலைகள் இருப்பது, பாறைகள் மற்றும் மண்ணின் வலிமை, மற்றும் உலகின் புவியியல் வரைபடம், 3 வது பதிப்பு, பிலிப் பௌயிஸ் (2009) எழுதிய தவறுகளின் இடங்கள் உள்ளிட்ட முக்கிய காரணிகளின் தரவுகளும் இதில் அடங்கும். அவர்கள் நிலச்சரிவுகளின் சாத்தியத்தை உருவாக்கிய ஒரு ஹியூரிஸ்டிக் தெளிவற்ற அணுகுமுறையைப் பயன்படுத்தி வரைபடத்தை உருவாக்கி, நிலச்சரிவு சரக்குகள் மூலம் அதை சரிபார்த்தனர். Resource Watch தரவுத் தொகுப்பின் ஒரு துணைக்குழுவை மட்டுமே காட்டுகிறது. முழு தரவுத் தொகுப்பு மற்றும் கூடுதல் தகவலுக்கான அணுகலுக்கு, மேலும் அறிக இணைப்பைப் பார்க்கவும்.  
  
### கூடுதல் தகவல்  
  
Resource Watch தரவுத்தொகுப்பின் ஒரு துணைக்குழுவை மட்டுமே காட்டுகிறது. முழு தரவுத்தொகுப்பு மற்றும் கூடுதல் தகவலுக்கான அணுகலுக்கு, "மேலும் அறிக" பொத்தானைக் கிளிக் செய்க.  
  
### பொறுப்புத்துறப்பு  
  
இந்த விளக்கப் பக்கத்தின் பகுதிகள் மூல மெட்டாடேட்டாவிலிருந்து எடுக்கப்பட்டன.
info.technical_title: உலகளாவிய மண்சரிவு உணர்திறன் வரைபடம்
info.functions: நிலச்சரிவுகளுக்கு ஆளாகக்கூடிய தன்மையின் உலகளாவிய வரைபடம்
info.cautions: வரைபடத்தின் உருவாக்கத்திற்கான ஒரு ஹீயூரிஸ்டிக் தெளிவற்ற அணுகுமுறையின் ஒரு குறைபாடு என்னவென்றால், வெளியீடு ஒரு "சாத்தியம்" ஆகும், இது கிளாசிக்கல் புள்ளிவிவரங்களால் உருவாக்கப்படும் நிகழ்தகவுகளுடன் கண்டிப்பாக ஒப்பிட முடியாது; இவ்வாறு வரைபடத்தின் பல அம்சங்கள் அதன் பயன்பாட்டைக் கட்டுப்படுத்தலாம். முதலாவதாக, வரைபடத்தின் தெளிவுத்திறன் தோராயமாக 1 கி.மீ ஆகும், மேலும் நிலப்பரப்பு பல பிக்சல்களுக்குள் கணிசமாக வேறுபடுகிறது. அதிகபட்ச மதிப்பைக் கணக்கிடுவதன் மூலம் சாய்வை ஒருங்கிணைப்பதற்கான தேர்வு என்பது சில பிக்சல்கள் செங்குத்தான நிலப்பரப்பின் மிகச் சிறிய பகுதியைக் கொண்டிருக்கலாம், மீதமுள்ளவை நிலச்சரிவுகளுக்கு ஆளாகாது என்பதாகும். இரண்டாவதாக, பாதிக்கப்படக்கூடிய வரைபடத்தை மதிப்பிடுவதற்கு பக்கச்சார்பான மற்றும் முழுமையற்ற நிலச்சரிவு சரக்குகளைப் பயன்படுத்துவது முடிவுகளை விளக்குவது மிகவும் கடினமாக்குகிறது. மூன்றாவதாக, உலகின் புவியியல் வரைபடம் மிகப் பெரிய பகுதிகளில் பயன்படுத்துவதற்கு மட்டுமே பொருத்தமானது. உள்ளூர் மற்றும் தேசிய அளவுகளில், மேலும் விரிவான தகவல்கள் பெரும்பாலும் கிடைக்கின்றன, ஆனால் அது தரம், வடிவம் மற்றும் செலவில் வேறுபடுகிறது. நான்காவதாக, இந்த வரைபடம் அனைத்து வெகுஜன இயக்கங்களையும் ஒரே சிகிச்சையுடன் மாதிரிப்படுத்துகிறது. உண்மையான உலகம் மிகவும் சிக்கலானது, மேலும் கனடாவில் பாறைகளை கவிழ்க்கும் காரணிகள் நியூ கினியாவில் சிதைவுகளை ஏற்படுத்தும் காரணிகளைப் போலவே இல்லை. ஐந்தாவதாக, இந்த வரைபடம் சரிவு தோல்வியின் வருடாந்திர நிகழ்தகவு வடிவத்தில் வெளிப்படையான ஆபத்து மட்டத்தை வழங்கவில்லை. எனவே மிகவும் பாதிக்கப்படக்கூடிய அனைத்து இடங்களிலும் நிலச்சரிவுகள் ஏதேனும் ஒரு தேதியில் ஏற்பட வாய்ப்புள்ளது, ஆனால் அந்த நிகழ்வுகளின் அளவு, அதிர்வெண் மற்றும் நேரம் ஆகியவை தெரியவில்லை. உலகளாவிய நிலச்சரிவு ஹாட்ஸ்பாட்கள் மற்றும் சாத்தியமான நிகழ்வுகள் பற்றிய சூழ்நிலை விழிப்புணர்வு, உலகளாவிய முடிவு ஆதரவு அமைப்புகளின் வளர்ச்சி மற்றும் எதிர்கால நிலச்சரிவு ஆராய்ச்சிக்கு முன்னுரிமை அளித்தல் போன்ற ஒரு சில நோக்கங்களுக்காக உலகளாவிய உணர்திறன் வரைபடம் சிறந்த முறையில் பயன்படுத்தப்படுகிறது என்று இந்த வரம்புகள் தெரிவிக்கின்றன. உள்கட்டமைப்பு வடிவமைப்பு, கட்டிட குறியீடு சட்டம் அல்லது உள்ளூர் நிலப் பயன்பாட்டுத் திட்டமிடல் பற்றிய முடிவுகளுக்கு இது பொருத்தமானதல்ல.

info.name: కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే అవకాశం
info.description:
నేషనల్ ఏరోనాటిక్స్ అండ్ స్పేస్ అడ్మినిస్ట్రేషన్ (నాసా) శాస్త్రవేత్తలు రూపొందించిన ఈ గ్లోబల్ కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే సున్నితత్వం మ్యాప్, 2017 లో 1 కి.మీ రిజల్యూషన్ తో ప్రచురించబడింది, అత్యంత తాజా డేటాను చేర్చడం ద్వారా గత కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే సంభావ్యత మ్యాప్ లను మెరుగుపరుస్తుంది. నాసా శాస్త్రవేత్తలు షటిల్ రాడార్ టోపోగ్రఫీ మిషన్ నుండి వాలుపై కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే సంభావ్యతను మరియు మేరీల్యాండ్ విశ్వవిద్యాలయం బృందం సంకలనం చేసిన లాండ్ శాట్ ఆధారిత అటవీ మార్పు రికార్డు నుండి అటవీ నష్టాన్ని అంచనా వేశారు. ఓపెన్ స్ట్రీట్ మ్యాప్ నుండి రహదారుల ఉనికి, రాతి మరియు నేలల బలం, మరియు ఫిలిప్ బోయిస్సే (2009) చే జియోలాజికల్ మ్యాప్ ఆఫ్ ది వరల్డ్, 3 వ ఎడిషన్ నుండి లోపాల యొక్క స్థానాలు సహా కీలక కారకాలపై డేటాను కూడా వారు చేర్చారు. కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే అవకాశం ఉన్న ఒక హ్యూరిస్టిక్ మసక విధానాన్ని ఉపయోగించి వారు మ్యాప్ ను రూపొందించారు మరియు కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే జాబితాల ద్వారా దానిని ధృవీకరించారు. రిసోర్స్ వాచ్ డేటా సెట్ యొక్క ఉపసమితిని మాత్రమే చూపుతుంది. పూర్తి డేటా సెట్ మరియు అదనపు సమాచారానికి ప్రాప్యత కోసం, మరింత తెలుసుకోండి లింక్ చూడండి.  
  
### అదనపు సమాచారం  
  
రిసోర్స్ వాచ్ డేటాసెట్ యొక్క ఉపసమితిని మాత్రమే చూపుతుంది. పూర్తి డేటాసెట్ మరియు అదనపు సమాచారాన్ని యాక్సెస్ చేసుకోవడానికి, "మరింత తెలుసుకోండి" బటన్ మీద క్లిక్ చేయండి.  
  
### డిస్ క్లెయిమర్  
  
ఈ వివరణ పేజీ యొక్క సారాంశాలు మూల మెటాడేటా నుండి తీసుకోబడ్డాయి.
info.technical_title: గ్లోబల్ కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే సంభావ్యత మ్యాప్
info.functions: కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడటం యొక్క సున్నితత్త్వం యొక్క గ్లోబల్ మ్యాప్
info.cautions: పటం యొక్క సృష్టికి ఒక హ్యురిస్టిక్ మసక విధానం యొక్క ప్రతికూలత ఏమిటంటే, ఉత్పత్తి అనేది ఒక "సంభావ్యత", ఇది క్లాసికల్ స్టాటిస్టిక్స్ ద్వారా ఉత్పత్తి చేయబడిన సంభావ్యతలతో ఖచ్చితంగా పోల్చదగినది కాదు; అందువల్ల పటం యొక్క అనేక లక్షణాలు దాని ఉపయోగాన్ని పరిమితం చేయవచ్చు. మొదట, పటం యొక్క రిజల్యూషన్ సుమారు 1 కి.మీ, మరియు భూభాగం అనేక పిక్సెల్స్ లోపల గణనీయంగా మారుతుంది. గరిష్ట విలువను లెక్కించడం ద్వారా వాలును అగ్రిగేట్ చేయడానికి ఎంపిక అంటే కొన్ని పిక్సెల్స్ నిటారుగా ఉన్న భూభాగం యొక్క చాలా చిన్న ప్రాంతాన్ని కలిగి ఉండవచ్చు, మిగిలినవి కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే అవకాశం లేదు. రెండవది, సున్నితత్త్వ పటాన్ని మదింపు చేయడానికి పక్షపాత మరియు అసంపూర్ణ కొండచరియల ఇన్వెంటరీలను ఉపయోగించడం వల్ల ఫలితాలను వ్యాఖ్యానించడం మరింత కష్టంగా మారుతుంది. మూడవది, ప్రపంచ భౌగోళిక పటం చాలా పెద్ద ప్రాంతాలలో ఉపయోగించడానికి మాత్రమే తగినది. స్థానిక మరియు జాతీయ ప్రమాణాల వద్ద, మరింత సవిస్తరమైన సమాచారం తరచుగా అందుబాటులో ఉంటుంది, అయితే ఇది నాణ్యత, ఆకృతి మరియు ఖర్చులో మారుతుంది. నాల్గవది, ఈ పటం అన్ని సామూహిక కదలికలను ఒకే చికిత్సతో నమూనా చేస్తుంది. వాస్తవ ప్రపంచం మరింత సంక్లిష్టమైనది, మరియు కెనడాలో రాక్ పడగొట్టడానికి దారితీసే కారకాలు న్యూ గినియాలో శిధిలాల ప్రవాహాలకు కారణమయ్యే కారకాలతో సమానంగా ఉండవు. ఐదవది, ఈ మ్యాప్ వాలు విఫలం కావడం యొక్క వార్షిక సంభావ్యత రూపంలో స్పష్టమైన ప్రమాద స్థాయిని అందించదు. అందువల్ల చాలా సున్నితమైన ప్రదేశాలన్నింటిలో ఏదో ఒక తేదీలో కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడే అవకాశం ఉంది, కానీ ఆ సంఘటనల పరిమాణం, పౌనఃపున్యం మరియు సమయం తెలియదు. ఈ పరిమితులు గ్లోబల్ ససెప్టిబిలిటీ మ్యాప్ ను కొన్ని ప్రయోజనాల కోసం ఉత్తమంగా ఉపయోగిస్తారని సూచిస్తున్నాయి: గ్లోబల్ కొండచరియల హాట్ స్పాట్ లు మరియు సంభావ్య సంభవం యొక్క సందర్భోచిత అవగాహన, గ్లోబల్ డెసిషన్ సపోర్ట్ సిస్టమ్ ల అభివృద్ధి, మరియు భవిష్యత్ కొండచరియల పరిశోధన యొక్క ప్రాధాన్యత. మౌలిక సదుపాయాల రూపకల్పన, బిల్డింగ్ కోడ్ చట్టం లేదా స్థానిక భూ వినియోగ ప్రణాళిక గురించి నిర్ణయాలు తీసుకోవడం సముచితం కాదు.

Land Cover Map
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The global land use and land cover maps were created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution for 2000 and 2020. The GLAD laboratory used the spatiotemporally consistent [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard) to quantify changes in forest extent and height, cropland, built-up lands, surface water, and perennial snow and ice extent over the twenty year period. Each thematic product was independently derived using state-of-the-art, locally and regionally calibrated machine learning tools. The dataset was validated using a statistical sampling which confirms its high accuracy.  
  
  
The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change.  Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) laboratory derived most global thematic products, except open water, using consistently processed [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard). The annual GLAD ARD data time series were integrated into a set of phenological metrics that enabled global model calibration and application. The water mapping was performed using the Landsat data processed in the Google Earth Engine using an approach similar to the GLAD ARD. GLAD used a separate supervised classification model to map each thematic class. The decision tree models calibrated with manually collected training data were implemented for water, cropland, and perennial snow and ice mapping. Forest height was estimated using the regression tree model calibrated with Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation Lidar (GEDI)  forest structure measurements. The built-up lands were mapped using a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm trained using Open Street Map (OSM) data. The models were calibrated locally (for forest height and cropland mapping) or regionally (all other products). GLAD independently validated each global thematic product using statistical sample analysis. The sample reference data were collected through visual image interpretation using the best available high-resolution satellite data and Landsat time series.
  
  
The GLAD ARD product consists of 16-day global Landsat normalized surface reflectance and brightness temperature composites combined from the best quality observations. Each 16-day composite includes the normalized surface reflectance for visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared Landsat bands and brightness temperature, along with the data quality layer. GLAD integrated the annual GLAD ARD 16-day clear-sky time series into a set of rank-based statistics, hereafter named phenology metrics, that enabled the application of the multitemporal classification and regression models. GLAD augmented the Landsat reflectance metrics with topographic metrics, including elevation and slope.
  
  
GLAD defined forest as wildland, managed, and planted tree cover, including agroforestry and orchards. The forest extent was defined as an area with tree cover ≥ 5 m, to ensure consistency with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) forest definition. Nevertheless, their forest definition differs from the one used by the FAO by the inclusion of trees outside forests (agroforestry, orchards, parks) and the exclusion of temporally unstocked forest areas. GLAD employed the global Landsat-based forest height model calibrated for the year 2019 using GEDI observations. For the boreal forests north of 52°N, where GEDI data are absent, GLAD used a regional model approach. Three separate models were calibrated for North America, Europe, and Northern Asia. The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to 2000, 2001, 2003, 2017, 2019, and 2020 annual metrics.The forest height values for the years 2000 and 2020 were calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003, and 2017, 2019, 2020 products, respectively, unless forest loss for the years 2001-2003 or 2017-2020 was indicated by the forest disturbance data (in such case, only the year 2000 or 2020 product value was used, respectively). GLAD produced the year 2000 and 2020 forest extent maps by attributing pixels with ≥ 5 m forest height as the “forest” land cover class. The forest extent change (net forest extent loss and gain) was derived directly from the year 2000 and 2020 map comparison.
  
  
Cropland was defined as land used to produce annual and perennial herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage, and biofuel. The definition excludes tree crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation. Consistent with the FAO arable land category, the fallow length was limited to four years for the cropland class. The cropland mapping was performed for two four-year epochs, 2000-2003 and 2016-2019. For each epoch, they attributed a GLAD ARD pixel as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any year within the interval. The cropland mapping model was calibrated with manually delineated training areas which were extrapolated in space and time through a three-stage algorithm. Supervised classification (bagged decision tree ensembles) was implemented at each of these three steps. The final products were filtered by removing artifacts and cropland patches smaller than 0.5 ha.
  
  
Built-up land consists of man-made land surfaces associated with infrastructure, commercial and residential land uses. At the Landsat spatial resolution, GLAD defined the built-up land class as pixels that include man-made surfaces, even if such surfaces do not dominate within the pixel. Due to the contextual nature of built-up lands, particularly settlements, they employed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm to map this thematic class. Final 2000 and 2020 per-pixel class presence probabilities were generated, and validation data were used to assist in the final thresholding of the layers in depicting 2000 and 2020 extents and 2000-2020 gain in built-up lands. Loss of built-up lands, which represents a small proportion of the year 2000 class area, was not mapped by this provisional product.
  
  
Open surface water, or simply water, is defined as inland water that covers ≥ 50% of a pixel and is not obscured by objects above the surface.The presented multidecadal surface water change product is based on the annual water presence dataset produced by Pickens et al. (2020). Water presence is a percent of Landsat observations classified as surface water of all annual clear-sky observations calculated per pixel. Instead of the GLAD ARD, the algorithm employed the original Collection 1 Tier 1 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes from 1999-2020. GLAD classified each Landsat scene into the land, water, and unusable data classes using an ensemble of hierarchical, bagged classification trees developed for ARD data processing.
  
  
The perennial snow and ice layer includes land covered by glaciers and snow which remains during the entire year. The map is limited to the GLAD ARD tiles where perennial snow and ice areas were detected using the ARD observation quality layer. GLAD mapped permanent snow and ice using regionally calibrated supervised classification models (decision tree ensembles). Overall, they used fourteen models, one model per mountain system or a geographic region. Each classification model was calibrated with manually collected training data from multitemporal Landsat metrics.
  
  
 Wetlands are treated as a landform containing multiple land cover classes. Topographical metrics, including slope, curvature, and a series of relative elevation layers from variably sized catchments were used to determine wetland versus terra firma. Percent bare ground was included from a previous assessment.   
  
GLAD validated each thematic product separately using an independently collected reference data sample. GLAD used different strata designs for each thematic product to target not only the LCLU class of interest but also the potential class omission errors. For product validation, the map and reference data were presented as discrete LCLU classes. The map accuracy metrics include overall accuracy (the proportion of correctly mapped sample pixels), user’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class commission), and producer’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class omission). Map accuracy statistics were accompanied by the standard error of the estimate (s.e.). We also estimated sample-based areas of LCLU classes and changes with the corresponding s.e. 
  
  
The global composite maps were created by layering an annual vegetation fraction layer with the bare land, wetland landform, followed by the superseding classes of ice, water, cropland, and built-up. The 2019 global composite map can be viewed and downloaded [here](https://glad.umd.edu/dataset/global-land-cover-land-use-v1). For the full documentation of the [landform classes](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ac46ec) and other [thematic classes](https://doi.org/10.3389/frsen.2022.856903), please see the original methodology.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), and [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer

info.name: Land Cover Map
info.technical_title: Global Land Cover and Land Use Change, 2000-2020
info.functions: Global land use and land cover map for 2000 and 2020
info.cautions:
- Land cover mapping was limited by the Landsat clear-sky data availability. The incompleteness of the Landsat observation time series decreases the map accuracy in regions with persistent cloud cover.
  
  
- Discrete land cover classes mapping in heterogeneous landscapes was constrained by the high proportion of mixed pixels at the Landsat spatial resolution. Most LULC classes have higher map accuracy over large homogeneous areas compared to fragmented landscapes and class patch edges.
  
  
- The spectral similarity between different LCLU classes may preclude class discrimination.
  
  
- The forest height product has issues related to GEDI data quality and Landsat data availability. Small changes in forest height between the years 2000 and 2020 may not indicate the actual forest structure change but represent the noise in the model outputs.
  
  
- Dynamic classes (LCLU class loss and gain) have lower accuracies compared to static maps.
  
  
- Map-based estimates are not adequate for national and international reporting due to unknown spatial and temporal variability of map uncertainty.

attributes.name: Trees in Mosaic Landscapes
attributes.description:
### Overview    
  
The trees in mosaic landscapes (TML) data maps tree extent at the ten-meter scale and enables accurate monitoring of trees in urban areas, agricultural lands, and in open canopy and dry forest ecosystems. The data extent covers 1.4 billion hectares of mosaic landscapes in Latin America and Africa. Mosaic landscapes are defined as regions that can support a wide variety of tree distributions, including sparse tree cover, scattered or clustered open canopy forests, and fragmented closed-canopy forests. 
The data is derived from multi-temporal convolutional neural network models applied to Sentinel optical and radar imagery. Each pixel demarcates the presence of one or more trees with canopy diameters larger than 3 meters and height greater than 5 meters. The value for each pixel represents the sigmoidal probability of detecting a tree , and can be converted to tree cover by averaging the values within a desired window size (e.g. 30 x 30 meter or half-hectare). The data relies on 3 cloud-free observations for 2020 (<97.5% average cloud cover) and less than 1% of the processing area is missing due to the lack of cloud-free observations. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data is generated by analyzing monthly cloud-free mosaics of Sentinel-2 optical imagery and Sentinel-1 radar imagery. We utilize the 10- and 20-meter bottom-of-atmosphere (L2A) bands from Sentinel-2 and the co-polarized vertical transmit/vertical receive (VV) and cross-polarized vertical transmit/horizontal receive (VH) imagery from Sentinel-1. The model used is a modified U-Net convolutional neural network with a temporal gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder. The methodology is derived from [Brandt and Stolle (2020)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01431161.2020.1841324) with additional improvements to be detailed in a forthcoming paper. Code and model specifics can be accessed on the project [GitHub page](https://github.com/wri/sentinel-tree-cover).

For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.  
  
### Visualizing the Data

info.name: Trees in Mosaic Landscapes
info.technical_title: Trees in Mosaic Landscapes
info.functions: Tree extent in urban areas, agricultural lands, and in open canopy and dry forest ecosystems.
info.cautions:
The TML data is still a draft product and data for some regions are subject to change in the future. In its draft form, TML provides complimentary monitoring data for mosaic and non-forested ecosystems when utilized with the [Hansen et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1244693) data. Combining with the Hansen et al. (2013) data achieves complete coverage, as TML does not currently cover steppe grasslands or dense, contiguous forests. While the dataset properly excludes non-tree crops, such as tea, sugar, banana, and cacti, it currently does not disambiguate plantation trees from non-plantation trees. 

  
  
Inconsistent imagery selection during the data production process may cause inaccurate predictions or visual artifacts in the data. Visual artifacts are artificial distortions in the image that degrade the performance of the image analysis. The issue, which can appear as a line of partially inconsistent pixel values in the image, stems from inconsistent imagery selection between neighboring tiles. Corrections will be retroactively applied in version 1.1 of the data product, but the following regions may be affected in the draft data: 

  
  
- Mali near the border with southern Mauritania 
  
  
- Sudan near the borders with Central African Republic and South Sudan 
  
  
- Parts of coastal Kenya, Tanzania, and Somalia 

  
  
In some cases, data quality issues arise at the boundary between Sentinel orbits, which takes place at 290 km longitudinal intervals. Canopy shapes and brightness can be represented differently due to the different angles at which Sentinel satellites acquire images, resulting in high variability in a canopy’s spectral signature. This makes it much harder to use remote sensing vegetation indices, which are based on special characteristics in spectral features, to distinguish mosaic tree cover. This issue primarily affects regions where the algorithm attempts to distinguish between closed canopy shrubs and closed canopy forests.

  
  
TML defines mosaic landscapes based on the pre-existing stratification of land cover classes in the 2015 European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative (CCI) 300 meter land cover product. The processing extent and analysis use these classifications to extract areas of interest, and therefore are subject to its associated limitations and errors. This can manifest as the irregular/inconsistent processing of a single 6 x 6 km tile.
info.citation: Brandt, J. & Ertel., J. 2021. The extent of trees in mosaic landscapes. Working Paper
info.geographic_coverage: The current processing extent covers 1.4 billion hectares across Latin America and Africa.
info.frequency_of_updates: The draft TML data will be finalized for the current processing area in early 2022 and will be extended across non-deserted regions in the tropics and subtropics during the latter half of 2022. A yearly or biannual change detection map is planned for 2023.

attributes.name: Intact Forest Landscapes
attributes.description:
The Intact Forest Landscapes (IFL) data set identifies unbroken expanses of natural ecosystems within the zone of forest extent that show no signs of significant human activity and are large enough that all native biodiversity, including viable populations of wide-ranging species, could be maintained. To map IFL areas, a set of criteria was developed and designed to be globally applicable and easily replicable, the latter to allow for repeated assessments over time as well as verification. IFL areas were defined as unfragmented landscapes, at least 50,000 ha in size, and with a minimum width of 10 km. These were then mapped from Landsat satellite imagery for the year 2000. Changes in the extent of IFLs were identified within year 2000 IFL boundary using the global wall-to-wall Landsat image composite for year 2013 and the global forest cover loss data set (Hansen et al. 2013). Areas identified as “reduction in extent” met the IFL criteria in 2000 but no longer met the criteria in 2013. The main causes of change were clearing for agriculture and tree plantations, industrial activity such as logging and mining, fragmentation due to infrastructure and new roads, and fires assumed to be caused by humans. These data can be used to assess forest intactness, alteration, and degradation at global and regional scales. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

cli.057.rw1 Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation
Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).  
  
### Disclaimer

- The downscaling approaches used to produce these indicators inherently assume that the relative spatial patterns in temperature and precipitation will remain constant under future climate change. Dramatic shifts in global weather patterns, such as the slowing or reversal of major air and ocean currents are possible, but will not be captured in these indicators.

attributes.name: Cambio proyectado en la precipitación acumulada
attributes.description:
### Visión general  
  
El conjunto de datos de cambio proyectado en la precipitación acumulativa muestra el cambio en la precipitación total promedio anual a intervalos de diez años entre 2000 y 2080, en comparación con un período de referencia de 1960-1990. Los datos mostrados en cada intervalo de diez años representan un promedio de 31 años, centrado en torno al año indicado. Por ejemplo, la precipitación total en 2000 es en realidad un promedio de la precipitación acumulada entre los años 1985 y 2015. Las proyecciones de precipitación se basan en las futuras tasas de emisión de gases de efecto invernadero determinadas por las Vías de Concentración Representativa (RCP) 8.5 del Grupo Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático (IPCC). RCP 8.5 es un escenario hipotético en el que no hay disminución en las tasas de emisión de gases de efecto invernadero dentro del siglo XXI. La precipitación media acumulada se divide por el promedio de referencia para calcular el cambio proyectado. Los valores mayores que 1 indican que la precipitación acumulada está aumentando, mientras que los valores menores de uno indican que el número está disminuyendo. Los datos se presentan a una resolución espacial de 0,25°.
  
El aumento en las concentraciones globales de gases de efecto invernadero, y el cambio resultante en el clima, alterará fundamentalmente nuestra relación con el planeta, afectando la agricultura, la infraestructura, la gestión de desastres y los conflictos humanos. Con el fin de anticipar y adaptarse a estos cambios, el conjunto de datos de cambio proyectado en la precipitación acumulativa proporciona proyecciones sobre cómo es probable que cambien los patrones de precipitación en las próximas décadas. Se proyecta que los cambios en las precipitaciones serán más variados en todo el mundo, mostrando generalmente aumentos en la precipitación media en las regiones de latitudes altas y un cambio de polos de las regiones áridas subtropicales. Además, se proyecta que la precipitación ocurra en menos eventos, pero más intensos. Excepto en las pocas áreas que se proyecta que verán un secado sustancial, se espera que los eventos de precipitación históricamente extremos se vuelvan más frecuentes en todo el mundo. Incluso a medida que aumenta la precipitación, se proyecta que los períodos secos aumentarán en longitud y frecuencia. 
  
Este conjunto de datos ha sido procesado por Vizzuality y el Instituto de Recursos Mundiales utilizando el National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). El conjunto de datos NEX-GDDP está destinado a ayudar a la comunidad científica a realizar estudios de los impactos del cambio climático a escala local a regional, y mejorar la comprensión pública de los posibles patrones climáticos globales futuros a escala espacial de pueblos, ciudades y cuencas hidrográficas individuales. Una versión anterior de este conjunto de datos fue procesada y producida por la [Asociación para la Resiliencia y la Preparación (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), ayudando en la misión de PREP de construir resiliencia al cambio climático mejorando el acceso a los datos climáticos.  
  
### Metodología  
  
El conjunto de datos de cambio proyectado en la precipitación acumulativa se creó con datos de precipitación de NEX-GDDP. Los conjuntos de datos NEX-GDDP se derivaron de los experimentos del Modelo de Circulación Global (GCM) que se produjeron para el [Quinto Informe de Evaluación (AR5) del Grupo Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático (IPCC)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). Estos experimentos, conocidos como el Proyecto de Intercomparación de Modelos Acoplados fase 5 (CMIP5) incluyeron resultados de modelos climáticos diseñados para simular el clima bajo diferentes niveles de concentraciones de gases de efecto invernadero.  

Los datos de CMIP5 incluyen un gran número de modelos (45), escenarios climáticos (4), años (más de 150) y variables (20-40). Incluso a su resolución gruesa (1-4 °) esto resulta en miles de millones de capas. Al reducir la escala, NEX-GDDP extrae solo los datos que requieren y reduce el tamaño general de los datos, utilizando el conjunto de datos [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) como referencia histórica.  

La precipitación acumulada para cada año, modelo climático y escenario se calculó utilizando datos de NEX-GDDP por píxel. Esto se hizo agregando todos los datos de precipitación diaria durante un año determinado. Las precipitaciones acumuladas se combinaron en promedios de 31 años para el período de referencia de 1960-1990 y nueve períodos centrados en el comienzo de cada década de 2000 a 2080. Luego, cada una de las nueve décadas proyectadas se dividió por el promedio de referencia para calcular el cambio proyectado en la precipitación acumulada. Los valores superiores a 1 indican que la precipitación acumulada está aumentando, mientras que los valores inferiores a uno indican que la precipitación acumulada está disminuyendo.

Los datos mostrados en cada intervalo de diez años representan un promedio de 31 años, centrado en torno al año indicado. Por ejemplo, la precipitación acumulada en 2000 se calculó como un promedio de la precipitación acumulada entre los años 1985 y 2015. Se eligieron promedios de 31 años porque minimizan los efectos de la variación anual y decenal y resaltan la señal climática a largo plazo. El período de referencia se seleccionó para alinearse con la orientación de larga data de la Asociación Meteorológica Mundial.
  
### Información adicional  
  
Resource Watch también muestra el cambio proyectado NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 datos para [Cambio proyectado en la temperatura media anual](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Cambio proyectado en la temperatura mínima promedio anual](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Cambio proyectado en la temperatura máxima promedio anual](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Proyectado Cambio en los días de grado de calefacción](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Cambio proyectado en los días de grado de enfriamiento](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Cambio proyectado en la temporada libre de heladas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Cambio proyectado en días de calor extremo](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [ Cambio proyectado en períodos secos](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Cambio proyectado en días de precipitación extrema](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

Resource Watch muestra solo un subconjunto de los datos. Se dispone de datos adicionales para el escenario de emisiones RCP 4.5. Para obtener acceso al conjunto de datos original de NEX-GDDP e información adicional, consulte el vínculo Más información.
  
### Visualización de los datos  
  
Nuestro equipo reformateó este conjunto de datos antes de mostrarlo en Resource Watch. Consulte la documentación sobre cómo Resource Watch procesó los datos en [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).  
  
### Descargo de responsabilidad  
  
Extractos de esta página de descripción fueron tomados de los metadatos de origen.

info.functions: Variación proyectada en la precipitación acumulada anual
info.cautions:
- Algunos GCM se desempeñan mejor que otros en la recreación de patrones climáticos regionales, como los monzones, en hindcasts. Para aplicaciones específicas, puede ser apropiado seleccionar modelos individuales basados en el rendimiento regional.
Los enfoques de reducción de escala utilizados para producir estos indicadores asumen inherentemente que los patrones espaciales relativos en temperatura y precipitación se mantendrán constantes bajo el cambio climático futuro. Los cambios dramáticos en los patrones climáticos globales, como la desaceleración o reversión de las principales corrientes aéreas y oceánicas son posibles, pero no se capturarán en estos indicadores.
- Los datos históricos utilizados para la reducción de escala varían en calidad en todo el mundo. En particular, las áreas que tienen registros cortos o una cobertura escasa de observaciones meteorológicas in situ pueden tener una precisión reducida.
Debido a que los GCM son desarrollados por equipos de investigación independientes e incorporan diferentes supuestos y mecanismos, es probable que cubran un rango sustancial de futuros probables. Proporcionamos estimaciones bajas y altas para que los usuarios puedan ver y evaluar este rango probable de resultados.
info.citation:
Gassert, F., E. Cornejo y E. Nilson. 2021. Nota técnica "Making Climate Data Accessible: Methods for Producing NEX-GDDP and LOCA Downscaled Climate Indicators". Washington, DC: Instituto de Recursos Mundiales. Disponible en línea en https://www.wri.org/research/making-climate-data-accessible. [www.resourcewatch.org] (https://www.resourcewatch.org/).

Reconocemos al Grupo de Trabajo sobre Modelización Acoplada del Programa Mundial de Investigación Climática, que es responsable de CMIP, y agradecemos a los grupos de modelado climático por producir y poner a disposición sus resultados de modelos. El Programa de Diagnóstico e Intercomparación de Modelos Climáticos del Departamento de Energía de los Estados Unidos proporciona apoyo coordinado y desarrollo de infraestructura de software en asociación con la Organización Global de Portales de Ciencias del Sistema Terrestre para CMIP.

Los escenarios climáticos utilizados fueron del conjunto de datos NEX-GDDP, preparado por el Climate Analytics Group y el Centro de Investigación Ames de la NASA utilizando el NASA Earth Exchange, y distribuido por el Centro de Simulación Climática de la NASA (NCCS).
