attributes.name: [Archived] Tree Cover Gain
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d305958d-3468-4a35-9660-5e18aa3e3190) as a replacement.**_
  
This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and  the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, measures areas of tree cover gain across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at 30 × 30 m resolution, displayed as a 12-year cumulative layer. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. Over 600,000 Landsat 7 images were compiled and analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis. The clear land surface observations (30 × 30 m pixels) in the satellite images were assembled, and a supervised learning algorithm was then applied to identify per pixel tree cover gain. Tree cover gain was defined as the establishment of tree canopy at the Landsat pixel scale in an area that previously had no tree cover. Tree cover gain may indicate a number of potential activities, including natural forest growth or the crop rotation cycle of tree plantations. The tree cover canopy density of the displayed data is >50%. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

info.name: [Archived] Tree Cover Gain
info.technical_title: Global Forest Change 2000–2016
info.functions: Areas of tree cover gain
info.cautions: In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 m in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. “Gain” is defined as the establishment of tree canopy at the Landsat pixel scale in an area that previously had no tree cover. Tree cover gain may indicate a number of potential activities, including natural forest growth or the crop rotation cycle of tree plantations. Due to variation in research methodology and date of content, tree cover, loss, and gain data sets cannot be compared accurately against each other. Accordingly, “net” loss cannot be calculated by subtracting figures for tree cover gain from tree cover loss, and current (post-2000) tree cover cannot be determined by subtracting figures for annual tree cover loss from year 2000 tree cover. The authors evaluated the overall prevalence of false positives (commission errors) in these data at 24%, and the prevalence of false negatives (omission errors) at 26%, though the accuracy varies by biome and thus may be higher or lower in any particular location.

attributes.name: Food Price Spikes
attributes.description: The Alert for Price Spices (ALPS) is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP). This alert indicates when prices of key staple food commodities have deviated from seasonal trends, and by how much. Early detection of food price increases can alert the international community to the possibility of current and future food insecurity in a region.    Seasonal price trends are determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Food and Commodity Price Database, which is collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. A linear regression is used to determine the contributions that 2 components make to seasonal price trends: the month of the year (related to harvest times) and the overall passage of time (related to population growth, inflation rates, etc.).    The current ALPS value for a food commodity is the number of standard deviations the current price is above the commodity's expected price for that month. Based on this ALPS value, markets are assigned to 1 of 4 situations, where all nominal values are measured in standard deviations from the seasonal mean price:     Normal, ALPS < 0.25  Stress, 0.25 < ALPS < 1  Alert, 1 < ALPS < 2  Crisis, ALPS >= 2 Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

info.name: Food Price Spikes
info.technical_title: Food Price Forecasting and Alert for Price Spikes
info.functions: Indicates when prices of key staple food commodities have deviated from seasonal trends, and by how much.
info.cautions: These alerts are a result of a statistical process that compares current prices to seasonal trends in prices. It does not account explicitly for other factors in the general economy, such as general price inflation rates, that may impact how seriously fluctuations in key staple food prices affect local buying power and food security.    The linear regression used to calculate the seasonal trends and variability in prices assumes that the time series of prices is stationary for each market---i.e., that the nature of the trend doesn't vary over time for each market. The general economic forces affecting prices, such as population growth and inflation, are implicitly represented by the coefficient of the trend term in the linear regression. Under the assumption of stationarity these forces are assumed to be constant for each market, but this may not be realistic.     For more information on ALPS methodology and limits of interpretation, refer to the WFP's technical note on how to calculate and interpret the ALPS: http://documents.wfp.org/stellent/groups/public/documents/manual_guide_proced/wfp264186.pdf.

attributes.name: wat.011 Global riverine Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (p) input, retention, and export
Riverine Nitrogen (N) and Phosphorus (P) Input, Retention, and Export
attributes.description:
The Integrated Model to Assess the Global Environment—Global Nutrient Model (IMAGE-GNM) is a global distributed, spatially explicit model using hydrology as the basis for describing nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) delivery to surface water, transport, and in-stream retention in rivers, lakes, wetlands, and reservoirs. It is part of the integrated assessment model IMAGE, which studies the interaction between society and the environment over prolonged time periods. In the IMAGE-GNM model, grid cells receive water with dissolved and suspended N and P from upstream grid cells; inside grid cells, N and P are delivered to water bodies via diffuse sources (surface runoff, shallow and deep groundwater, riparian zones, litterfall in floodplains, atmospheric deposition) and point sources (wastewater); N and P retention in a water body is calculated on the basis of the residence time of the water and nutrient uptake velocity; subsequently, water and nutrients are transported to downstream grid cells. Differences between model results and observed concentrations for a range of global rivers are acceptable given the global scale of the uncalibrated model. Sensitivity analysis with data for the year 2000 showed that runoff is a major factor for N and P delivery, retention, and river export. For both N and P, uptake velocity and all factors used to compute the subgrid in-stream retention are important for total in-stream retention and river export. Soil N budgets, wastewater, and all factors determining litterfall in floodplains are important for N delivery to surface water. For P the factors that determine the P content of the soil (soil P content and bulk density) are important factors for delivery and river export. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Wind Energy Potential
attributes.description:
Vaisala created this global data set of average annual wind speeds at 80 m above the Earth's surface, a common height for wind turbines when the data set was originally created in 2008. The map resolution is 2 arc minutes and average wind speeds are measured in m/s. These data can be used to identify regions of the world likely to have sufficient wind resources to make wind energy generation a worthwhile investment. Vaisala pioneered the use of numerical weather prediction (NWP) models for producing realistic wind flows around the world to better understand and predict wind energy generation. NWP models are physically based and use powerful supercomputers to simulate the interaction between the entire atmosphere and the Earth's surface, even in places where no direct observations are available. This methodology captures the myriad processes responsible for wind—from jet-level dynamics to surface-level processes—and creates a more robust and accurate wind climatology. In essence, the models use numerical methods to obtain approximate answers to mathematical equations that describe the physics and dynamics of the atmosphere. To solve these equations for different locations on the globe, the atmosphere is divided into many small elements, both horizontally and vertically. The model computes what happens within each model element and how much mass, energy, and momentum is exchanged between the model elements. In 2008, with the release of its global wind data set, Vaisala was the first to map global wind potential at high resolution by using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and conducting a 10-year computer simulation at a 2 arc minute (approximately 5 km) resolution. This data set can be used for rapid prospecting for wind energy generation sites or conducting national or regional infrastructure, policy, or transmission planning. However, the development of specific utility-scale projects requires additional site-specific research after this step. The global wind data set is intended as a tool to help to narrow the focus of project developers and investors to accelerate the growth of wind energy worldwide. The data set was validated against publicly available wind speed observations from more than 4,000 globally distributed meteorological stations from the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Automated Data Processing (ADP) surface observations data set. For more validation information, please visit http://www.vaisala.com/en/energy/Documents/WEA-ERG-3TIER-Global%20Wind%20Dataset.pdf. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information

attributes.subtitle: Earthstat

attributes.name: [Archived] Observed and Potential Crop Yields
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](01ae2fd7-b818-429f-a27e-a36c8def971a) as a replacement.**_
  
The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Earthquake Frequency and Distribution
attributes.description:
The Global Earthquake Hazard Frequency and Distribution data set is created by the World Bank Group, the Columbia University Center for Hazards and Risk Research (Columbia CHRR), and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN). The data are released in a 2.5 minute grid utilizing Advanced National Seismic System (ANSS) Earthquake Catalog data of actual earthquake events exceeding 4.5 on the Richter scale during the time period 1976 through 2002. To produce the final output, the frequency of an earthquake hazard is calculated for each grid cell, and the resulting grid cells are then classified into deciles (10 classes consisting of an approximately equal number of grid cells). The greater the grid cell value in the final output, the higher the relative frequency of hazard posed by earthquakes. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Historical Sea Ice Medians
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Historical Sea Ice Medians dataset shows monthly median sea ice extent over the period of 1981-2010. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments for both the Arctic and Antarctic regions. Satellite data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Gridded ice concentration estimates were used to define the ice edge position that is typical for each month. This dataset shows the maximum (blue line) and minimum (yellow line) sea ice extent, and the typical sea ice extent for each month in between. In the Arctic, sea ice normally reaches its maximum extent in March and its minimum extent in September. Antarctic sea ice extent peaks in September and reaches its minimum in February. The lines in this dataset represent how sea ice expands and retreats between its maximum and minimum extent.

  
  
This dataset is the [baseline](https://nsidc.org/data/noaa/baseline-change) for sea ice index products from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Climate baselines are used as a historical reference to current trends and anomalies. A three-decade time period is ideal because it averages out short-term variability. This dataset can be used to understand how polar sea ice extent and melting season are changing. Antarctic sea ice behaves differently than Arctic sea ice, largely because the two regions have different land-ocean configurations. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has declined since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. Comparing current sea ice extent data to this baseline dataset can help define the rates and locations of sea ice retreat. 

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Historical Sea Ice Medians were generated from data collected by five sensors:
- [Nimbus-7](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987
- [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991
- DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995
- DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007
- DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to December 2017

  
  
The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. The SMMR sensor collected data on alternate days and the SSM/I and SSMIS sensor collected data on a daily basis. Daily satellite measurements were averaged each month to eliminate errors and smooth variations caused by short-term weather conditions. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell.

  
  
Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Median ice extents were calculated by applying the 15% cutoff to all gridded concentration data for each month between 1981 and 2010. Cells that classified as ice more than 50% of the time from 1981-2010 were designated as ice; cells that classified as ice less than 50% of the time were designated as water. This was done on a monthly basis: for example, the data from every January from 1981-2010 was analyzed together to create a single January dataset. Each month’s gridded concentration data was mapped and a contour line was drawn to mark the ice edge. This contour line represents the median sea ice extent. Because the sea ice extent varies considerably from year to year, the median extent is a better representation of the sea ice extent over time. The workflow was applied to both the Arctic and Antarctic regions.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a).


  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends dataset shows the average annual change in crop yield from 1989-2008. Agricultural crop yield is the amount of crop harvested per area of land. It is used to measure a crop’s performance. This study used approximately 1.8 million agricultural census reports from 13,500 political units around the world to determine how crop yield changed over time. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes, which is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.”
  
  
Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. In order to meet projected demand, [crop production needs to double by 2050](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2296#MOESM1532). Improving crop yield, instead of clearing new land for agriculture, is one of the preferred solutions. In many areas, yield is stagnant or has collapsed entirely. Understanding where improvement is most needed can guide new agricultural investments. It is also important to identify and continue improving yield of high-performing crops and regions.  

  
  
This dataset was produced by EarthStat, a collaboration between the Global Landscapes Initiative (GLI) at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment (LUGE) lab at the University of British Columbia (UBC). EarthStat’s mission is to provide data on the global food system to help others make science-based decisions. The GLI is a scientific initiative that develops and applies tools to characterize global land use and evaluate global agricultural supply and demand trends. The LUGE lab is a research group that studies links between land use, global environmental change, and food security.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Approximately 1.8 million census reports were used to determine yield of the four crops for the years between 1989 and 2008. Crop yield is the ratio of production (kilograms) and harvested area (hectares). According to the UN’s [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)](http://www.fao.org/waicent/faostat/agricult/pr_ele-e.htm), production is the amount of crop harvested. The harvested area is the area from which the crop is gathered. National-level data used in this study was provided by the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home), who collects data from the member countries’ statistical offices. At the time of the study, the FAO had crop data for 226 nations. In addition to national-level data, the study also used subnational data for the 51 countries that account for more than 70% of global production/harvested area for each of the four crops. Data was available at the state/province level for all 51 countries and county/district/município/department level for an additional 17 countries. This data was collected from these countries’ agricultural and statistical bureaus. 

  
  
According to the data provider, studies have used linear regression to project future crop yields. As such, the annual crop yields in this study (one data point per year) were linearly regressed to calculate the average change in yield from 1989-2008. A linear regression is a line modeled to fit the shape of a group of data points. The slope of the line gives the rate of change–in this case, the average yield change over the observed period. This calculation was performed for each crop at each political unit. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0066428#pone.0066428.s017).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer

info.cautions:
- This data does not contain unique data for each grid cell as it is aggregated based on administrative unit reporting.
- Reporting frequency varied among countries. Crop data was interpolated in situations where the crop was known to have been harvested, but data was missing for one or multiple years. Data was interpolated from the average production and harvested area data for the nearest five years before the missing year(s). 
- Data quality may be poor in some countries and years where complete or accurate information is lacking. Political strife, weak institutions, incentives to misreport data, or lack of access to proprietary data can diminish data quality. 
- Yield was derived from production and harvested area figures. If yield data was available, but either production or harvested area data was missing, missing data was calculated from the provided yield.
- Subnational data was collected directly from the country’s governmental agencies. This data was quality checked by summing production and harvested area data and comparing it to national data from the FAO. FAO data was used if there was a discrepancy between the two.

attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](ac6dcdb3-2beb-4c66-9f83-565c16c2c914) as a replacement.**_
  
The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: Earthquakes
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Earthquakes dataset shows all earthquakes that have occurred within the last seven days, earthquakes with a magnitude of 5.0+ within the last 30 days, and significant earthquakes within the last 30 days. Earthquakes are deemed significant based on a combination of their magnitude, number of Did You Feel It (DYFI) responses, and Prompt Assessment of Global Earthquakes for Response (PAGER) alert level. The dataset shows earthquakes that have occurred globally and is updated within 15 minutes of an earthquake’s occurrence. The location of each earthquake is designated by longitude and latitude and listed with its magnitude.

  
  
The dataset is part of the Earthquake Hazards Program created by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) with assistance from contributing government agencies around the world. The Earthquake Hazards Program works to provide and apply relevant earthquake science information and knowledge for reducing deaths, injuries, and property damage from earthquakes through understanding of their characteristics and effects and by providing the information and knowledge needed to mitigate these losses. This dataset serves as a way to track and understand where earthquakes occur, which is integral in mitigating earthquake hazards for the future.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The USGS created this dataset by collecting and compiling near-real-time seismological information, alerts, and reports of earthquakes from over 100 contributing institutions and government agencies around the world. Seismological information was largely collected by remote sensors placed and monitored by these groups. The USGS then utilized the information collected to calculate the significance level for each earthquake. An earthquake’s significance was determined by using the following formula based on magnitude (mag), PAGER alert level (pager), and Did You Feel It Score (DYFI):

  
  
Significance = max(mag_significance, pager_significance) + dyfi_significance

  
  
mag_significance = magnitude  x  100  x  (magnitude / 6.5)
  
  
pager_significance = red is 2000, orange is 1000,  yellow is 500, and green is 0
  
  
dyfi_significance = min(num_responses, 1000)  x  (max_cdi / 10)
  
  
Any event that received a significance score over 600 was considered a significant event in the dataset. 
  
  
PAGER is an automated system that rapidly estimates earthquake shaking and the scope and impact of earthquakes around the world. PAGER delivers rapid estimates of the total number of people and settlements exposed to a wide range of shaking from light to catastrophic. Additionally, it provides estimates of potential fatalities, as well as the approximate economic impact an earthquake may cause. PAGER alert levels are assigned as follows:
- Red = 1000+ fatalities and $1 billion+ estimated losses
- Orange = 100-999 fatalities and $100 million - $1 billion estimated losses
- Yellow = 1-99 fatalities and $1 million - $100 million estimated losses
- Green = 0 fatalities and less than $1million estimated losses
  
  
Did You Feel It (DYFI) is a program run by the USGS. It is a system that was developed to tap the abundant information available about earthquakes from the people who experience them. It is made up of an online questionnaire where people provide a description of what they experienced, the effects of the earthquake, and the extent of damage. For each earthquake the responses are aggregated for users in each community and a single intensity score is assigned, called “Community Decimal Intensity” (CDI), to that community.
  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data specifically for the U.S.z on all earthquakes that have occurred over the last 1 day, 7 days, and 30 days is available. Further data on each earthquake’s depth of occurrence, Did You Feel It score, ShakeMap score, and PAGER alert level is also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/dis_001_significant_earthquakes). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.   
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.name: Earthquakes
info.technical_title: Earthquake Catalog
info.functions: Significant earthquakes or earthquakes over a magnitude of five that have occured within the last 30 days
info.cautions:
- This should not be considered to be a complete list of all events in the U.S. and adjacent areas. Additionally, it should not be considered to be a complete list of all 4.5+ magnitude events in the world. 

- The USGS may not rapidly locate earthquakes smaller than 5.0 outside the U.S. unless they have caused significant damage or are widely felt. Earthquakes this small rarely cause significant damage. 

- Other agencies may report an earthquake with a larger magnitude than what the USGS computes, especially for non-U.S. events near magnitude 5.0. If the USGS magnitude for the event is less than magnitude 5.0, it may not have a rapid report issued for it. 

- Earthquakes occurring outside the U.S. and smaller than about magnitude 4.5 can be difficult for the USGS to locate if there is not enough data. The USGS continues to receive data from observatories throughout the world for several months after the events occur. Using this data, it adds new events and revises existing events in later publications. 

- PAGER loss estimates will always have a level of  uncertainty due to its rapid approach, uncertain earthquake information, and uncertain building vulnerability data. For this reason, the human and economic loss results that PAGER produces fall under ranges of likelihoods. In most cases, with time and additional information available, PAGER's results become more accurate.
info.citation: United States Geological Survey. N.D. "Latest Earthquakes." Retrieved from [www.earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/map/](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/map/). Accessed through Resource Watch, (date). [www.resourcewatch.org](https://www.resourcewatch.org/).

depth_in_km.description: Depth of the event in kilometers.

mag.description: Earthquake magnitude is a measure of the size of an earthquake at its source. It is a logarithmic measure. At the same distance from the earthquake, the amplitude of the seismic waves from which the magnitude is determined are approximately 10 times as large during a magnitude 5 earthquake as during a magnitude 4 earthquake. The total amount of energy released by the earthquake usually goes up by a larger factor: for many commonly used magnitude types, the total energy of an average earthquake goes up by a factor of approximately 32 for each unit increase in magnitude.

place.description: Textual description of named geographic region near to the event. This may be a city name, or a Flinn-Engdahl Region name.

sig.description: A number describing how significant the event is. Larger numbers indicate a more significant event. This value is determined on a number of factors, including: magnitude, maximum MMI, felt reports, and estimated impact.

alert.description: The alert level from the PAGER earthquake impact scale, includes “green”, “yellow”, “orange” and “red”.

cdi.description: The maximum reported intensity for the event. Computed by DYFI. While typically reported as a roman numeral, for the purposes of this API, intensity is expected as the decimal equivalent of the roman numeral.

felt.alias: Number of 'Did You Feel It?' Reports
felt.description: The total number of felt reports submitted to the Did You Feel It (DYFI)? system.

gap.description: The largest azimuthal gap between azimuthally adjacent stations (in degrees). In general, the smaller this number, the more reliable is the calculated horizontal position of the earthquake. Earthquake locations in which the azimuthal gap exceeds 180 degrees typically have large location and depth uncertainties.

dmin.description: Horizontal distance from the epicenter to the nearest station (in degrees). 1 degree is approximately 111.2 kilometers. In general, the smaller this number, the more reliable is the calculated depth of the earthquake.
dmin.alias: Horizontal distance from epicenter to nearest station

mmi.description: The maximum estimated instrumental intensity for the event.

net.description: The ID of a data contributor. Identifies the network considered to be the preferred source of information for this event.

tsunami.description: This flag is set to "1" for large events in oceanic regions and "0" otherwise. The existence or value of this flag does not indicate if a tsunami actually did or will exist

magtype.description: The method or algorithm used to calculate the preferred magnitude for the event.

rms.description: The root-mean-square (RMS) travel time residual, in sec, using all weights. This parameter provides a measure of the fit of the observed arrival times to the predicted arrival times for this location. Smaller numbers reflect a better fit of the data. The value is dependent on the accuracy of the velocity model used to compute the earthquake location, the quality weights assigned to the arrival time data, and the procedure used to locate the earthquake.

nst.description: The total number of seismic stations used to determine earthquake location.

attributes.name: Female & Male Population Densities
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset provides estimates of population counts by age and sex for the year 2010. It uses national censuses and population registers for the year 2010. The global data is presented as gridded raster data with a 30 arc second resolution (about 1 km at the equator). This dataset was created by Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) and is the fourth version and 11th revision of the Gridded Population of the World (GPWv4) estimates.  
  
GPWv4 consists of estimates of age and sex disaggregated population as counts (number of persons per pixel) and densities (number of persons per km²).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4): Basic Demographic Characteristics, Revision 11 provides estimates of population counts by age and sex for the year 2010, consistent with national censuses and population registers. To estimate the male and female populations by age in 2010, the proportions of males and females in each five-year age group from ages 0-4 to ages 85+ for the given census year were calculated. These proportions were then applied to the 2010 estimates of the total population to obtain 2010 estimates of male and female populations by age.   
  
In some cases, the spatial resolution of the age and sex proportions was coarser than the resolution of the total population estimates to which they were applied. The population density rasters were created by dividing the population count rasters by the land area raster. The data files were produced as global rasters at 30 arc second (about 1 km at the equator) resolution. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on male and female counts, and distribution of populations disaggregated by age, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: Water Stress Country Ranking
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available freshwater. The dataset was calculated by comparing water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. Higher water stress values indicate that there is more competition among people for available freshwater. The dataset was grouped by water usage for different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand which sectors had the greatest impact on water stress. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high.
  
  
Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production.
  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments in creating water use policies.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Water Stress Country Ranking is based on baseline water stress measurements. Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Gridded output data from the [PCRaster Global Water Balance](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/2429/2018/) (PCRGLOBWB 2) hydrological model was used for both water withdrawal and available water. The water withdrawal output data from PCRGLOBWB 2 included monthly data from January 1960 to December 2014 for four sectors: domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock. Output data for available water was also available over the same time frame. Data from the model was then aggregated spatially to the sub-basin level using the World Wildlife Fund’s (WWF) [HydroBASINS level 6](https://hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) hydrological sub-basins. Next, the data was regressed at the sub-basin level using an ordinary least square (OLS) regression with a trailing moving window size of 10 years to reduce noise in the data. This process resulted in gross water withdrawal and available water for each month for each sub-basin in the dataset. 
  
  
Next, the overall baseline water stress per month, per year, per sub-basin was determined. This was done by dividing the gross total water withdrawal by the difference between the available water and consumptive water withdrawal. This resulted in 12 time series of baseline water stress for each sub-basin: one time series for each month, with each time series spanning the years 1960-2014. Then, a single baseline water stress value for each month in each sub-basin was calculated by fitting a second OLS regression to each of the 12 time series and using the value for 2014 as the baseline water stress for that month. While the 2014 regression value is used, this value actually represents the baseline value, rather than an estimate of the water stress in 2014.
  
  
To compute national baseline water stress scores, the sub-basins had to be aggregated to a national scale. Aggregation was made possible by following the steps outlined on page 4 of the [2013 version](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct_coutnry_rankings_010914.pdf) of the methodology. This resulted in raw country score percentages in which water stress was classified as follows:
- Low (0-1): <10%
- Low to medium (1-2): 10-20%
- Medium to high (2-3): 20-40%
- High (3-4): 40-80%
- Extremely high (4-5): >80%
  
  
Each category represents the risk of water stress in the country. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct-30-updated-decision-relevant-global-water-risk-indicators_1.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [interannual variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat052-Aqueduct-Interannual-Variability) and [seasonal variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat053-Aqueduct-Seasonal-Variability) in water supply from the same dataset.  
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on drought risk and riverine flood risk is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_036_rw1_water_stress_country_ranking). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

attributes.name: National Infant Mortality
attributes.description:
The 'mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)' dataset released by the World Bank data catalog is the number of infants dying before reaching one year of age, per 1,000 live births in a given year.  The main sources of mortality data are vital registration systems and direct or indirect estimates based on sample surveys or censuses. A "complete" vital registration system - covering at least 90 percent of vital events in the population - is the best source of age-specific mortality data. Estimates of neonatal, infant, and child mortality tend to vary by source and method for a given time and place. Years for available estimates also vary by country, making comparisons across countries and over time difficult. To make neonatal, infant, and child mortality estimates comparable and to ensure consistency across estimates by different agencies, the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), which comprises the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank Group, the United Nations Population Division, and other universities and research institutes, developed and adopted a statistical method that uses all available information to reconcile differences. The method uses statistical models to obtain a best estimate trend line by fitting a country-specific regression model of mortality rates against their reference dates.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Thus estimates must be obtained from sample surveys or derived by applying indirect estimation techniques to registration, census, or survey data. Survey data are subject to recall error, and surveys estimating infant/child deaths require large samples because households in which a birth has occurred during a given year cannot ordinarily be preselected for sampling. Indirect estimates rely on model life tables that may be inappropriate for the population concerned. Extrapolations based on outdated surveys may not be reliable for monitoring changes in health status or for comparative analytical work

attributes.name: Fertility Rates
attributes.description:
The Fertility rate, total (births per woman) data set released on the World Bank data catalog, represents the number of children that would be born to a woman if she were to live to the end of her childbearing years and bear children in accordance with age-specific fertility rates of the specified year.  Data is collected from the "World Population Prospects" of the United Nations Population Division,Census reports and other statistical publications from national statistical offices, "Demographic Statistics" of Eurostat, the "Population and Vital Statistics Report" of the United Nations Statistical Division, theU.S. Census Bureau's  International Database, and the Statistics and Demography Programme of the Secretariat of the Pacific Community.  Total fertility rates are based on data on registered live births from vital registration systems or, in the absence of such systems, from censuses or sample surveys. The estimated rates are generally considered reliable measures of fertility in the recent past. Where no empirical information on age-specific fertility rates is available, a model is used to estimate the share of births to adolescents. For countries without vital registration systems fertility rates are generally based on extrapolations from trends observed in censuses or surveys from earlier years. attributes.name: Arctic Sea Ice Extent
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Arctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Arctic region. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand the current Arctic sea ice extent. Typically, Arctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in March and minimum in September. However, Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property - albedo -  keeps polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns.

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset.  

  
  
The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. 

  
  
Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cli_005_polar_sea_ice_extents).

info.functions: Near real-time extent of Arctic sea ice
info.cautions:
- Monthly extent is a better measure of conditions from year to year than is daily ice extent. Monthly data should be used for climatology studies instead of daily data.  
- Temporal and spatial monthly ice concentration averages can be ambiguous. For example, a mean concentration of 50% for a particular grid cell for the month of September could result from 100% concentration at that location for 15 days and 0% concentration for 15 days, or 50% concentration for 30 days, or some other combination. 
- Concentration values from 1% to 15% are statistically irrelevant because data values less than 15% from passive microwave instruments are too uncertain to use. Any cell with an ice concentration of less than 15% was automatically classified as water. 
- Occasionally, data from one or more days within a month are missing for a given 25 km grid cell. Monthly averages are computed from the daily data only if there are at least 20 days of data for that cell.
- Due to orbit inclination, the satellite instruments that provided data for this study did not image a circular area over the North pole. This area is assumed to be covered by ice at greater than 15% concentration.

attributes.name: cit.004a.rw0.nrt Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts
Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of PM2.5 for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to a 24-hour average.

  
  
PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) the size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even go into the bloodstream.  The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world.

  
  
These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/).
Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md).  
 
   
  
Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). 
 
  
  
Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry.  The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions.
 
  
  
The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/403726e5-6852-49f4-9dce-b82b599b09fc) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea).

info.technical_title: CityAQ
info.functions: Forecast of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) at monitoring station level for the next five days
info.cautions:
- Factors affecting air quality can change over the course of a day, which can lead to differences between the forecast and the actual levels observed.

  
  
- The forecasts were adjusted using validated monitoring data where available. Where validated data was not available, the raw data observations were used to adjust the forecast model.
  
  
- A concentration level of zero indicates that the forecast is not available for that station. This is the case for those stations that didn't have validated or raw data of enough quality to train the machine learning algorithm.
  
  
- The performance of the forecast model for each monitoring site has not been determined.

attributes.name: Agro-Ecological Zones
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the First Theme, Land and Water Resources, is displayed here and allows for the uniform classification of [biophysical](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/biophysics) resources that are relevant for agricultural production systems. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

​​Information on the current and future use of land resources is important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on the biophysical limitations of land, current crop suitability, and information on how different agricultural resources may be impacted by climate change. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security.

The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data for AEZ is derived from climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps.
 
The Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) sub-theme outputs fall under the first Theme, Land and Water Resources, and provides an inventory of land resources for the assessment of land productivity under specific agro-ecological conditions. Thermal and moisture layers are combined with broad categories of soil and terrain qualities allowing for the identification of land areas with biophysical constraints. 

A rigorous methodology and set of explicit principles are followed to assemble the AEZ classes and definitions. The following principles ensure that: 1) the map classes align with major climate zones based on the baseline historical period of 1981-2010, 2) map classes reflect broad ranges of the length of growing period boundaries, and 3) AEZ classes have generalized information about the prevailing soil and terrain limitations that are derived from GAEZ v4 terrain and soil resources inventories. The final AEZ layer has 57 different classes that are mapped at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator).
 
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Agro-Ecological Zones data has additional data for 2071-2100 and additional RCPs (2.6 and 6). For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_068_rw0_agro_ecological_zones/).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.cautions:
- GAEZ v4 assessment does not encompass all activities related to agriculture. It primarily focuses on the potential for growing crops.
- Results of this dataset should be utilized at the appropriate aggregation levels, which are dependent on the underlying resolution of the input datasets. Input datasets have different spatial resolutions.
- Input datasets are known to have uneven quality and reliability.
- Newer datasets with improved resolution and accuracy were made available after GAEZ datasets were frozen, for example, land cover.
- Land degradation was minimally or not at all accounted for in GAEZ outputs.
- Global generalizations were necessary for certain variables, such as the data on environmental requirements for some crops.
- Socioeconomic data use is limited to the specifications of modes and purpose of agricultural production, the quantification of levels of inputs and management, the inclusion of agricultural prices, and the consideration of population numbers and distributions.
- GAEZ utilized an exclusion layer to denote land that is marked either as protection or exclusion status from reliable datasets.

attributes.name: Zonas Agroecológicas
attributes.description:
### Visión general  
  
El conjunto de datos Global Agro-Ecological Zoning versión 4 (GAEZ v4) evalúa los recursos agrícolas actuales y futuros y su potencial. Es un marco estandarizado que permite la caracterización de las condiciones climáticas, del suelo y del terreno que son relevantes para la producción agrícola. Los datos del primer tema, Recursos de tierra y agua, se muestran aquí y permiten la clasificación uniforme de los recursos [biofísicos] (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/biophysics) que son relevantes para los sistemas de producción agrícola. Las salidas se presentan a una resolución de 5 minutos de arco, que es de aproximadamente 9 km x 9 km en el ecuador, pero [cambia con la distancia] (https://www.thoughtco.com/degree de latitud y longitud-distancia-4070616) desde el ecuador.

La información sobre el uso actual y futuro de los recursos de tierras es importante para la toma de decisiones agrícolas con implicaciones en la seguridad alimentaria, la sostenibilidad de los recursos de tierra y agua, y el desarrollo y las políticas agrícolas. El conjunto de datos GAEZ v4 reúne múltiples fuentes de datos para proporcionar información sobre las limitaciones biofísicas de la tierra, la idoneidad actual de los cultivos e información sobre cómo los diferentes recursos agrícolas pueden verse afectados por el cambio climático. Comprender qué cambios pueden ocurrir en el futuro permitirá a los diferentes actores la capacidad de aumentar la resiliencia, desarrollar técnicas o políticas para aliviar los desafíos potenciales y mantener la seguridad alimentaria.

La Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Agricultura y la Alimentación (FAO) junto con el Instituto Internacional de Análisis de Sistemas Aplicados (IIASA) comenzaron a desarrollar el marco de modelado GAEZ a principios de la década de 1980 para proporcionar datos actuales sobre el estado de los recursos agrícolas. Desde entonces, se ha expandido para apoyar el desarrollo agrícola sostenible y proporcionar información clave sobre los riesgos actuales y futuros para la producción agrícola, el desarrollo de cultivos, la productividad de la tierra y los impactos del cambio climático.
  
### Metodología  
  
Se utilizaron múltiples conjuntos de datos como insumos para el marco de modelado GAEZ v4 y proporcionan datos sobre atributos climáticos históricos y futuros, recursos de suelo y terreno, cobertura terrestre, tierras protegidas, áreas de biodiversidad, recursos hídricos, unidades administrativas, población y ganado. Los datos climáticos históricos provienen de los conjuntos de datos TS v3.21 de la Unidad de Investigación Climática que incluyen información climática mensual. Los datos climáticos futuros para AEZ se derivan de los resultados de los modelos climáticos para cuatro (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Vías de Concentración Representativas (PCR) del quinto Informe de Evaluación (AR5) del Grupo Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático.

El procesamiento de datos se dividió en varios pasos y siete módulos principales resumen los pasos necesarios dentro del marco de modelado GAEZ v4. Los resultados de cada uno de los módulos se clasifican en seis temas principales: 1) Recursos de tierra y agua, 2) Recursos agroclimáticos, 3) Rendimiento potencial agroclimático, 4) Idoneidad y rendimiento alcanzable, 5) Rendimientos y producción reales, y 6) Brechas de rendimiento y producción.
 
Los resultados del subtema de las Zonas Agroecológicas (ZEE) se incluyen en el primer Tema, Recursos de tierra y agua, y proporcionan un inventario de los recursos de tierras para la evaluación de la productividad de la tierra en condiciones agroecológicas específicas. Las capas térmicas y de humedad se combinan con amplias categorías de calidades del suelo y el terreno, lo que permite la identificación de áreas terrestres con restricciones biofísicas. 

Se sigue una metodología rigurosa y un conjunto de principios explícitos para ensamblar las clases y definiciones de AEZ. Los siguientes principios aseguran que: 1) las clases de mapas se alinean con las principales zonas climáticas basadas en el período histórico de referencia de 1981-2010, 2) las clases de mapas reflejan amplios rangos de la duración de los límites del período de crecimiento, y 3) las clases de AEZ tienen información generalizada sobre las limitaciones prevalecientes del suelo y el terreno que se derivan de los inventarios de terreno y recursos de suelo gaez v4. La capa final de AEZ tiene 57 clases diferentes que se mapean a una resolución espacial de 5 minutos de arco (aproximadamente 9 km en el ecuador).
 
Para obtener la documentación completa, consulte la fuente [metodología](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf).
  
### Información adicional  
  
Nuestro catálogo de datos muestra solo un subconjunto del conjunto de datos. Los datos de la Zonificación Agroecológica Global versión 4 de zonas agroecológicas tienen datos adicionales para 2071-2100 y PCR adicionales (2.6 y 6). Para acceder al conjunto de datos completo e información adicional, haga clic en el botón "Más información".  
  
### Visualización de los datos  
  
Nuestro equipo reformateó este conjunto de datos antes de mostrarlo en el catálogo de datos de la IRG. Consulte la documentación sobre cómo recuperamos los datos en [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_068_rw0_agro_ecological_zones/).  
  
### Descargo de responsabilidad  
  
Extractos de esta página de descripción fueron tomados de los metadatos de origen.

info.functions: Clasificación de la Zona Agroecológica por clima, suelo, terreno y cobertura del suelo
info.cautions:
- La evaluación GAEZ v4 no abarca todas las actividades relacionadas con la agricultura. Se centra principalmente en el potencial para el crecimiento de los cultivos.
- Los resultados de este conjunto de datos deben utilizarse en los niveles de agregación apropiados, que dependen de la resolución subyacente de los conjuntos de datos de entrada. Los datasets de entrada tienen diferentes resoluciones espaciales.
- Se sabe que los conjuntos de datos de entrada tienen una calidad y confiabilidad desiguales.
- Los conjuntos de datos más nuevos con una resolución y precisión mejoradas se pusieron a disposición después de que los conjuntos de datos GAEZ se congelaron, por ejemplo, la cubierta terrestre.
- La degradación de la tierra se tuvo en cuenta mínimamente o no se tuvo en cuenta en absoluto en los resultados de la GAEZ.
- Las generalizaciones globales fueron necesarias para ciertas variables, como los datos sobre los requisitos ambientales para algunos cultivos.
- El uso de datos socioeconómicos se limita a las especificaciones de los modos y el propósito de la producción agrícola, la cuantificación de los niveles de insumos y la gestión, la inclusión de los precios agrícolas y la consideración de los números y distribuciones de la población.
- GAEZ utilizó una capa de exclusión para denotar la tierra que está marcada como estado de protección o exclusión de conjuntos de datos confiables.
