Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of an index that measures the presence of aerosols that absorb ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the atmosphere, such as dust and smoke. This index may be referred to as the absorbing aerosol index (AAI) or the UV Aerosol Index (UVAI).

  
  
Absorbing Aerosols are solid and liquid particles suspended in the atmosphere. They are made up of primary aerosols and secondary aerosols. Primary aerosols are emitted directly, whereas secondary aerosols are formed by gases reacting in the atmosphere. Absorbing aerosols are mostly made of dust and smoke. The main sources of aerosols are combustion, like burning biomass, and natural sources, like volcanoes. The AAI can show dust and smoke particles coming from events like dust storms, volcanic eruptions, fires, and biomass burning around the world.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as absorbing aerosols, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO),  [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI AAI dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. UV-absorbing aerosol data was collected by determining the amount of Rayleigh scattering that occured in the UV spectral range for a pair of wavelengths. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure, and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that UV-absorbing aerosol molecules emit in the atmosphere. Rayleigh scattering is the scattering of light particles without causing a change in their wavelength. The UV-absorbing aerosol data collected was then compared with a calculated theoretical Rayleigh scattering value based on no UV-absorbing aerosols being present in the troposphere. The difference in scattering between the two data points represents the amount of UV-absorbing aerosols present and is the absorbing aerosol index. A positive AAI value indicates that UV-absorbing aerosols are present. 

  
  
The dataset was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “UV-Aerosol Index”.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO),  [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.technical_title: Sentinel 5 Precursor Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (S5P/TROPOMI) Offline (OFFL) Level 3 (L3) Absorbing Aerosol Index (AAI)
info.functions: Average monthly absorbing aerosol index (AAI), which can be used to determine the presence of UV-absorbing aerosols, like dust and smoke
info.cautions:
- The presence of ozone (O₃) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) can interfere with UV-absorbing aerosol readings. Both O₃ and NO₂ are also present in the UV spectral range and have been found to cause errors up to 3%.
  
  
- Validation results have found the systematic difference between S5P/TROPOMI and other instruments measuring aerosol index to be just within 1 AAI, where TROPOMI values are lower than both the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) and Ozone Mapping Profiler Suite (OMPS). The UV Aerosol Index has a large negative bias compared to other satellite-derived aerosol index products, especially in the presence of clouds. Overall, index values are likely low due to wavelength-dependent degradation in the diffuser.
  
  
- For more information on the data quality, please see the [product readme file] (https://sentinel.esa.int/documents/247904/3541451/Sentinel-5P-Aerosol-Level-2-Product-Readme-File).

attributes.name: Marine Protected Areas
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Marine Protected Area (MPA) dataset contains officially designated parks, reserves, and other formal conservation areas around the world that have a substantial maritime component. Protected area data are provided via [Protected Planet](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas), the online interface for the World Database for Protected Areas (WDPA). The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data is provided as shapefiles and updates monthly. Each record is either represented as a polygon boundary, or if unavailable, a point location, along with descriptive information, such as the name, legal designation, and mode of administration. As of May 2019, the WDPA included data on 242,784 protected areas, of which 91% were polygons and 9% were points.

  
  
Over 70% of the surface of Earth is ocean, comprised of highly diverse ecosystems, and providing a wide range of marine ecosystem services that support human society, health and the economy. Much of the recent growth in MPA coverage has been driven by the establishment of very large MPAs over 100,000 (square kilometers) km². These vast MPAs each contribute a significant part of the total global ocean coverage, with the 20 largest making up the majority of the world’s MPA coverage. While these represent huge commitments to conservation, there is a need for international collaboration to ensure that MPAs achieve their desired conservation value. The information contained in the MPA dataset contributes to the UNEP-WCMC's mission to place biodiversity at the heart of environment and development decision-making to enable enlightened choices for people and the planet.

  
  
The mandate of the database dates back to 1959 when the UN Economic and Social Council called for a list of national parks and equivalent reserves in recognition that they "are valuable for economic and scientific reasons and also as areas for the future preservation of fauna and flora and geologic structures in their natural state." The first UN List of Protected Areas was published in 1962, and subsequently evolved into the WDPA. The database is also used to generate indicators to track progress towards the Convention on Biological Diversity Aichi Biodiversity Target 11 and UN Sustainable Development Goals 14 and 15.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data for protected area records in the WDPA have been obtained from nearly 500 sources. Along with information on the data verifier, these sources are listed in the source table that is included with each monthly release. Data for protected areas designated under international agreements and conventions are often sourced from the relevant convention secretariats. Data for national-level protected areas have been sourced from national authorities wherever possible. Information may also be supplemented by data from other agencies, organizations or individuals. All data in the WDPA have been verified either by the national authorities or by non-government expert partners, with the exception of some data included before the verification process was established.

  
  
Data in the WDPA must meet the Protected Planet data standards. These were developed in 2010, regularly updated and subsequently revised in 2015 to ensure consistency in the way the WDPA is compiled, checked, managed, and presented. Standards are important to ensure all information is supplied in a common format that is interoperable and useful for a wide variety of reporting and analytical purposes. There are four key requirements:

  
  
 1. All sites must meet the IUCN definition of a protected area
  
  
 2. Spatial data from Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and an associated list of attributes must be provided
  
  
 3. Source of information must be provided
  
  
 4. The WDPA Data Contributor Agreement must be signed
 
  
  
The Protected Planet data standards also encompass standards specific to other databases, such as the Global Database on Protected Area Management Effectiveness.

  
  
The MPA dataset comprises protected areas in the WDPA that intersect with the marine part of an internal base layer—generally, the ocean or seas, but not lakes.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/resources/wdpa-manual).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA dataset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) as accessed through the [Protected Planet API](https://api.protectedplanet.net/documentation#get-v3protectedareas).

info.name: Marine Protected Areas

sources.source-description: United Nations Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC)
International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)

info.technical_title: The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECM) database
info.functions: Global database of marine protected areas, including boundaries and descriptive information
info.cautions:
- The WDPA dataset is not necessarily a complete representation of all the protected areas which have been designated globally; the quality of the WDPA depends on the accessibility of accurate, comprehensive, up-to-date protected areas information from data holders. Thus, mismatches between on the ground protected areas and protected areas in the WDPA may be due to a number of reasons that include but are not restricted to: new data being quality checked to fit the WDPA standards, data not submitted to the WDPA yet, new protected area boundaries not being accurately digitized or simply not yet being digitised. In many areas, several (up to eight) designations overlap; it is hence necessary to dissolve the dataset before any surface area calculations are carried out. Details on the common issues and quality limitations of the WDPA are described in detail in the User Manual.
  
  
 - The WDPA is formally paired with a sister dataset: the other effective area-based conservation measures (OECM) database. Resource Watch displays only entries from the WDPA. The OECM database is in development and cannot yet be considered to be a comprehensive representation of OECMs globally. Populating the database will require a concerted effort and long-term collaborations with governments and other data providers. 
  
  
 - Although records should not be submitted to the WDPA if they do not meet the IUCN or CBD definition of a protected area, it cannot be guaranteed that data-providers consistently follow this standard. In part, this is because countries often have national definitions of protected areas that may not fully align with the IUCN or CBD definition. It should therefore not be assumed that all records in the WDPA meet the IUCN or CBD definition. However, the majority of these sites are reviewed via discussions with data providers periodically via data updates and tend to be removed before being entered into the WDPA. 
  
  
 - The WDPA stores both management categories and governance types as reported by the data provider. In May 2019, 66% of protected areas in the WDPA had an IUCN Management Category, and 88% had a governance type. UNEP-WCMC encourages the adoption of the IUCN standards but does not assign or review the application of the categories by countries.
  
  
 - There are still many protected areas for which there is no IUCN Protected Area Management Category assigned. The absence of a management category does not in any way reduce the importance of a protected area, nor does it imply that the site is not being adequately managed or should be excluded from analyses. 
  
  
 - The IUCN management categories are not intended to be hierarchical. They cannot be used to make assumptions about the biodiversity value, management effectiveness, or conservation performance of a protected area. 
  
  
 - It is important to note that different designations of protected areas may occupy the same geographical space, in which case each will have a different WDPA identifier (ID). For example, Yellowstone National Park in the United States is a National Park, but this same location is also a natural World Heritage Site. The two designations have different WDPA IDs. For more information on the WDPA ID, see the User Manual.
  
  
 - Due to the inherent variability of data submitted by a wide range of data providers, with different capacity and resources to support the digitization of boundaries, issues with the accuracy of the WDPA database data should be expected. For more information about common issues with the data, see section 5 of the User Manual.

attributes.name: Hourly Precipitation
attributes.description:
This data set published by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives hourly precipitation estimates in mm/hr from latitudes 60N - 60S at a 0.1° resolution. The Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP) is a product of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission.   
  
 Values are estimated using multi-band passive microwave and infrared radiometers from the GPM Core Observatory satellite and with the assistance of a constellation of other satellites. GPM's precipitation rate retrieval algorithm is based on a radiative transfer model. The gauge-adjusted rate is calculated based on the optimization of the 24h accumulation of GSMaP hourly rain rate to daily precipitation by NOAA/CPC gauge measurement.   
  
  Data is available from 2014 through present day and is made available with a four hour latency as JAXA processes the satellite data.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

Land Deals
attributes.description:
The Land Matrix Online Database on Land Deals tracks large-scale land deals that are made for agricultural production, timber extraction, carbon trading, industry, renewable energy production, conservation, and tourism in low- and middle-income countries. A deal is referred to as an intended, concluded, or failed attempt to acquire land through purchase, lease, or concession that must (1) entail a transfer of rights to use, control, or ownership of land through sale, lease, or concession; (2) have been initiated since the year 2000; (3) cover an area of 200 ha or more; and (4) imply the potential conversion of land from smallholder production, local community use, or important ecosystem service provision to commercial use. Resource Watch shows the number of concluded deals that cover an area of 200 ha or more per year since 2000. Because of the nature of land acquisitions, it is difficult to obtain this information from official sources, therefore data are attained from (1) research papers and policy reports by international and local organizations and NGOs; (2) personal information contributed through the Global Observatory website; (3) field-based research projects; (4) official government records; (5) company websites; and (6) media reports. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

info.name: Land Deals
info.technical_title: Land Matrix Online Public Database on Land Deals
info.functions: Prevalence of large-scale land acquisitions of 200 ha or more in low- and middle-income countries
info.cautions: The data set is inherently unreliable, but over time it is expected to become more accurate. Land deals are notoriously opaque. In many countries, established procedures for decision-making on land deals do not exist, and negotiations and decisions do not take place in the public realm. Furthermore, a range of government agencies and levels of government are usually responsible for approving different kinds of land deals. Even official data sources in the same country can therefore vary, and none may actually reflect reality on the ground. Decisions are often changed, and this may or may not be communicated publicly. Therefore, the data of the Global Observatory rely extensively on unofficial sources. Data errors may arise if the information provided by the source is inaccurate. As the information source is provided, users may decide the extent to which they determine the source to be trustworthy. Errors may also arise from mistakes in entering the data. The new database management system accompanying the June 2013 upgrade contains safeguards to detect likely mistakes, but the latter are impossible to eliminate. Furthermore, errors may arise from the information becoming out of date; we rely on our networks in different countries and users of the website to provide updates. Additional errors or bias may include the following: (1) open data policies in certain countries may give the impression that they have a higher proportion of land deals; (2) media and research interest is often higher in certain regions (e.g., Africa), on certain investors (e.g., emerging investor countries), and in certain sectors (e.g., agriculture and specifically biofuels); (3) foreign investors generally attract more attention than domestic investors, which leads to an underrepresentation of purely domestic deals; (4) networks of Land Matrix partners are important information providers and checkers, leading to a likely underrepresentation of deals in regions such as Eastern Europe and Central Asia where our networks do not have a strong presence; and (5) failed deals and domestic deals are particularly hard to get reliable information for, so these are likely to be underrepresented in the data set. Consequently, trends evident in the database should be taken as indicative, since they are likely to change as the data become more accurate.

attributes.name: wat.046 Sea Surface Temperature and Salinity
Water Temperature and Salinity
attributes.description:
Water Temperature and Salinity are two products from the Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM), created by the HYCOM Consortium, the National Ocean Partnership Program (NOPP), and the United States Global Ocean Data Assimilation Experiment (GODEA). HYCOM is a fully three dimensional, multivariate, variational ocean data assimilation system that produces simultaneous analyses of temperature, salinity, geopotential and vector velocity.   
  
The analysis is run in real-time and updates daily. The data have been interpolated to a uniform 0.08 degree lat/long grid between 80.48°S and 80.48°N. The salinity, temperature, and velocity variables have been interpolated to 40 standard z-levels (vertical depth).   
  
The high resolution makes HYCOM eddy resolving. Eddy-resolving models can more accurately simulate western boundary currents and the associated mesoscale variability and they better maintain more accurate and sharper ocean fronts. In particular, an eddy resolving ocean model allows upper ocean topographic coupling via flow instabilities. The coupling occurs when flow instabilities drive abyssal currents that in turn steer the pathways of upper ocean currents. In ocean prediction this coupling is important for ocean model dynamical interpolation skill in data assimilation/nowcasting and in ocean forecasting, which is feasible on time scales up to about a month.   
  
Sea surface temperature (SST) retrievals are empiracally derived using stored regressions between cloud cleared satellite SST radiances and drifting buoy SSTs. The regressions are global, calculated once, and held constant.

cli.086.crt0 Near term climate projections for India - SSP585
Near-Term climate hazard indicators across India – Early Century Projection - SSP 585
attributes.description:
### Overview
 
 
 This dataset provides insights into India’s climate projections for the period 2021–2040, focusing on extreme weather events such as heat waves, droughts, and intense rainfall. The data is essential for understanding the regional risks posed by climate change and for supporting targeted strategies to safeguard lives and livelihoods across the country. The data is provided at district level. 
 
 
 ### Methodology
 
 
 **Layers of interest**: Average Annual Maximum Temperature Change (℃), Average Annual Minimum Temperature Change (℃), Average Annual Precipitation Change (%), Average Annual Relative Humidity (%), Average Southwest Monsoon Precipitation Change (%), Average Northeast Monsoon Precipitation Change (%), Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Southwest Monsoon (number of days), Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Northeast Monsoon (number of days). 
 
 
**Data sources**: The dataset integrates outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models. The daily precipitation dataset (grid resolution: 0.25° × 0.25°), maximum, minimum and mean temperature datasets (grid resolution: 1°×1°) developed by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) have been used as observed data. 
 
 
### Estimation Methods
 
 
 The India Meteorological Department (IMD) have been used for statistical downscaling of the coarser resolution CMIP6 model simulations to 25 km. The study employed bias-correction procedure for daily datasets for precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature, as developed by Mishra et al. (2020). Climate projections are analysed for various temperature and precipitation changes under both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. 
 
 
 The projections include two key scenarios: 
 
 
 SSP2-4.5 (Middle of the Road): Moderate emissions and adaptation. 
 
 
 SSP5-8.5 (Fossil-Fueled Development): High emissions and heavy reliance on fossil fuels. 
 
 
 The historical simulation period 1951 – 1970 was selected as the ‘baseline period’ and for future climate projections, the time period 2021–2040 was used. In the present format, all the model simulations and observations have been maintained to a uniform grid resolution of 0.25°×0.25° for making them consistent for computing the Multi-Model Mean (MMM). For precise diagnosis of precipitation and temperature changes on a space and time scale in the present and future climate, the final parameters are presented at district level through district level mean aggregates. 
 
 
 For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Mishra V, Bhatia U, Tiwari AD (2020) Bias corrected climate projections from CMIP6 models for Indian sub-continental river basins. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3874046 and https://azimpremjiuniversity.edu.in/data-and-methods. 
 
 
### Description of the Layers
 
 
**Average Annual Maximum Temperature Change (℃):** The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in temperature was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Annual Minimum Temperature Change (℃):** The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in temperature was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Annual Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for each year is extracted and averaged across years to calculate the yearly average precipitation. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Annual Relative Humidity (%):** The annual average relative humidity for each year is calculated considering all the parallel to the temperatures available and presented for the period 2021–2040. 
 
 
 **Average Southwest Monsoon Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for the southwest monsoon season covering June-July-August-September of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation for the season was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Northeast Monsoon Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for the northeast monsoon season covering October-November-December of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation for the season was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Southwest Monsoon (number of days):** A heavy rainfall day as per IMD is whenever daily rainfall exceeds 64.5 mm. The number of heavy precipitation days for the southwest monsoon season covering June-July-August-September of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in number of heavy rainy days for the season was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Northeast Monsoon (number of days):** A heavy rainfall day as per IMD is whenever daily rainfall exceeds 64.5 mm. The number of heavy precipitation days for the southwest monsoon season covering October-November-December of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in number of heavy rainy days for the season was calculated. 
 
 
### Visualizing the Data
 
 
The data is presented district wise with a time slider with a dropdown selector for changing between the layers. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shades of yellow (indicating low values) to darker shades of green (representing higher values).

attributes.name: Global roads
attributes.description:
The Global Roads Inventory Project (GRIP) dataset was developed to provide a more recent and consistent global roads dataset for use in global environmental and biodiversity assessment models. 
 The GRIP dataset is mainly aimed at providing a roads dataset that is easily usable for scientific global environmental and biodiversity modelling projects. The dataset is not suitable for navigation. GRIP4 is based on many different sources (including OpenStreetMap) and to the best of our ability we have verified their public availability, as a criteria in our research. The UNSDI-Transportation datamodel was applied for harmonization of the individual source datasets. 
 We have only included included highways, primary and secondary roads as part of this dataset. The original GRIP dataset consists of tertiary and local roads as well.

attributes.name: Out-Of-School Rate
attributes.description:
The rate of out-of-school children, generated by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), is the percentage of children not in school by year per country. The data extend back to 2014. The UIS gathers these statistics using questionnaires, which are sent to UNESCO Member States annually. The questionnaires are based on international standards, classifications, and measures that are regularly reviewed and modified by the UIS in order to address emerging statistical issues and improve the quality of data. The UIS collaborates with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and Eurostat to collect data with surveys (collectively UOE). The UOE questionnaire compiles data from high- and middle-income countries that are members or partner countries of the OECD or Eurostat. The UOE survey gathers more detailed education statistics. Midyear population estimates for countries with at least 90,000 inhabitants are provided by the UN Population Division to calculate the percentages. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for black carbon (BC). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
Black carbon is the sooty black material emitted from gas and diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, and other sources that burn fossil fuel. It is made up of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that is 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter. PM2.5 can have significant health risks for people with compromised respiratory systems, the young, and the old. Black carbon is a global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate. Inhalation of black carbon is associated with health problems including respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, and even birth defects. Black carbon also contributes to climate change causing changes in patterns of rain and clouds.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The black carbon station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer

Mangrove Extent Change
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the change in the global extent of mangroves between 1996 and 2016. Comparable maps of mangrove gain and loss (corresponding to smaller timesteps) were part of the creation of the first global map of mangrove extent produced via an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, which used a combination of optical and radar satellite data. The data have an effective resolution of approximately 25 meters at the equator.

  
  
Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology.

  
  
The underlying mangrove extent dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The net extent change in global mangrove area from 1996 to 2016 was calculated by comparing the [global mangrove extent maps](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/45) provided by [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) for the corresponding years.

  
  
**1996 and 2016 extent maps:**

  
  
To develop the 1996 and 2016 mangrove extent maps, GMW first created a baseline map of mangroves for 2010 at a global level through a random forests classification of both Landsat sensor spectral composite data (all spectral wavebands) and Advanced Land Observing Satellite (ALOS) Phased Arrayed L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data.The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017).

  
  
The maps for 1996 and 2016 were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0%. 

  
  
**1996–2016 mangrove extent change map:**

  
  
WRI derived the 1996 to 2016 extent change map by directly comparing the corresponding extent layers provided by GMW (rather than combining the change layers calculated by the authors). This comparison was performed by calculating the geometric intersection of the 1996 and 2016 extent layers. The intersection was erased from the 1996 extent to obtain loss polygons and erased from the 2016 extent to obtain gain polygons.

  
  
For the full documentation for the 1996 and 2016 extent maps, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [mangrove extent time series](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/386314c4-ab42-47a7-b2cd-596b788e114d), which shows total mangrove forest cover, rather than change.   
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_005a_mangrove).  
  
### Disclaimer

- Several different factors can affect the classification accuracy, including satellite data availability, mangrove species composition and level of degradation.
- While the original pixel spacing of the satellite data used for the mapping is in the order of 25-30 metres, a minimum mapping unit of approximately 1 ha is recommended. The classification error typically increases in regions of disturbance and fragmentation such as aquaculture ponds, as well as along riverine or coastal reef mangroves that form narrow shoreline fringes. 
- In general, the mangrove seaward border is more accurately defined than the landward side where distinction between mangrove and certain terrestrial vegetation species can be unclear.
- Striping artefacts due to Landsat-7 scanline error are also present in some areas, particularly West African regions due to lack of Landsat-5 data and persistent cloud cover
- Areas known to be missing in this version (v2.0) of the dataset: Aldabra island group (Seychelles); Andaman and Nicobar Islands (India); Bermuda (U.K.); Chagos Islands; Europa Island (France); Fiji - east of Antemeridian; Guam and Saipan (U.S.); Kiribati; Maldives; Marshall Islands; Peru - south of latitude S4°; and Wallis and Futuna Islands (France).

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](1ae29c41-a9bb-498e-9b72-9f59ef1d1c62) as a replacement.**_
  
The Fragile States Index (FSI), produced by the Fund for Peace (FFP), measures the vulnerability of states to collapse. It not only highlights the normal pressures that all states experience but also identifies when pressures exceed a state’s capacity to manage them. The FFP collects millions of reports and information from around the world, detailing existing social, economic, and political pressures. Based on the comprehensive social science approach of their Conflict Assessment System Tool (CAST), data from 3 main streams--preexisting quantitative data sets, content analysis, and qualitative expert analysis—are triangulated and subjected to critical review to obtain final scores for the index. The higher the index score the closer a state is to failure. The index is produced annually and covers 178 countries. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index measures how restrictive foreign direct investment (FDI) is in a country. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is an investment made by an entity in one country into another country’s business interests. FDI is particularly important in developing countries and emerging markets as it can provide capital for technology and infrastructure and create jobs for local workers. However, some countries that receive foreign investment impose restrictions on FDI. For a given country, the four main FDI restrictions in each economic sector were evaluated and scored based on how discriminatory they are to foreign investors. These restrictions are foreign equity limitations; screening and approval requirements; restrictions on foreign key personnel; and other operational restrictions. Scores range from 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions). The scores of each sector were averaged to calculate the country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. This dataset includes FDI data from 22 economic sectors for OECD and G20 countries and is updated annually.
  
  
The index captures a country’s ability to attract FDI. It can also be used to measure changes in regulatory restrictions over time and how these changes affect FDI inflow. Highly restrictive countries receive less FDI compared to less restrictive countries with similarly sized economies. FDI restrictions can be costly to governments in terms of loss of potential investments. They also increase costs in service sectors and negatively impact stocks. Studies of this dataset have shown that countries that reform FDI restrictions attract more foreign investors. FDI restrictions reform can positively impact developing countries by promoting economic growth and investment in human capital. 
  
  
The OECD created the FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. The OECD is an international organization founded in 1961. The 36 member states work to shape policies that foster prosperity, equality, opportunity and well-being.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictions Index uses data from 22 economic sectors. Economic sectors include industries like agriculture, media, electricity, transportation and financial services. 
  
  
Scoring for each sector was based on the following restriction types:
Limits on the amount of foreign equity ownership permitted
Screening and approval procedures applied to inward foreign direct investment
Restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel
Other restrictions (e.g., land ownership, reciprocity requirements, access to local finance)
  
  
Scoring was based on the discriminatory nature of a country’s measures, i.e. whether the measures applied to only foreign investors. Restrictions were evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. The restrictiveness of each sector was calculated by adding the scores for each of the four types of FDI restrictions (with a maximum score of 1). A country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index is the average of the scores from all 22 economic sectors. 

  
  
The score for **foreign equity limits** differentiated between three key thresholds: full exclusion of foreign participation, restrictions on foreign majority control and limits on full foreign ownership. The score further distinguished between start-up businesses and takeovers. If the measure only applied to takeovers, the score was reduced by half. **Screening and approval mechanisms** that applied only to foreign investors were scored based on a monetary threshold. Restrictive countries required approval of new FDI/acquisitions worth less than $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Less restrictive countries did not require approval of new FDI/acquisitions until they exceeded $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Open countries required no screening, only pre-notification from foreign investors. Restrictions on **foreign key personnel** were scored on two criteria: limitations on foreign employment and board of directors members. The OECD defines key personnel as employees in a managerial role or employees with essential technical skills. Restrictive countries did not allow employment of foreign key personnel. Less restrictive countries imposed time limits or required economic justification of foreign key personnel employment. Nationality/residence requirements for board of directors members are common. Restrictive countries required the majority of board members to be citizens. In contrast, less restrictive countries required only one board member to be a citizen. **Other restrictions** are measures that could affect the potential operations of foreign investors. These include restrictions on the following: land ownership, access to local finance, capital/profit repatriation, and establishment of local branches. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_007_rw1_fdi_regulatory_restrictiveness_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

info.cautions:
- The FDI Index is not a full measure of a country’s investment climate. A country’s ability to attract foreign investment is affected by a range of other factors.
- The FDI Index only accounts for statutory restrictions on FDI. It is important to note that OECD countries commit to treating foreign-controlled enterprises operating on their territory equal to similar domestic enterprises. 
- Implementation and enforcement of FDI rules were not factored into the index. 
- State ownership and state monopolies that do not discriminate against foreigners were not scored. 
- Aspects of the regulatory framework that may deter FDI were not factored into the index. These include the nature of corporate governance and institutional or informal restrictions.

attributes.name: wat.065.rw0 Hydropolitical Tension and Institutional Vulnerability
Hydropolitical Tension and Institutional Vulnerability
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Transboundary Freshwater Dispute Database (TFDD) catalogs the number and delineation of the world's international river basins and also contains physical, socioeconomic, and political data relating to each of them. In the context of these datasets, an international river basin is defined by its ultimate outlet to an ocean, sea, or inland water body and has year-round flow crossing or drawing a political border. This database includes data at the scale of basins as well as basin country units, which is an area of an international river basin that falls within a particular country. 

The Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension estimates the relative level of risk a basin or basin country unit has for political tension over its transboundary rivers. This risk is based on:
  
  
 1. **water infrastructure development**: the ability to deal with disputes arising from the development of new water infrastructure
  
  
 2. **institutional vulnerability**: the capacity of a basin country unit to absorb tension, which is expressed by the presence or absence of treaties, treaty provisions, and river basin organizations

This data was calculated by TFDD-affiliated researchers as a part of the Governance thematic group within the Transboundary Water Assessment Programme's River Basin Component.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The delineation and count of international river basins and basin country units were determined using the [Register of International River Basins](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/content/register-international-river-basins) and watershed boundaries from the [HydroBASINs](https://www.hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) dataset. HydroBASINS provides global coverage of watershed boundaries with several levels of sub-basin delineations, including watersheds that range in scale from tens to millions of square kilometers (see [Lehner & Gill, 2013](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.9740)).  For full documentation on the spatial boundary data, please see the [methodology](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07900627.2019.1572497).

Institutional Vulnerability is measured by five components of formal transboundary cooperation. The five components are:
  
  
 1. at least one water treaty
  
  
 2. at least one treaty with an allocation mechanism
  
  
 3. at least one treaty with a flow variability management mechanism
  
  
 4. at least one treaty with a conflict resolution mechanism
  
  
 5. at least one river basin organization
  
  
The presence of a component is summed to give the institutional vulnerability score from 0 to 5, with 0 being the most vulnerable and 5 being the least vulnerable. 

Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension is calculated based on the basin country unit's institutional vulnerability score and the presence of a large dam or water diversion project in the basin country unit or upstream of it. If a basin country unit has a lower score for its institutional vulnerability and has infrastructure development in the basin country unit or upstream, it is in a higher risk category for Hydropolitical tension. Relative Risk ranges from 1 (very low risk) to 5 (very high risk). 

For full documentation on the metrics shown in this dataset, please see the [Transboundary River Basins report](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/sites/transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/files/Database/ResearchProjects/TWAP/GEF_TWAPRB_FullTechnicalReport_compressed.pdf).   
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for fine particulate matter (PM2.5). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even get into the bloodstream. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of health problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).

  
  
### Methodology  
  
The fine particulate matter (PM2.5) station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.

Tree Cover
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Tree Cover dataset measures areas of tree cover in 2000. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

  
  
Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the tree cover density of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity.

  
  
The dataset was created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. 

  
  
The following steps were taken to pre-process the images:
  
  
1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed.
  
  
2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water.
  
  
3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another.

  
  
Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information

Tropical Cyclones
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the paths cyclones have followed and their intensities, from 1980 to the present. The data includes information on tropical cyclones by location, ocean basin, scale, name, wind speed, and other intensity parameters. The International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) is run by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

  
  
According to NOAA, a tropical cyclone is a weather event that produces rotating clouds, high winds, and thunderstorms. These cyclones are called hurricanes in the North Atlantic, central North Pacific, and eastern North Pacific. Elsewhere they are called typhoons or tropical typhoons. The disruptions from tropical cyclones have significant impacts on human life, property, and ecology. By compiling data in one place, this dataset can support scientific research efforts in understanding the distribution, frequency, and intensity of tropical cyclones, and assist emergency managers with disaster mitigation efforts. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers obtained this data from various agencies either directly through agency websites or via personal communication. The data originated from satellite observations. The data files were then converted into a common format with two general steps. To solve the double-reporting issue with various data sources, step 1 identified each unique storm with an algorithm based on the storm’s position. Step 2 harmonized intensity estimates across data sources so that the intensity parameters are comparable. In cases of different sources having different positions and intensities, researchers calculated the average values from all available reports. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/pdf/10.1175/2009BAMS2755.1).   
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1842 and 1979 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/blob/master/dis_015a_tropical_cyclones/README.md).

number.description: The cardinal number of the system for that season.

basin.description: Basins include: NA - North Atlantic EP - Eastern North Pacific WP - Western North Pacific NI - North Indian SI - South Indian SP - Southern Pacific SA - South Atlantic MM - Missing - should not appear in final IBTrACS product

subbasin.description: Subbasins include: MM - missing - no sub basin for this basin (no subbasins provided for WP, SI) CS - Caribbean Sea GM - Gulf of Mexico CP - Central Pacific BB - Bay of Bengal AS - Arabian Sea WA - Western Australia EA - Eastern Australia

iso_time.description: ISO Time provided in Universal Time Coordinates (UTC). Format is YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss Most points are provided at 6 hour intervals. Some agencies provided 3 hour points (e.g., New Delhi) or times at important observations (e.g., landfall times in the North Atlantic, etc.).

nature.description: Combined storm type. This is assigned based on all available storm types. They include: DS - Disturbance TS - Tropical ET - Extratropical SS - Subtropical NR - Not reported MX - Mixture (contradicting nature reports from different agencies)

wmo_wind.description: Maximum sustained wind speed from the WMO agency for the current location. NO adjustment is made for differences in wind speed averaging periods. hurdat/atcf = North Atlantic - U.S. Miami (NOAA NHC) - 1-minute winds tokyo = RSMC Tokyo (JMA) - 10-minute newdelhi = RSMC New Delhi (IMD) - 3-minute reunion = RSMC La Reunion (MFLR) - 10 minute bom = Australian TCWCs (TCWC Perth, Darwin, Brisbane) - 10-minute nadi = RSMC Nadi (FMS) - 10 minute wellington = TCWC Wellington (NZMS) - 10-minute

wmo_agency.description: This is the reporting agency responsible for the basin as currently listed. Therefore the WMO agency is used loosely todescribe the currently reponsible agency.

track_type.description: Tropical storms can interact. This identifies : PROVISIONAL - Real time data used to populate the position and other parameters of this system. This is a provisional track that will be replaced when reanalysis of the storm is performed. (Usually within 2 years of the storm's occurence) PROVISIONAL_spur - Real time data (see provisional description above) but due to differences in positions between various inputs, algorithm can not identify accurate position. When counting storms, these should not likely be counted. These should be rare for PROVISIONAL data. MAIN - primary track associated with a storm system. This is a track that has had some reanalysis and is higher quality than provisional data. spur - usually short lived tracks associated with a main track and often represents alternate positions at the beginning of a system. dist2land.alias: Distance to land from the current position (km)

landfall.description: Nearest location to land within next 6 hours. This can be thought of a landfall flag: =0 -- Landfall within 6 hours. >0 -- No landfall within next 6 hours. storm_spd.description: Translation speed of the system as calculated from the positions in LAT and LON

storm_dr.description: Translation direction of the system as calculated from the positions in LAT and LON. Direction is moving toward the vector pointing in degrees east of north [range = 0-360 deg]

attributes.name: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature (RCP4.5)
Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature (RCP4.5)
attributes.description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at https://doi.org/10.46830/writn.19.00117. [www.resourcewatch.org](https://www.resourcewatch.org/).

We acknowledge the World Climate Research Programme's Working Group on Coupled Modelling, which is responsible for CMIP, and we thank the climate modeling groups for producing and making available their model output. The U.S. Department of Energy's Program for Climate Model Diagnosis and Intercomparison provides coordinating support and development of software infrastructure in partnership with the Global Organization for Earth System Science Portals for CMIP.

Climate scenarios used were from the NEX-GDDP dataset, prepared by the Climate Analytics Group and NASA Ames Research Center using the NASA Earth Exchange, and distributed by the NASA Center for Climate Simulation (NCCS).

attributes.name: Fragile States Index
attributes.description:
The Fragile States Index (FSI), produced by the Fund for Peace (FFP), measures the vulnerability of states to collapse. It not only highlights the normal pressures that all states experience but also identifies when pressures exceed a state’s capacity to manage them. The FFP collects millions of reports and information from around the world, detailing existing social, economic, and political pressures. Based on the comprehensive social science approach of their Conflict Assessment System Tool (CAST), data from 3 main streams--preexisting quantitative data sets, content analysis, and qualitative expert analysis—are triangulated and subjected to critical review to obtain final scores for the index. The higher the index score the closer a state is to failure. The index is produced annually and covers 178 countries. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

attributes.name: Non-CO₂ Agricultural Emissions
attributes.description:
The non-CO₂ agricultural emissions data set, published the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in its FAOSTAT database, contains all the non-CO₂ emissions produced in the different agricultural emissions subdomains (enteric fermentation, manure management, rice cultivation, synthetic fertilizers, manure applied to soils, manure left on pastures, crop residues, cultivation of organic soils, burning of crop residues, burning of savanna, energy use) and provides a picture of their contribution to the total amount of GHG emissions from agriculture. GHG emissions from agriculture tabulated here consist of non-CO₂ gases—namely, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—produced by crop and livestock production and management activities. The FAOSTAT emissions database is computed following Tier 1 IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National GHG Inventories. GHG emissions data are provided by countries, regions, and special groups, with global coverage, relative to the period 1961-present (with annual updates) and with projections for 2030 and 2050. GHG emissions are expressed as Gg CO₂ and CO₂e (from CH₄ and N₂O), by underlying agricultural emission subdomain and by aggregate (agriculture total, agriculture total plus energy, agricultural soils). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](b2483333-693a-44e2-ae00-47f21c6a00bd) as a replacement.**_
  
The rate of out-of-school children, generated by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), is the percentage of children not in school by year per country. The data extend back to 1999. The UIS gathers these statistics using questionnaires, which are sent to UNESCO Member States annually. The questionnaires are based on international standards, classifications, and measures that are regularly reviewed and modified by the UIS in order to address emerging statistical issues and improve the quality of data. The UIS collaborates with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and Eurostat to collect data with surveys (collectively UOE). The UOE questionnaire compiles data from high- and middle-income countries that are members or partner countries of the OECD or Eurostat. The UOE survey gathers more detailed education statistics. Midyear population estimates for countries with at least 90,000 inhabitants are provided by the UN Population Division to calculate the percentages. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

Projected Change in Heating Degree Days (RCP4.5)
attributes.description:
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings.
