attributes.name: Electricity Installed Capacity
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
Electricity installed capacity measures the [maximum electric output](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3) an electricity generator can produce under specific conditions. This dataset reveals the amount of electricity all the power plants in a country can produce within a year and helps quantify the [growth of energy resources](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/what-generation-capacity). However, considering many generators do not operate at their full capacity all the time, a generator's actual electric output [varies based on conditions at the power plant, fuel costs, and/or as instructed by the electric power grid operator](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3). Therefore, this dataset represents the theoretical electricity output that is possible, rather than the actual electricity generation.
  
  

The Electricity Installed Capacity dataset was released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). This data was reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is available for the years 1980-2019, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
EIA compiled data from a list of external sources including  
- International Energy Agency (IEA)
- Power Reactor Information System (PRIS) from International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
- Platts World Power Plants Database
- International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)
- International Hydropower Association (IHA)
- United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database
- BP Statistical Review of World Energy
- Other government agencies, research institutes, and companies
  
  

Electricity data shows the capacity as of December 31 each year. Data from both utility and non-utility sources was used. EIA is in the process of creating specific country-level metadata for this dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. 
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [Total Energy Consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/67cf410f-4cdf-4437-aa09-187e5fa590ae) dataset and [Electricity Consumption] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/eef10736-8d8b-4ac9-a715-ef0653a83196) dataset by EIA.
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the electricity installed capacity of different energy resources from 1980 through 2018 is available from the data provider. 

For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_eia_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. 
  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: [Archived] Non-CO₂ Agricultural Emissions
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](460e6d91-ce17-46b0-b23d-d37751f1f607) as a replacement.**_
  
The non-CO₂ agricultural emissions data set, published the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in its FAOSTAT database, contains all the non-CO₂ emissions produced in the different agricultural emissions subdomains (enteric fermentation, manure management, rice cultivation, synthetic fertilizers, manure applied to soils, manure left on pastures, crop residues, cultivation of organic soils, burning of crop residues, burning of savanna, energy use) and provides a picture of their contribution to the total amount of GHG emissions from agriculture. GHG emissions from agriculture tabulated here consist of non-CO₂ gases—namely, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—produced by crop and livestock production and management activities. The FAOSTAT emissions database is computed following Tier 1 IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National GHG Inventories. GHG emissions data are provided by countries, regions, and special groups, with global coverage, relative to the period 1961-present (with annual updates) and with projections for 2030 and 2050. GHG emissions are expressed as Gg CO₂ and CO₂e (from CH₄ and N₂O), by underlying agricultural emission subdomain and by aggregate (agriculture total, agriculture total plus energy, agricultural soils). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: Plastic density in the oceans
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The dataset represents the count (pieces per square kilometer) and weight (grams per square kilometer) densities of plastic particles floating in the ocean. The data was created from an oceanographic model of floating debris dispersal and calibrated using data from surveys done during 24 expeditions conducted from 2007-2013. The results have been adjusted for a variety of factors like particle fragmentation and wind driven mixing of water. The data is presented in four particle size categories ranging from 0.33 millimeters to >200 millimeters. The final results are shown in raster format at a spatial resolution of 20 kilometers. 
  
  

Plastic pollution is globally distributed across all oceans and is regarded as a major health issue for marine and human life. As plastic degrades it forms microplastics that are often consumed by marine fauna, slowly working up the food chain. In addition, floating plastics can move across oceans and transport species to non-native regions. 
  
  

This study was conducted to help countries understand their impacts on the ocean and to be used in implementing plastic waste reduction policies. It was authored by researchers from a variety of organizations and funded by an array of environmental and educational groups. The data has global coverage and is available at a spatial resolution of 0.2° or about 20 kilometers.  
  
### Methodology  
  
To gather the mass and count of the ocean’s plastics, the researchers conducted 24 expeditions (2007–2013) across all five subtropical gyres, coastal Australia, Bay of Bengal, and the Mediterranean Sea. During these expeditions 680 surface net tows and 891 visual survey transects of large plastic debris were conducted. Surface net tows were done using a mesh size of 0.33 millimeters towed at 0.5 to 2 meters below the ocean surface for 15 to 60 minutes. Visual surveys were carried out using dedicated observers viewing 20 meter sections next to the boat noting large floating debris. Debris observations were broken into nine categories, four categories for fishing-related debris: buoy, line, net, and other fishing gear, and five categories for other plastics: bucket, bottle, foamed polystyrene, bag/film, or miscellaneous plastics. All 1,571 mesh and visual surveys included data on plastic counts and 1,333 of them also included data on debris weight.
  
  

The data was used to create debris estimates and calibrate an oceanographic model based on water movement to show the dispersal of floating debris. The model used to describe oceanic currents was the US Navy’s Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM). This was combined with a Lagrangian particle-tracking model Pol3DD to mimic how plastic particles move through the ocean. The model assumes that amounts of plastic entering the ocean depends on three principal variables: watershed outfalls, population density, and maritime activity. The results were adjusted to compensate for wind driven mixing of the surface layer that forces plastic particles below the surface. Additionally, conservative estimates for particle fragmentation rates were used when determining particle count. Through this methodology, estimated values were generated for the count and weight of ocean plastic in four size classes: 0.33-1.0 millimeters, 1.01-4.75 millimeters, 4.76-200 millimeters, and >200 millimeters.
  
  

For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0111913).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_016_rw0_ocean_plastics).

attributes.name: Local Threats to Coral Reefs
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The health of coral reefs is threatened from many nearby human activities. This dataset describes, individually and in aggregate, the threat posed by the following nearby activities: coastal development, marine-based pollution, watershed-based pollution, and overfishing and other destructive fishing practices. This dataset expresses these threats via an index of low, medium, or high threat severity at a 1 km resolution (the integrated threat index also includes a "very high" category).   
  
The dataset was created at the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the Reefs at Risk Revisited study and represents threats for the year 2011. The coral reef location dataset used was based on 500 meter resolution gridded data reflecting shallow, tropical coral reefs of the world. Organizations contributing to the data and development of the map include the Institute for Marine Remote Sensing at the University of South Florida (IMaRS USF), Institut de Recherche pour le Développement (IRD), United Nations Environment World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), WorldFish Center, and WRI.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Local threats to coral reefs include: coastal development; marine-based pollution and damage; watershed-based pollution; and overfishing and destructive fishing practices. To combine these into one index, the authors defined the factors that contribute to each threat in the following way:  
  
The coastal development threat includes the number, size, population density, and population growth rates of human settlements on the coast; locations of seaports, airports and hotels; and traffic from tourism.  
  
The marine-based pollution and damage threat includes datasets on distance from commercial and cruise ports, shipping intensity as measured by a voluntary reporting scheme, and presence of oil infrastructure.   
  
The watershed-based pollution threat to coral reefs includes sediment deposits accumulated throughout watersheds and released at river mouths. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) is used to calculate the relative erosion potential (REP) for all land areas. The REP levels in a watershed are used to determine how much sediment gets loaded into the water courses of the watershed. Factors such as mangroves and dams reduce the total sediment delivery at the river mouth. A model is used to disperse the accumulated sediment amount in the surrounding ocean area. Thresholds are established to differentiate between ocean grid cells at low, medium, or high threat from sediment deposits.  
  
Severity of overfishing was estimated based on proxies for demand for fish products---coastal population density, extent of official fishing areas, and reef and shallow shelf areas---with special adjustments made to account for increased demand when in proximity to large populations and market centers. Areas where destructive fishing practices occur, such as using explosives or poisons, were included based on observations from monitoring and mapping exercises undertaken by field experts.   
  
The overfishing and destructive fishing threat level may be reduced by one level if a grid cell was inside a marine protected area that had been rated as having “effective” or “partially effective” management. These ratings were sourced from regional experts, who were asked to rate marine protected areas on a three-point scale for management effectiveness.   
  
Depending on the size of these threat factors, distance thresholds are established for whether that threat factor puts a nearby ocean grid cell at low, medium, or high risk of damage to coral reefs. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://wriorg.s3.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/pdf/reefs_at_risk_revisited.pdf?_ga=2.65485742.1818236267.1556558259-801875434.1487936749).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for global threats to coral are available from the data provider.  For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

info.technical_title: Reefs at Risk Revisited: Local Threats
info.functions: Estimated threat to coral reefs from combined local activities such as development, pollution and fishing
info.cautions:
Certain assumptions or simplifications were made about each of the four types of threats considered in this study. The assumptions, listed by category, are described below:
  
  

  
  
Coastal development:
  
  
• Some tourist locations were missed in the modeling process, especially new locations.
  
  
• The model did not directly capture sewage discharge, but relied on population as a proxy.
  
  

  
  
Watershed-based pollution:
  
  
• The model used a proxy for sediment, nutrient, and pollutant delivery.
  
  
• Nutrient delivery to coastal waters might have been underestimated due to a lack of spatial data on crop cultivation and fertilizer application. However, agricultural land was treated as a separate category of land cover, weighted for a higher influence.
  
  
• The model did not incorporate nutrient and pollutant inputs from industry or from intensive livestock farming, which could be considerable.
  
  
• Sediment plumes accumulated through inland watersheds and discharged at river mouths can drive reef degradation. After reaching the river mouth, sediment matter disperses according to currents, but the movements of currents were not taken into account in modeling the plume dispersal process. The model designers decided for the sake of simplicity to model the dispersion process as depositing an equal proportion of the plume in successive concentric circles around the river mouth until all of the plume matter has been allocated. This data did not include threats from nutrient deposits released at river mouths, which can cause algal blooms which damage coral reefs.
  
  

  
  
Marine-based pollution and damage:
  
  
• Threats associated with shipping intensity may have been underestimated because the data source was based on voluntary ship tracking, and did not include fishing vessels.
  
  
• The threat model did not account for marine debris (such as plastics), discarded fishing gear, recreational vessels, or shipwrecks, due to a lack of global spatial data on these threats.
  
  
• The drivers of coral reef degradation include discharged oil, bilge, and ballast liquids from ships involved in world trade. There were no available datasets that measure these discharges, so port and ship traffic density were used as a proxy.
  
  

  
  
Overfishing and destructive fishing:
  
  
• Accurate, spatially referenced global data on fishing methods, catches, and the number of fishers was not available; therefore, population pressure was used as a proxy for overfishing.    
  
  
• This model didn’t capture the targeting of high-value species, which affects most reefs globally but has fewer ecosystem impacts than wider-scale overfishing.
  
  
• Management effectiveness scores were only available for about 83% of the reefs within marine protected areas.

attributes.name: Annual Surface Water Coverage
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the locations of seasonal water and permanent water for each year between 1984 and 2020. A permanent water surface is an area that is underwater for all 12 months of the year, while a seasonal water surface is underwater for less than 12 months of the year. This dataset has a 30 meter resolution. 
  
  

Water is essential for Earth’s plant and animal life, as well as for many human activities. Surface water also affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between Earth’s surface and atmosphere. The dataset can be used to support sectors such as water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. 
  
  

This data is a part of the Global Surface Water dataset, created by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Water coverage was detected using satellite imagery from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 that was collected between 1984 and  2020. To detect water, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques such as expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. An expert system is a classification process that can account for data uncertainty and incorporate image interpretation expertise. 
  
  

In some places, observations for all 12 months of the year were not available. For example, some parts of the world experience a polar night during parts of the year, in which the night lasts for more than 24 hours. These areas do not have adequate imagery to detect surface water coverage for all 12 months. In cases where 12 months of data was not available, water is considered to be permanent if the number of months where water is present is equal to the number of months where valid observations were acquired. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal.
  
  

Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. 
  
  

If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. 
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly recurrence and monthly water history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer

info.cautions:
- The accuracy of this dataset was calculated using over 40,000 control points from around the world and across the 32 years. The validation results show that the water detection expert system produced less than 1% of false water detections and that less than 5% of water surfaces were missed.
- Known omissions include bodies of water smaller than 30 meters by 30 meters, as well as those obscured by floating, overhanging, and standing vegetation or hidden by infrastructure such as bridges. There are also issues with irrigated fields that stand in open water and paddy fields in steep terrain. 
- Detections are problematic in high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, particularly latitudes above 78° N,  due to the short observation season, as well as other reasons described in the [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584).
- Melt ponds and streams on the surface of glaciers are identified as permanent water surfaces, but this permanence is questionable.
- Some isolated errors are present in urban areas, where roofs, coal and waste heaps, and runways are the most common sources of confusion.
- Additional known issues and planned improvements of the dataset can be found in this [publication](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584).

attributes.name: Frost Free Season
attributes.description:
Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. attributes.name: Antarctic Sea Ice Extent
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Antarctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Antarctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Antarctic region. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand the current Antarctic sea ice extent. Typically, Antarctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in September and minimum in February. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. According to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent), natural variability in the Southern Ocean and in atmospheric circulation patterns have a greater impact on Antarctic sea ice extent than climate change. However, climate change is disrupting wind patterns, currents and ocean temperatures across the globe. These changes may eventually impact Antarctic sea ice extent.

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Antarctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset. 

  
  
The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. 

  
  
Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f) and [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cli_005_polar_sea_ice_extents).  
  
### Disclaimer

info.technical_title: Sea Ice Index, Version 3
info.functions: Near real-time extent of Antarctic sea ice
info.cautions:
- Monthly extent is a better measure of conditions from year to year than is daily ice extent. Monthly data should be used for climatology studies instead of daily data. 
- Temporal and spatial monthly ice concentration averages can be ambiguous. For example, a mean concentration of 50% for a particular grid cell for the month of September could result from 100% concentration at that location for 15 days and 0% concentration for 15 days, or 50% concentration for 30 days, or some other combination. 
- Concentration values from 1% to 15% are statistically irrelevant because data values less than 15% from passive microwave instruments are too uncertain to use. Any cell with an ice concentration of less than 15% was automatically classified as water. 
- Occasionally, data from one or more days within a month are missing for a given 25 km grid cell. Monthly averages are computed from the daily data only if there are at least 20 days of data for that cell.

Dry spells represent the annual average count of 5-day periods without precipitation, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: Extreme Heat Days
attributes.description:
Extreme heat days represent the annual average count of days with heat greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA).

LOCA is a technique for downscaling climate model projections of the future climate. The method estimates finer-scale climate detail using the systematic historical effects of topography on local weather patterns. The LOCA downscaled climate projections provide temperature and precipitation on pixels that are six kilometers (3.7 miles) across. The data are daily, covering the period 1950-2100 for 32 global climate models. LOCA attempts to better preserve extreme hot days and heavy rain events than the previous generation of downscaling approaches. While previous downscaling techniques typically formed the downscaled model day using a weighted average of 30 similar historical days, LOCA looks locally around each point of interest to find the one best matching day. The data spans from Mexico through southern Canada and can be used to assess climate impacts across much of North America, including the entire conterminous U.S. The work represents a collaboration across many groups, including SIO, the California Energy Commission, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Geological Survey, the Bureau of Reclamation, the NOAA Regional Integrated Sciences and Assessments (RISA) program, the Climate Analytics Group, the nonprofit group Climate Central, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, NASA Ames Research Center, Santa Clara University, the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder, and the Southwest Climate Science Center.

The LOCA data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 32 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the LOCA data set. For access to the original LOCA data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: U.S. Wildfire Hazard Potential
attributes.description:
Federal wildfire managers often want to know, over large landscapes, where wildfires are likely to occur and how intense they may be. To meet this need we developed a map that we call wildfire hazard potential (WHP) – a raster geospatial product that can help to inform evaluations of wildfire risk or prioritization of fuels management needs across very large spatial scales (millions of acres). Our specific objective with the WHP map was to depict the relative potential for wildfire that would be difficult for suppression resources to contain. To create the 2014 version, we built upon spatial estimates of wildfire likelihood and intensity generated in 2014 with the Large Fire Simulation system (FSim) for the national interagency Fire Program Analysis system (FPA), as well as spatial fuels and vegetation data from LANDFIRE 2010 and point locations of fire occurrence from FPA (ca. 1992 – 2012). With these data sets as inputs, we produced an index of WHP for all of the conterminous United States at 270 m resolution. We present the final WHP map in two forms: 1) continuous integer values, and 2) five WHP classes of very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. On its own, WHP is not an explicit map of wildfire threat or risk, but when paired with spatial data depicting highly valued resources and assets such as structures or powerlines, it can approximate relative wildfire risk to those specific resources and assets. WHP is also not a forecast or wildfire outlook for any particular season, as it does not include any information on current or forecasted weather or fuel moisture conditions. It is instead intended for long-term strategic fuels management.

attributes.name: U.S. Flood Hazards
attributes.description:
The National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) is a digital database that contains flood hazard mapping data from FEMA’s National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). This map data is derived from Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases and Letters of Map Revision (LOMRs).The NFHL is for community officials and members looking to view effective regulatory flood hazard information in a Geographic Information Systems (GIS) application.

The NFHL provides users with the ability to determine the flood zone, base flood elevation and floodway status for a particular geographic location. It also has National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) community information, map panel information, cross section and hydraulic structure information, Coastal Barrier Resource System information (if applicable) and base map information, such as road, stream and public land survey data.  A full list of the layers available in the NFHL may be found in the NFHL GIS Services User Guide.

The NFHL data set represents the current effective flood risk data for those parts of the country where maps have been modernized. It is a compilation of effective Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases and Letters of Map Revision (LOMR). The NFHL is updated as new data reaches its designated effective date and becomes valid for regulatory use under the NFIP.

Note: this data set is only visible at high zoom levels.

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

attributes.name: U.S. Billion-Dollar Disasters
attributes.description: The National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) is the Nation's Scorekeeper in terms of addressing severe weather and climate events in their historical perspective. As part of its responsibility of monitoring and assessing the climate, NCEI tracks and evaluates climate events in the U.S. and globally that have great economic and societal impacts. NCEI is frequently called upon to provide summaries of global and U.S. temperature and precipitation trends, extremes, and comparisons in their historical perspective. Found here are Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters: the weather and climate events that have had the greatest economic impact from 1980 to 2018. The U.S. has sustained 233 weather and climate disasters since 1980 where overall damages/costs reached or exceeded $1 billion (including Consumer Price Index adjustment to 2018). The total cost of these 233 events exceeds $1.5 trillion. Please note that the map reflects a summation of billion-dollar events for each state affected (i.e., it does not mean that each state shown suffered at least $1 billion in losses for each event).

attributes.name: Cooling Degree Days
attributes.description:
A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. 

This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts.

This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA).

info.description:
The graph below offers several temperature and precipitation variables for U.S. counties. Switch between counties, variables, and temporal resolutions using the dropdown menu above the graph.

Average Daily Maximum Temperature (°F): 
 •  A day’s highest (maximum) temperature usually occurs in the afternoon. Averaging the daily high temperatures over any period results in a mean maximum temperature for that period. Maximum temperature serves as one measure of comfort and safety for people and for the health of plants and animals. When maximum temperature exceeds particular thresholds, people can become ill and transportation and energy infrastructure may be stressed.

Average Daily Minimum Temperature (°F):
 •  A day’s lowest (minimum) temperature usually occurs in the early morning, just before sunrise. Averaging the daily low temperatures for any period results in a mean minimum temperature for that period. Periods of low temperature give plants, animals, and people a chance to recover from daytime heat. When minimum temperatures aren’t sufficiently cool, plant and animal responses can trigger ecosystem changes and increased demand for energy can stress energy infrastructure.

Days per year with Maximum Temperature Above 90, 95, 100, or 105°F
 •  The total number of days per year with maximum temperature above various thresholds is an indicator of how often very hot conditions occur. Depending upon humidity, wind, and physical workload, people who work outdoors or don’t have access to air conditioning may feel very uncomfortable or experience heat stress or illness on very hot days. Hot days also stress plants, animals, and human infrastructure such as roads, railroads, and electric lines. Increased demand for electricity to cool homes and buildings can place additional stress on energy infrastructure.

Days per year with Maximum Temperature below 32°F
 •  The total number of days per year when the highest temperature is less than 32°F (0°C) is an indicator of how often very cold days occur. Days when the highest temperature doesn’t rise above the freezing point of water are called “icing days.” The annual number of icing days tells us how much rest plants get from growing; with too few icing days, some plants do not perceive a “reset” signal to begin budding or blooming in the spring. The annual number of icing days can also help predict if populations of insects, such as tree-killing bark beetles, will survive the winter or not.

Days per year with Minimum Temperature below 32°F
 •  The total number of days per year when the temperature dips below 32°F (0°C) is an indicator of how often cold days occur. A decrease in the number of days temperature drops below freezing promotes earlier spring snowmelt and runoff, with important consequences for managing water resources. Below-freezing temperatures can cause driving hazards, aircraft icing, and damage to infrastructure, yet ski resorts and other winter recreation businesses depend on sufficiently cold days to maintain snowpack. Some plants require a cumulative number of days below freezing before they can begin budding or blooming in the spring.

Days With Minimum Temperature above 80 or 90°F
 •  The total number of days per year when the lowest temperature doesn’t drop below a given threshold is an indicator of how often very warm nights occur. When the lowest temperature of a 24-hour period doesn’t dip below 80 or 90°F, plants, animals, and people don’t have a chance to cool down. They can become stressed and susceptible to other negative health impacts. As the number of very warm nights increases, sensitive plants may not produce flowers or viable seeds.

Total Precipitation
 •  Total precipitation over a year, season, or month indicates the average amount of water added to the environment over the indicated period. The graph for this variable shows total precipitation in inches. To help users perceive trends in this variable over time however, the map shows precipitation as the percentage change from the long-term average (1961 to 1990).

Days with Precipitation Above 1, 2, 3, or 4 inches
 •  The number of days per year when locations receive more than 1, 2, or 3 inches of precipitation is an indicator of how often very heavy precipitation events occur. This measurement may also be used as an indicator of flood risk. Comparing the number of days with heavy precipitation at a single location over time can reveal a trend of increasing or decreasing flood risk.

Dry Days
 •  The number of dry days per year—days when precipitation is less than 0.01 inches—gives a sense of the portion of the year when no moisture is being added to the environment. Changes in the number of dry days can indicate a tendency toward drier or wetter conditions. The graph for this variable shows counts of Dry Days. To help users perceive trends in numbers of dry days over time however, the map shows dry days as the projected annual number of dry days for each decade minus the 1961-1990 average. Positive values indicate more dry days while negative values indicate fewer dry days.

Heating Degree Days
 •  The number of heating degree days at any location reflects the amount of energy people use to heat a building when it is cool outside. Lower numbers of heating degree days indicate lower demand for energy. Heating degree days measure how much (in degrees), and for how long (in days), outside air temperature is below 65°F. For example, on a day when the average outdoor temperature is 35°F, raising the indoor temperature to 65°F would require 30 degrees of heating multiplied by 1 day, or 30 heating degree days. Engineers and utility companies use a location’s annual number of heating degree days as one input when estimating demand for energy in the cold season.

Cooling Degree Days
 •  The number of cooling degree days at any location reflects the amount of energy people use to cool a building when it is warm outside. Higher numbers of cooling degree days indicate higher demand for energy. Cooling degree days measure how much (in degrees), and for how long (in days), outside air temperature is higher than 65°F. For example, on a day when the average outdoor temperature is 85°F, reducing the indoor temperature to 65°F would require 20 degrees of cooling multiplied by 1 day, or 20 cooling degree days. Engineers and utility companies use a location’s annual number of cooling degree days as one input when estimating demand for energy in the warm season.

Growing Degree Days
 •  The number of growing degree days per year is used to estimate the growth and development of plants (or insects) during the growing season. Higher numbers of growing-degree days indicate longer and warmer growing conditions. As growth occurs only when temperature exceeds a species’ base temperature (for example, 50°F), the number of days times the number of degrees above the base indicates the duration and magnitude of growing conditions.

Modified Growing Degree Days
 •  Corn growers use the number of modified growing degree days to monitor the development of corn crops. As corn development occurs only when temperature is above 50°F but below 86°F, the standard calculation for growing-degree days is modified to omit conditions outside this range. In future decades, regions where temperatures regularly exceed 86°F may be less successful in growing corn.

attributes.name: Cropland Extent
attributes.description:
The NASA Making Earth System Data Records for Use in Research Environments (MEaSUREs) Global Food Security Support Analysis Data (GFSAD) Crop Mask Global 1 kilometer (km) data set was created using multiple input data including: remote sensing such as Landsat, Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), Satellite Probatoire d'Observation de la Terre (SPOT) vegetation and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (MODIS); secondary elevation data; climate 50-year precipitation and 20-year temperature data; reference sub-meter to 5-meter resolution ground data and country statistics data.

The GFSAD1KCM provides spatial distribution of a disaggregated five class global cropland extent map derived for nominal 2010 at 1-km based on four major studies: Thenkabail et al. (2009a, 2011), Pittman et al. (2010), Yu et al. (2013), and Friedl et al. (2010). The GFSAD1KCM nominal 2010 product is based on data ranging from years 2007 through 2012.

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

attributes.name: Projected Change in Frost Free Season (RCP4.5)
Projected Change in Frost Free Season (RCP4.5)
attributes.description:
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

attributes.name: Average Temperature
attributes.description:
Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: cit.002 GEOS-CF Air Quality Forecast NO2
Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Modeled 5-day Forecast
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). NO₂ is a highly reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which includes nitrous acid and nitric acid.  
  
NO₂ emissions contribute to the [formation of smog](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-nitrogen-dioxide-no2) and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposure to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions, and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators.  
  
GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model.  
  
To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module.  
  
All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b).

  
  


Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere is also produced by GEOS-CF. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_002_gmao_air_quality).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days (RCP8.5)
Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days (RCP8.5)
attributes.description:
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in extreme precipitation is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average days of extreme precipitation during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India
attributes.description:
Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India

SOURCE: Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India

LINK: https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web; https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf

Overview

The dataset comprises five-year averages of production (in tonnes), productivity/yield (in tonnes per hectare), and area (in hectares) for 55 major crops across India from 1997–98 to 2022–23. The information is provided at the district level, covering major seasonal time periods of each crop within each year. The yearly datasets were derived from crop-wise APY dataset (https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web).

Methodology

Pre-Processing: The dataset available as excel report was processed and joined with district shapefile (recent by mid of year 2022, containing 755 districts) obtained from Survey of India website. To simplify the presentation, the raw yearly data was averaged into five-year intervals to highlight trends in crop production and acreage across each district. The periods were labelled as follows: 1995-2000 as 2000, 2001-2005 as 2005, 2006-2010 as 2010, 2011-2015 as 2015, 2016-2020 as 2020, and 2021-2023 as 2023. This approach was adopted based on feedback from stakeholder engagements.

Layers of interest: Rice Area (in Hectares), Rice Production (in Tonnes), Rice Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare), Cotton Area (in Hectares), Cotton Production (in Tonnes), Cotton Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare)

Seasons considered for Rice crop: Kharif, Rabi, Autumn, Summer
Seasons considered for Cotton crop: Kharif, Rabi

The agricultural crop year in India runs from July to June. The cropping season is divided into two main seasons: (i) Kharif and (ii) Rabi, based on the monsoon. The Kharif season occurs from June/July to September/October during the southwest monsoon. It aligns with the Asian summer monsoon and is mostly rainfed, with limited irrigation arrangements. The Rabi season lasts from October to March and is grown under irrigated conditions. The Summer and Autumn seasons are shorter and found only in a few states. The Summer season runs from February/March to April/May and is mostly grown under irrigated conditions. The Autumn season, from May/June to October, is mainly for long-duration crops like sugarcane and some vegetable crops. For rice crop, the season is followed in particular states of India that do not receive considerable rains from the Asian summer monsoon.

Area, Yield, and Production Estimation Methods

The methods for estimating area, yield, and production of crops follow standardized processes under India's agricultural statistical framework.

1. Area Estimation Methods

1.1. Temporarily Settled States (Land Record States)
Crop area is estimated through field-to-field enumeration by a village accountant (Patwari/Karnam). The data is recorded in the Khasra register (a field-wise crop record). The area statistics are aggregated at village, tehsil, district, and state levels.

1.2. Permanently Settled States (Non-Land Record States)
Establishment of Agency for Reporting Agricultural Statistics (EARAS) is used:
- A random sample of at least 20% of villages is surveyed annually.
- Complete enumeration is conducted within selected villages.
- The process ensures coverage of all villages over five years.

1.3. Non-Reporting Areas
Area estimates are derived using remote sensing technology and aerial photography. Ground truthing and validation methods are used to improve accuracy.

2. Yield Estimation Methods

General Crop Estimation Surveys (GCES)
The yield is estimated through scientifically designed crop-cutting experiments (CCE). The methodology is as follows:

2.1. Sampling Design
Stratified Multistage Random Sampling:
- Strata: Administrative divisions (tehsil/block).
- Primary Sampling Units: Villages (selected randomly).
- Second-Stage Sampling Units: Fields within selected villages.
- Ultimate Sampling Units: Experimental plots of standard size (e.g., 5m x 5m).

2.2. Plot Selection
Two fields are randomly selected per village. A random plot (e.g., 5m x 5m) is located within each field using random numbers. For row-planted crops (like cotton), longer plots (e.g., 10m x 5m) are used.

2.3. Harvesting and Recording
The experimental plot is harvested before the rest of the field. The produce is:
- Weighed immediately for gross yield.
- Adjusted if required (e.g., driage experiments for rice).

2.4. Driage Adjustments
- Rice: Driage experiments are conducted to adjust for moisture content, ensuring yields are reported as dried grain weight.
- Cotton: In the case of cotton, the final produce is expressed in terms of lint after adopting ginning percentage (kapas to lint) as obtained from the ginning factories.

3. Production Estimation Methods
Area and yield are multiplied to estimate production at village, district, state, and national levels.

4. Validation of the Area, Production and Yield estimates
Final aggregation and validation occur at the national level by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES). Production estimates are validated using:
- Remote sensing data,
- Historical trends,
- Market and trade data,
- Reports from local agricultural officers.

For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf.

Visualizing the Data
The data is available as district-level aggregates. By selecting a specific crop, area, production, yield statistic, and preferred season, the relevant layer is displayed with a gradient based on the 2023 crop year, ranging from yellow (for low values) to green (with darker shades representing higher values). The cursor can be dragged over districts and clicked to view the 5-yearly averaged values from 1995 to 2023. The 'No Data' value, represented by black, indicates either that the season was not practiced in the district during that year or that data is unavailable from the source.

Disclaimer
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source.

attributes.name: Extreme Precipitation Days
attributes.description:
Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

attributes.name: Average Low Temperature
attributes.description:
Annual average low temperature, as derived from the Localized Constructed Analogs (LOCA). 

LOCA is a technique for downscaling climate model projections of the future climate. The method estimates finer-scale climate detail using the systematic historical effects of topography on local weather patterns. The LOCA downscaled climate projections provide temperature and precipitation on pixels that are six kilometers (3.7 miles) across. The data are daily, covering the period 1950-2100 for 32 global climate models. LOCA attempts to better preserve extreme hot days and heavy rain events than the previous generation of downscaling approaches. While previous downscaling techniques typically formed the downscaled model day using a weighted average of 30 similar historical days, LOCA looks locally around each point of interest to find the one best matching day. The data spans from Mexico through southern Canada and can be used to assess climate impacts across much of North America, including the entire conterminous U.S. The work represents a collaboration across many groups, including SIO, the California Energy Commission, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Geological Survey, the Bureau of Reclamation, the NOAA Regional Integrated Sciences and Assessments (RISA) program, the Climate Analytics Group, the nonprofit group Climate Central, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, NASA Ames Research Center, Santa Clara University, the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder, and the Southwest Climate Science Center.

The LOCA data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 32 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm

attributes.name: Fires (VIIRS)
attributes.description:
The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGTDL_NRT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS.  The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot / fire pixels. 

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.
