காஸெர்ட், எஃப்., ஈ. கார்னெஜோ, மற்றும் ஈ. நில்சன். 2021. "காலநிலை தரவை அணுகக்கூடியதாக ஆக்குதல்: நெக்ஸ்-ஜி.டி.டி.பி மற்றும் எல்.ஓ.சி.ஏ கீழ்மட்ட காலநிலை குறிகாட்டிகளை உற்பத்தி செய்வதற்கான முறைகள்" தொழில்நுட்ப குறிப்பு. வாஷிங்டன், டி.சி: வேர்ல்ட் ரிசோர்சஸ் இன்ஸ்டிடியூட். https://www.wri.org/research/making-climate-data-accessible ஆன்லைனில் கிடைக்கிறது. [www.resourcewatch.org] (https://www.resourcewatch.org/).

சி.எம்.ஐ.பி.க்கு பொறுப்பான உலக காலநிலை ஆராய்ச்சித் திட்டத்தின் ஒருங்கிணைந்த மாடலிங் பணிக் குழுவை நாங்கள் அங்கீகரிக்கிறோம், மேலும் அவற்றின் மாதிரி வெளியீட்டை உற்பத்தி செய்து கிடைக்கச் செய்த காலநிலை மாடலிங் குழுக்களுக்கு நாங்கள் நன்றி தெரிவிக்கிறோம். அமெரிக்க எரிசக்தித் துறையின் காலநிலை மாதிரி நோய் கண்டறிதல் மற்றும் இண்டர்கம்பரிசன் திட்டம் சிஎம்ஐபிக்கான புவி அமைப்பு அறிவியல் போர்ட்டல்களுக்கான உலகளாவிய அமைப்புடன் இணைந்து மென்பொருள் உள்கட்டமைப்பின் ஒருங்கிணைப்பு ஆதரவு மற்றும் மேம்பாட்டை வழங்குகிறது.

பயன்படுத்தப்படும் காலநிலை காட்சிகள் நெக்ஸ்-ஜி.டி.டி.பி தரவுத்தொகுப்பில் இருந்து வந்தன, இது காலநிலை பகுப்பாய்வு குழு மற்றும் நாசா அமேஸ் ஆராய்ச்சி மையத்தால் நாசா எர்த் எக்ஸ்சேஞ்சைப் பயன்படுத்தி தயாரிக்கப்பட்டது, மேலும் காலநிலை உருவகப்படுத்துதலுக்கான நாசா மையத்தால் (என்.சி.சி.எஸ்) விநியோகிக்கப்பட்டது.

attributes.name: వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రతలో అంచనా వేయబడ్డ మార్పు
attributes.description:
### అవలోకనం  
  
1960-1990 బేస్ లైన్ కాల వ్యవధితో పోలిస్తే, 2000 మరియు 2080 మధ్య పది సంవత్సరాల విరామాల వద్ద వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత డేటాసెట్ లో అంచనా వేయబడ్డ మార్పు వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత డేటాసెట్ లో అంచనా వేసిన మార్పు చూపిస్తుంది. ప్రతి పది సంవత్సరాల విరామం వద్ద చూపించబడ్డ డేటా 31 సంవత్సరాల సగటుకు ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహిస్తుంది, ఇది సూచించబడ్డ సంవత్సరం చుట్టూ కేంద్రీకృతమై ఉంటుంది. ఉదాహరణకు, 2000 లో సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత వాస్తవానికి 1985 మరియు 2015 సంవత్సరాల మధ్య గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత యొక్క సగటు. వాతావరణ మార్పులపై ఇంటర్ గవర్నమెంటల్ ప్యానెల్ (ఐపిసిసి యొక్క) ప్రాతినిధ్య ఏకాగ్రత మార్గాలు (ఆర్ సిపి) 8.5 ద్వారా నిర్ణయించబడే భవిష్యత్తు గ్రీన్ హౌస్ వాయువు ఉద్గార రేట్లపై సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత అంచనాలు ఆధారపడి ఉంటాయి. ఆర్ సిపి 8.5 అనేది 21వ శతాబ్దంలో గ్రీన్ హౌస్ వాయువుల ఉద్గార రేట్లు ఏమాత్రం తగ్గని ఒక ఊహాజనిత దృశ్యం. డేటాసెట్ 0.25° ప్రాదేశిక రిజల్యూషన్ వద్ద డిగ్రీల సెల్సియస్ (°C)లో చూపించబడింది.
  
గ్లోబల్ గ్రీన్హౌస్ వాయువుల సాంద్రతలు పెరగడం, ఫలితంగా వాతావరణంలో మార్పు, వ్యవసాయం, మౌలిక సదుపాయాలు, విపత్తు నిర్వహణ మరియు మానవ సంఘర్షణను ప్రభావితం చేస్తూ, గ్రహంతో మన సంబంధాన్ని ప్రాథమికంగా మార్చడానికి సెట్ చేయబడింది. ఈ మార్పులను అంచనా వేయడానికి మరియు స్వీకరించడానికి, వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత డేటాసెట్ లో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ చేంజ్ రాబోయే దశాబ్దాల్లో ఉష్ణోగ్రత నమూనాలు ఎలా మారే అవకాశం ఉందనే దానిపై అంచనాలను అందిస్తుంది. ఈ డేటాసెట్ గ్లోబల్ క్లైమేట్ సమాచారాన్ని సంక్షిప్తీకరించడం ద్వారా మరియు సమాచారాన్ని ఒక సాధారణ జియోస్పేషియల్ ఫార్మెట్ లో ఓపెన్ డేటాసెట్ వలే అందించడం ద్వారా వాతావరణ డేటా యొక్క ప్రాప్యతను మెరుగుపరుస్తుంది. 
  
నేషనల్ ఏరోనాటిక్స్ అండ్ స్పేస్ అడ్మినిస్ట్రేషన్ (నాసా) ఎర్త్ ఎక్స్ఛేంజ్ గ్లోబల్ డైలీ డౌన్ స్కేల్డ్ ప్రొజెక్షన్స్ (నెక్స్-జిడిడిపి) ను ఉపయోగించి విజ్జువాలిటీ మరియు వరల్డ్ రిసోర్సెస్ ఇనిస్టిట్యూట్ ద్వారా ఈ డేటాసెట్ ప్రాసెస్ చేయబడింది. ఎన్ ఈఎక్స్-జిడిడిపి డేటాసెట్ అనేది స్థానిక మరియు ప్రాంతీయ స్థాయిల వద్ద వాతావరణ మార్పు ప్రభావాల యొక్క అధ్యయనాలను నిర్వహించడంలో శాస్త్రీయ సమాజానికి సహాయపడటానికి మరియు వ్యక్తిగత పట్టణాలు, నగరాలు మరియు వాటర్ షెడ్ ల ప్రాదేశిక స్థాయిలో భవిష్యత్తు ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ నమూనాలపై ప్రజా అవగాహనను పెంపొందించడానికి ఉద్దేశించబడింది. ఈ డేటాసెట్ యొక్క మునుపటి వెర్షన్ [పార్టనర్ షిప్ ఫర్ రెజిలియెన్స్ అండ్ ప్రిపేర్డ్ నెస్ (ప్రెప్)]](https://prepdata.org/) ద్వారా ప్రాసెస్ చేయబడింది మరియు ఉత్పత్తి చేయబడింది, ఇది వాతావరణ డేటాకు ప్రాప్యతను మెరుగుపరచడం ద్వారా వాతావరణ మార్పులకు స్థితిస్థాపకతను నిర్మించడానికి పి.ఆర్.ఇ.పి యొక్క మిషన్ కు సహాయపడుతుంది.  
  
#### మెథడాలజీ  
  
ఎన్ ఈఎక్స్-జిడిడిపి నుండి ఉష్ణోగ్రత డేటాతో వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత డేటాసెట్ లో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ చేంజ్ సృష్టించబడింది. ఎన్ ఈఎక్స్-జిడిడిపి డేటాసెట్ లు గ్లోబల్ సర్క్యులేషన్ మోడల్ (జిసిఎమ్) ప్రయోగాల నుండి తీసుకోబడ్డాయి, ఇవి [ఇంటర్ గవర్నమెంటల్ ప్యానెల్ ఆన్ క్లైమేట్ చేంజ్ (ఐపిసిసి) ఐదవ అసెస్ మెంట్ రిపోర్ట్ (ఎఆర్ 5)] (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf) కొరకు ఉత్పత్తి చేయబడ్డాయి. కపుల్డ్ మోడల్ ఇంటర్ కంపారిసన్ ప్రాజెక్ట్ ఫేజ్ 5 (సిఎమ్ ఐపి5) గా పిలువబడే ఈ ప్రయోగాల్లో గ్రీన్ హౌస్ వాయువు సాంద్రతల యొక్క వివిధ స్థాయిల కింద శీతోష్ణస్థితిని అనుకరించడానికి రూపొందించిన వాతావరణ నమూనాల నుండి ఫలితాలు ఉన్నాయి.  

సిఎమ్ఐపి5 డేటాలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో మోడల్స్ (45), క్లైమేట్ దృష్టాంతాలు (4), సంవత్సరాలు (150+), మరియు వేరియబుల్స్ (20-40) ఉన్నాయి. దాని ముతక రిజల్యూషన్ (1-4°) వద్ద కూడా ఇది బిలియన్ల కొద్దీ పొరలకు దారితీస్తుంది. డౌన్ స్కేలింగ్ ద్వారా, నెక్స్-జిడిడిపి తమకు అవసరమైన డేటాను మాత్రమే సంగ్రహిస్తుంది మరియు [షెఫీల్డ్ ఎట్ అల్. (2006)] (https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-ఆఫ్-ఎ-50-ఇయర్-హై-రిజల్యూషన్-గ్లోబల్) డేటాసెట్ ను చారిత్రాత్మక రిఫరెన్స్ గా ఉపయోగించి డేటా యొక్క మొత్తం పరిమాణాన్ని తగ్గిస్తుంది.  

ప్రతి సంవత్సరం వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత, వాతావరణ నమూనా, మరియు దృష్టాంతం ప్రతి-పిక్సెల్ ప్రాతిపదికన నెక్స్-జిడిడిపి డేటాను ఉపయోగించి లెక్కించబడ్డాయి. ఇవ్వబడ్డ సంవత్సరంలో రోజువారీ గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత డేటా మొత్తాన్ని వెలికితీయడం మరియు సరాసరి చేయడం ద్వారా ఇది చేయబడింది. సగటు వార్షిక గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రతలు 1960-1990 బేస్ లైన్ కాలానికి 31-సంవత్సరాల సగటులుగా మరియు 2000 నుండి 2080 వరకు ప్రతి దశాబ్దం ప్రారంభంలో తొమ్మిది కాలాలు కేంద్రీకృతమై ఉన్నాయి. వార్షిక సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రతలో అంచనా వేయబడిన మార్పును సృష్టించడానికి బేస్ లైన్ సగటును తొమ్మిది ప్రొజెక్ట్ చేసిన దశాబ్దాలలో ప్రతి దాని నుండి తీసివేయబడింది.

ప్రతి పది సంవత్సరాల విరామం వద్ద చూపించబడ్డ డేటా 31 సంవత్సరాల సగటుకు ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహిస్తుంది, ఇది సూచించబడ్డ సంవత్సరం చుట్టూ కేంద్రీకృతమై ఉంటుంది. ఉదాహరణకు, 2000లో సగటు గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రత వాస్తవానికి 1985 మరియు 2015 సంవత్సరాల మధ్య వార్షిక గరిష్ట ఉష్ణోగ్రతల సగటుగా ఉంది. 31-సంవత్సరాల సగటులు ఎంచుకోబడ్డాయి ఎందుకంటే అవి వార్షిక మరియు దశాబ్ధ వైవిధ్యం యొక్క ప్రభావాలను కనిష్టం చేస్తాయి మరియు దీర్ఘకాలిక వాతావరణ సంకేతాన్ని హైలైట్ చేస్తాయి. ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ సంఘం నుండి దీర్ఘకాలిక మార్గదర్శకత్వంతో సమలేఖనం చేయడానికి బేస్ లైన్ కాలం ఎంచుకోబడింది. అదనంగా, యూనిట్లను ఒరిజినల్ డేటాసెట్ యూనిట్లు (కెల్విన్) నుండి °C కు మార్చారు.   
### అదనపు సమాచారం  
  
[వార్షిక సగటు ఉష్ణోగ్రతలో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ చేంజ్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7d7ed62c), [వార్షిక సగటు కనిష్ఠ ఉష్ణోగ్రతలో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ చేంజ్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82 కొరకు ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ ఛేంజ్ NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 డేటాను కూడా రిసోర్స్ వాచ్ చూపిస్తుంది https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae. డిగ్రీ డేస్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [ఫ్రాస్ట్ ఫ్రీ సీజన్ లో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ ఛేంజ్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [ఎక్స్ ట్రీమ్ హీట్ డేస్ లో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ చేంజ్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434aa-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [క్యుమిలేటివ్ అవపాతంలో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ ఛేంజ్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-4591-4591-4591-181b-434735,0001-181000000000001000000000000000050000000005000000001000000000000000001000000000010000000000100000100000000000000000000000010050100001001000000050000000050000050000000000000000000000000000000000005800000000500000000000500010000000000500000100000000000000000000000000005000 డ్రై స్పెల్స్ లో](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [ఎక్స్ ట్రీమ్ అవపాత రోజుల్లో ప్రొజెక్టెడ్ ఛేంజ్](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1ఈ6ఈ-4156-9బా2-875ఈసిఎబి665అఫ్).

రిసోర్స్ వాచ్ డేటా యొక్క ఒక ఉపసమితిని మాత్రమే చూపుతుంది. ఉద్గారాల సందర్భం RCP 4.5 కొరకు అదనపు డేటా లభ్యం అవుతుంది. ఒరిజినల్ NEX-GDDP డేటాసెట్ మరియు అదనపు సమాచారాన్ని యాక్సెస్ చేసుకోవడానికి, లెర్న్ మోర్ లింక్ చూడండి.
  
### డేటాను విజువలైజ్ చేయడం  
  
రిసోర్స్ వాచ్ లో ప్రదర్శించడానికి ముందు మా టీమ్ ఈ డేటాసెట్ ని రీఫార్మాట్ చేసింది. రిసోర్స్ వాచ్ [Github](https://github.com/resource-వాచ్/డేటా-ప్రీ-ప్రాసెసింగ్/ట్రీ/మాస్టర్/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca)పై డేటాను ఏవిధంగా ప్రాసెస్ చేసిందనే దానిపై డాక్యుమెంటేషన్ ని చూడండి.  
  
### డిస్ క్లెయిమర్  
  
ఈ వివరణ పేజీ యొక్క సారాంశాలు మూల మెటాడేటా నుండి తీసుకోబడ్డాయి.

- కొన్ని జిసిఎమ్ లు హిండ్ కాస్ట్ ల్లో రుతుపవనాలు వంటి ప్రాంతీయ వాతావరణ నమూనాలను పునఃసృష్టించడంలో ఇతరుల కంటే మెరుగ్గా పనిచేస్తాయి. నిర్దిష్ట అనువర్తనాల కొరకు, ప్రాంతీయ పనితీరు ఆధారంగా వ్యక్తిగత నమూనాలను ఎంచుకోవడం సముచితంగా ఉండవచ్చు.
- ఈ సూచికలను ఉత్పత్తి చేయడానికి ఉపయోగించే డౌన్ స్కేలింగ్ విధానాలు సహజంగానే ఉష్ణోగ్రత మరియు అవపాతంలో సాపేక్ష ప్రాదేశిక నమూనాలు భవిష్యత్తు వాతావరణ మార్పులలో స్థిరంగా ఉంటాయని ఊహిస్తాయి. ప్రధాన గాలి మరియు సముద్ర ప్రవాహాలు మందగించడం లేదా తిరోగమనం చెందడం వంటి ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ నమూనాలలో నాటకీయ మార్పులు సాధ్యమే, కానీ ఈ సూచికలలో సంగ్రహించబడవు.
- డౌన్ స్కేలింగ్ కోసం ఉపయోగించే చారిత్రక డేటా ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా నాణ్యతలో మారుతుంది. ప్రత్యేకించి, చిన్న రికార్డులు లేదా సిటు వాతావరణ పరిశీలనల యొక్క తక్కువ కవరేజీ ఉన్న ప్రాంతాలు కచ్చితత్త్వాన్ని తగ్గించి ఉండవచ్చు.
- జిసిఎమ్ స్వతంత్ర పరిశోధనా బృందాలచే అభివృద్ధి చేయబడి, విభిన్న ఊహలు మరియు యంత్రాంగాలను కలిగి ఉన్నందున, అవి సంభావ్య భవిష్యత్తు యొక్క గణనీయమైన శ్రేణిని కవర్ చేసే అవకాశం ఉంది. మేము తక్కువ మరియు అధిక అంచనాలు రెండింటినీ అందిస్తాము, తద్వారా వినియోగదారులు ఈ సంభావ్య శ్రేణి ఫలితాలను చూడవచ్చు మరియు మదింపు చేయవచ్చు.

"మేకింగ్ క్లైమేట్ డేటా యాక్సెసబుల్: మెథడ్స్ ఫర్ ప్రొడ్యూసింగ్ నెక్స్-జిడిడిపి అండ్ ఎల్ఓసిఎ డౌన్ స్కేల్డ్ క్లైమేట్ ఇండికేటర్స్" టెక్నికల్ నోట్. వాషింగ్టన్, డిసి: వరల్డ్ రిసోర్సెస్ ఇన్స్టిట్యూట్. https://www.wri.org/research/making-climate-data-accessible వద్ద ఆన్ లైన్ లో లభ్యం అవుతుంది. [www.resourcewatch.org] (https://www.resourcewatch.org/).

సిఎమ్ ఐపికి బాధ్యత వహించే కపుల్డ్ మోడలింగ్ పై వరల్డ్ క్లైమేట్ రీసెర్చ్ ప్రోగ్రామ్ యొక్క వర్కింగ్ గ్రూప్ కు మేం అభినందనలు తెలియజేస్తున్నాం, మరియు వారి మోడల్ అవుట్ పుట్ ని ఉత్పత్తి చేయడం మరియు లభ్యం చేయడం కొరకు క్లైమేట్ మోడలింగ్ గ్రూపులకు మేం ధన్యవాదాలు తెలియజేస్తున్నాం. యు.ఎస్. డిపార్ట్ మెంట్ ఆఫ్ ఎనర్జీ యొక్క ప్రోగ్రామ్ ఫర్ క్లైమేట్ మోడల్ డయాగ్నోస్టిక్స్ అండ్ ఇంటర్ కంపారిసన్ సిఎమ్ ఐపి కొరకు గ్లోబల్ ఆర్గనైజేషన్ ఫర్ ఎర్త్ సిస్టమ్ సైన్స్ పోర్టల్స్ భాగస్వామ్యంతో సాఫ్ట్ వేర్ ఇన్ ఫ్రాస్ట్రక్చర్ యొక్క కో ఆర్డినేటింగ్ సపోర్ట్ మరియు డెవలప్ మెంట్ ని అందిస్తుంది.

నాసా ఎర్త్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ ఉపయోగించి క్లైమేట్ ఎనలిటిక్స్ గ్రూప్ మరియు నాసా అమెస్ రీసెర్చ్ సెంటర్ ద్వారా తయారు చేయబడిన మరియు నాసా సెంటర్ ఫర్ క్లైమేట్ సిమ్యులేషన్ (ఎన్ సిసిఎస్) ద్వారా పంపిణీ చేయబడిన నెక్స్-జిడిడిపి డేటాసెట్ నుండి వాతావరణ దృశ్యాలు ఉపయోగించబడ్డాయి.

attributes.name: Maritime Boundaries
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2019 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries.

  
  
The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference).  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. VLIZ also provides boundaries of internal waters, archipelagic waters and high seas. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_011_rw1_maritime_boundaries)  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

info.cautions:
- VLIZ included the archipelagic waters and internal waters zones of each country in the EEZ. This is a deviation from the UNCLOS EEZ definition.
- There are several known issues in the Maritime Boundaries dataset, including overlapping claims between countries and changing maritime boundaries.
- The concept of maritime boundaries was introduced in 1982 by the UNCLOS. Many countries are still working to define maritime boundaries with their neighbors.

attributes.name: cli.055a Projected Change in Frost Free Season
Projected Change in Frost Free Season
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information

attributes.name: [Archived] Projected Heating Degree Days
attributes.description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2) as a replacement.**_
  
A heating degree day (HDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is below 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined HDD for those two days would be 30. HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. 

This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from heating in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts.

This Heating Degree Days data set shows projected change in HDDs in 2051-2080, relative to 1971-2000, under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. 

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). 

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on Resource Watch. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm. 

Resource Watch shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. For access to the processed data set, please contact the PREPdata team at https://www.prepdata.org/.

attributes.name: Standardised Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index
attributes.description:
The Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) Global Drought Monitor offers near real-time information about drought conditions at the global scale, with a 0.5 degrees spatial resolution and a monthly time resolution. SPEI provides a measure of change in water availability in a region by accounting for increases in available water through precipitation and decreases in available water through a process known as evapotranspiration, which includes both evaporation of water from the Earth's surface and transpiration of water which results during plants' photosynthesis. SPEI is calculated relative to historical seasonal averages. Different SPEIs can be calculated by accounting for water available change over different lengths of time. SPEI time-scales between one and 48 months are available through the CSIC website.The calibration period for the SPEI is January 1950 to December 2010. The dataset is updated during the first days of the following month based on the most reliable and updated sources of climatic data. Mean temperature data are obtained from the NOAA NCEP CPC GHCN CAMS gridded dataset. Monthly precipitation sums data are obtained from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC).   
  
### Additional Information

info.technical_title: Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index
info.functions: Near real-time information about drought conditions at the global scale
info.cautions: Currently, the SPEI Global Drought Monitor is based on the Thortnthwaite equation for estimating potential evapotranspiration (PET). This is due to the lack of real-time data sources for computing more robust PET estimations which have larger data requirements. The main advantage of the SPEI Global Drought Monitor is thus its near real-time character, a characteristic best suited for drought monitoring and early warning purposes. For long-term analysis, however, other datasets are to be preferred that rely on more robust methods of PET estimation. Use of the SPEIbase dataset, which is based on the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith model, is thus recommended for climatological studies of drought.

attributes.name: cli.070.rw0 Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.
Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset in the United States (U.S.) shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A dry spell is a five day period with less than 1 millimeter (mm) of precipitation. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Average annual dry spells are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is shown at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The average annual number of dry spells for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting precipitation data for a given year and summing the number of 5-day periods with less than 1 mm of precipitation. If a dry period lasted longer than 5 days, each additional day without precipitation was counted as a fractional (1/5) dry period. For example, a dry period of 8 days would count as 8/5 of a dry period (1 + 3/5). The average annual number of dry spells were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in dry spells. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).   
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

attributes.name: cli.058a Projected Change in Dry Spells
Projected Change in Dry Spells
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A dry spell is a five day period with less than 1 millimeter (mm) of precipitation. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Change in dry spells is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average dry spells during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is shown at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The average annual number of dry spells for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting precipitation data for a given year and summing the number of 5-day periods with less than 1 mm of precipitation. If a dry period lasted longer than 5 days, each additional day without precipitation was counted as a fractional (1/5) dry period. For example, a dry period of 8 days would count as 8/5 of a dry period (1 + 3/5). The average annual number of dry spells were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in dry spells. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Day](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), and [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

attributes.name: Volcanic Activity Report
attributes.description:
The Weekly Volcano Report, produced by the Smithsonian Institution and the USGS, displays activity from mostly terrestrial volcanoes that meet one of the following criteria:   
  
(1) a volcanic ash advisory has been released by a volcanic ash advisory center (VAAC) stating that an ash cloud has been produced from the volcano;   
  
(2) a verifiable news report of new activity or a change in activity at the volcano has been issued;   
  
(3) observers have reported a significant change in volcanic activity.   
  
This data set mostly excludes continuous eruptive activity and sea-floor volcanism. Volcanoes are included in the "New Activity/Unrest" section of the Weekly Volcanic Activity Report if the activity occurs after at least 3 months of quiescence. Once a volcano is included in the "New Activity/Unrest" section, updates will remain in that section unless the activity continues for more than 1 month without escalating, after which time updates will be listed in the "Continuing Activity" section. A volcano is also included in the "New Activity/Unrest" section if it is undergoing a period of relatively high unrest, or increasing unrest.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Disclaimer

info.functions: Weekly volcano activities report
info.cautions: The Weekly Volcanic Activity Report is intended to provide timely information about global volcanism on a weekly basis. Consequently, the report is generated rapidly by summarizing volcanic reports from various sources, with little time for fact-checking. The accuracy of the Weekly Volcanic Activity Report is dependent upon the quality of the volcanic activity reports it receives. Reports published in the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network are monthly, and more carefully reviewed, although all of the volcanoes discussed in the Weekly Volcanic Activity Reportare not necessarily reported in the Bulletin. Because of the Weekly Volcano Report's emphasis on rapid reporting on the web it has avoided diacritical marks. Reports are updated on the Weekly Volcanic Activity Report web page as they are received, therefore information may be included regarding events that occurred before the current report period.

Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.

  
  
The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).

### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).   
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

attributes.name: Projected Heating Degree Day U.S. (RCP8.5)
attributes.description:
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDD are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings.

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

attributes.name: Coral Bleaching Monitoring
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The dataset shows up-to-date status, trends, and alerts related to sea surface temperature anomalies, which have the potential to cause bleaching where coral are present. Sea surface temperature (SST) is the water temperature close to the ocean's surface. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Coral Reef Watch (CRW) program has developed a daily global 5 kilometer (km) product suite based on satellite observations to monitor SST and thermal stress on coral reefs.

  
  
Mass coral bleaching events due to anomalously warm ocean water have increased in frequency and severity and have become one of the most significant contributors to the deterioration of the world’s coral reefs. Thermal stress that persists for several weeks with ambient water temperatures as little as 1 to 2 degrees Celsius (°C) above a coral’s thermal tolerance level has been shown to cause bleaching, often on broad geographical scales. Corals can die if thermal stress is severe or long-lasting; furthermore, coral weakened by thermal stress may subsequently succumb to disease. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, reductions in fish productivity, and economic loss. Corals are capable of rebounding from bleaching, but not if the heat stress events are too severe or recur too quickly to permit recovery. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs.

  
  
Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities.

  
  
Reliable global monitoring and prediction of environmental conditions leading to bleaching is used to guide targeted observations and management responses. The NOAA CRW products fulfill requests from coral reef managers and researchers for higher resolution products by taking advantage of new satellites, sensors and algorithms.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Coral Bleaching Monitoring dataset draws its layers from Version 3.1 of NOAA Coral Reef Watch’s experimental [coral bleaching heat stress monitoring product suite](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php). This product suite spans January 1, 1985 to present and is derived from CRW's Version 3.1 daily global 5 km satellite sea surface temperature (SST) data product known as ['CoralTemp'](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php).

  
  
The Version 3.1 product suite was developed based on user requests and in order to address errors that were identified in the source SST data for CRW's Version 3.0 products for some coral reef regions during 2013-2016. It now comprises the core of CRW's Decision Support System (DSS) for coral reef management, providing service at or near reef-scales, allowing direct monitoring of 95% of global coral reefs and significantly reducing data gaps caused by cloud cover.

  
  
Note that SST variability is often considerably higher at the much finer 5 km spatial and daily temporal resolutions, when compared with CRW's heritage twice-weekly global 50 km (0.5 degree) monitoring products. Due to resulting day-to-day fluctuations between stress levels in highly variable locations, the single-day 5 km Bleaching Alert Area product does not consistently and adequately identify potentially harmful heat stress levels, especially with regard to accumulated heat stress impacts. Rather than requiring users to examine the single-day 5 km Bleaching Alert Area product over several days, a 7-day maximum Bleaching Alert Area composite product, updated daily, was introduced in the Version 2 product suite and is maintained here in Version 3.1. The evolution of CRW's daily global 5 km product suites can be found [here](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/history_5km_products.php). This 7-day composite product shows the maximum stress level that a satellite pixel has experienced during the most recent seven consecutive days. Data and images are dated on the last day of the 7-day period. Notably, it is compatible with CRW's heritage twice-weekly global 50 km Bleaching Alert Area product, as the 50 km Bleaching Alert Area is based on a half-week (3 or 4 days) composite of 50 km SSTs (but with much less SST variability due to its much coarser spatial resolution).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data about heat stress frequency, heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

  
  
CRW's first-generation (heritage) near real-time [twice-weekly global 50 km satellite coral bleaching heat stress monitoring products](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/50km/) were operational at NOAA until April 30, 2020, when they were officially retired, and succeeded by CRW's next-generation operational daily global 5 km coral bleaching heat stress monitoring products. The heritage 50 km products served the U.S. and international coral reef communities for more than 20 years (1997-2020). While the 50km products no longer update in near real-time, due to their retirement, since they served as vital tools for our users for so many years, [archived 50km data and images](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/50km/) are still available on the CRW website.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/ocn_007_coral_bleaching_monitoring).  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

attributes.name: Global Power Plant Database
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Power Plant Database is a comprehensive, open source database of power plants around the world. It centralizes power plant data to make it easier to navigate, compare, and draw insights for one’s own analysis. The database covers approximately 30,000 power plants from 164 countries and includes thermal plants (e.g., coal, gas, oil, nuclear, biomass, waste, geothermal) and renewables (e.g., hydro, wind, solar). Each power plant is geolocated, and entries contain information on plant capacity, generation, ownership, and fuel type. The database will be continuously updated as data becomes available.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Power Plant Database leverages existing data sources and methodologies to build a comprehensive and open-access power sector database. The database was built entirely from open sources, which are publicly available on the internet, including data from national government agencies, reports from companies that build power plants or provide their components, data from public utilities, and information from multinational organizations. Currently the Global Power Plant Database uses more than 600 sources to create the database.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](20cc5eca-8c63-4c41-8e8e-134dcf1e6d76) as a replacement.**_
  
The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Thermal Anomalies/Fire products are primarily derived from MODIS 4 and 11 micrometer radiances. The fire detection strategy is based on absolute detection of a fire (when the fire strength is sufficient to detect) and on detection relative to its background (to account for variability of the surface temperature and reflection by sunlight). The product includes fire occurrence (day/night), fire location, the logical criteria used for the fire selection, detection confidence, fire radiative power, and numerous other layers describing fire pixel attributes. The product distinguishes between fire, no fire, and no observation. Level 3 Daily fire products include 8 separate days of data detailing pixels according to their level of confidence as fires. This information will be used in monitoring the spatial and temporal distribution of fires in different ecosystems, detecting changes in fire distribution, and identifying new fire frontiers, wildfires, and changes in the frequency of the fires or their relative strength. MODIS data on Terra and Aqua are acquired from each platform twice daily at mid-latitudes. These 4 daily MODIS fire observations that are typically acquired serve operational fire management needs while also advancing global monitoring of the fire process and its effects on ecosystems, the atmosphere, and climate. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

attributes.name: cit.004c.rw0.nrt Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts
Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts
attributes.description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Ozone (O₃) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of O₃ for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to the maximum 8-hour concentration.
  
  
Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that is harmful to breathe and damages crops and other vegetation. Unlike stratospheric ozone in the upper atmosphere, which protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays and forms naturally, ground-level ozone forms when emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides react in the presence of heat and sunlight. Gasoline-burning vehicles are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Other sources include consumer products such as paints, insecticides, cleaners, as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/ground-level-ozone-pollution/health-effects-ozone-pollution), ozone irritates respiratory systems, can aggravate asthma, and can damage cells that line your lungs. Ozone may also aggravate chronic lung diseases such as emphysema and bronchitis and may cause permanent lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults.
The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world.

  
  
These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/).
Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md).  
 
   
  
Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). 
 
  
  
Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry.  The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions.
 
  
  
The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for fine particulate matter [(PM2.5)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/f5599d62-7f3d-41c7-b3fd-9f8e08ee7b2a) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea). 

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Forecasted data at an hourly time step is available from the source. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_004_city_aq).
